topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Finding halves and quarters (age 5+)
topic.description: Recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
evidence: Fold a shape into four equal parts and identify each as 'a quarter'
Find a quarter of 12 objects by sharing into 4 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into quarters (four equal parts)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you fold a square piece of paper into four equal parts, can {{name}} tell you that each part is a quarter — and point to just one quarter?

pedagogy.summary: A quarter is ONE OF FOUR EQUAL parts of a whole. It extends halving: fold in half and half again gives four equal parts (the IES 'powers of two' route). Quarters apply to single objects, lengths, and sets (a quarter of 12 = share into four equal groups, take one). Four quarters recompose the whole, and two quarters make a half — the seed of equivalence.
bestPractices: Reach quarters by repeated halving (halve, then halve each half) before free four-way partitioning — IES powers-of-two progression
Insist on four EQUAL parts; check by matching/overlaying
Work quarters of sets by sharing into four equal groups (not making groups of four)
Name and count: 'four quarters make one whole', 'two quarters make a half'
Use continuous and discrete models so 'a quarter' is not tied to one shape
keyRepresentations: A shape folded in half then half again into four matching parts
A strip/length marked into four equal parts
12 counters shared into four equal groups
Four quarters reassembling into the whole; two quarters overlaying a half
commonMisconceptions: Any four pieces count as quarters regardless of size (equal-parts missing)
Muddling the names — calling a quarter 'a half', or vice versa
A quarter of a set found by making groups OF four rather than four equal groups
Thinking a quarter is bigger than a half because 'four is more than two' (whole-number bias, developing here)

learn.summary: A quarter is one of FOUR EQUAL parts of a whole. Reach quarters by repeated halving (fold in half, then halve each half, giving four matching parts in total), work them on single objects, lengths, and sets (a quarter of 12 = share into four equal groups and take one), and show that four quarters recompose the whole while two quarters make a half — seeding equivalence. The core learner actions are partitioning/folding to make equal parts and sharing a set into four equal groups, with naming and counting attached to the number of equal parts.

activities.title: Halve, then halve again: making four equal quarters
feedback: If a learner accepts any four pieces as quarters, have them overlay the pieces: unequal pieces do not match, so they are not quarters.
When all four parts match after folding twice, confirm: 'Four equal parts — each one is a quarter, and all four make the whole.'
If two quarters joined line up exactly with the other two quarters (or with a half of the same shape), name it: 'Two quarters make a half.'
Use overlaying as a practical check — real paper folds have slight thickness and are only approximate, so look for parts that clearly match rather than treating the overlay as an exact proof.
activities.rationale: The IES/WWC powers-of-two route builds fourths by halving then halving again before free four-way partitioning, and insisting on equal parts (checked by matching) targets the common error of counting pieces regardless of size. A live fold/partition lets the child test equality rather than take it on trust; a static poster of quartered objects can show the result but does not let the child verify equality themselves.
sourceClaims: Quarters/fourths are reached via a halving (powers-of-two) strategy - halve then halve again - before partitioning into other numbers of parts
Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Fold (or partition) a symmetrical shape such as a square, rectangle or circle in half, then fold each half in half again so the shape opens into four matching parts.
Check the four parts are equal by matching or overlaying them; only equal parts count as quarters.
Count aloud: 'four quarters make one whole'.
Join two of the quarters to make a half, then place that pair over the other two quarters (or over an identical shape folded once into halves) to see that 'two quarters make a half'.
Compare with a shape cut into four UNEQUAL pieces and explain why those are not quarters.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter is one of four EQUAL parts; repeated halving is a reliable way to produce them, four quarters rebuild the whole, and two quarters together make a half.

activities.title: A quarter of a set: sharing 12 into four equal groups
feedback: If a learner makes groups of four (ending with three groups) or hands over four objects, redirect: the 4 in 'a quarter' means FOUR equal groups — share all 12 into four hoops and take one.
When the four groups are equal, confirm the count: 'Each group has 3, so a quarter of 12 is 3.'
If groups are unequal, prompt: 'Are all four groups the same? Move counters until they match.'
activities.rationale: Working quarters of discrete sets by equal sharing (not grouping-of-four) addresses a specific documented confusion and supports finding a quarter of a quantity as required by the Year 1 curriculum. Discovering 3 by sharing rather than guessing makes the division meaning concrete. An optional set mode that flags unequal groups until they match makes the equal-sharing requirement visible.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Take 12 counters and share them, one at a time, into four equal groups (four hoops or circles).
Keep going until all 12 are placed and every group has the same number.
Report how many are in one group — 'a quarter of 12 is 3'.
Contrast with making groups OF four and notice that gives three groups, which is a different question.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter of a set is found by sharing the whole set into four equal groups and taking one group — not by making groups of four.

activities.title: Naming by counting equal parts: halves vs quarters
feedback: If a learner calls a quarter 'a half' (or vice versa), count the equal parts together and re-attach the name to the count.
If a learner thinks a quarter is bigger than a half because 'four is more than two', overlay a quarter on a half of the SAME shape to show the quarter is smaller.
Confirm correct naming by restating the count: 'Four equal parts, so each is a quarter.'
activities.rationale: Explicit naming of quarters is needed because some children call all fractional parts 'one-half'; linking the name to the count and connecting half-to-quarters by halving addresses both the naming muddle and the whole-number-bias idea that more pieces means a bigger piece.
sourceClaims: Some children think all fractional parts are called 'one-half', so explicit naming of quarters is needed
learnerActions: Partition one shape into two equal parts and name each a 'half'; partition another into four equal parts and name each a 'quarter'.
Count the equal parts aloud and attach the name to the count: two equal parts = halves, four equal parts = quarters.
Use halve-then-halve-again on the same shape to see how a half becomes two quarters.
Decide, for a correctly-made part, whether it is a half or a quarter and justify by counting the equal parts.
activities.intendedInsight: The fraction name follows the number of equal parts: two equal parts are halves, four equal parts are quarters; of the SAME whole, a quarter is smaller than a half.

activities.title: Sorting quarters from not-quarters
feedback: If a learner marks a four-way UNEQUAL cut as 'quarters', point to the pieces: 'Count them — four pieces, but are they all the same size? If not, they are not quarters.'
Reinforce the fix: for a shape, fold in half and then in half again so all four parts match; for a set, share it into four groups with the same number in each.
For the quarter-of-12 question, confirm by sharing 12 into four equal groups to check the answer is 3.
activities.rationale: A recognition/sorting task that pairs the correct NUMBER of pieces (four) with unequal sizes discriminates children who merely count pieces from those who require equal parts. A sort of this kind can check and prompt discussion of classification, but on its own it does not require the child to independently construct four equal parts or share a set, so pair it with the folding and sharing activities.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Look at several shapes and sets, some divided into four EQUAL parts and some into four UNEQUAL parts.
Sort each into 'quarters' or 'not quarters', including a tricky case cut into four clearly unequal pieces.
For each 'not quarters' case, say what is wrong (the parts are not equal) and how to fix it (fold in half then half again, or divide into four equal parts).
Answer: 'A quarter of 12 is ___' and explain how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Having four pieces is not enough — the four parts must be equal to be quarters.

constraints: Insist on four EQUAL parts; check by matching or overlaying rather than by eye alone, treating the overlay as a practical check (real paper folds have slight thickness and are approximate), not an exact mathematical proof.
Work quarters of sets by sharing into four equal groups, not by making groups of four.
Use both continuous models (shapes, strips/lengths) and discrete models (sets of counters) so 'a quarter' is not tied to one shape or layout.

Sorting/recognition tasks can check whether a child requires equal parts and prompt discussion, but do not by themselves require the child to generate four equal parts or share a set; use them alongside hands-on folding and sharing.
A reference poster of quartered objects can show the result but does not let the child test equality; use it as support, not as the main way to learn.
Introduce the half/quarter link ('two quarters make a half', 'four quarters make a whole') as the seed of equivalence at an age-appropriate level, not as formal equivalent-fraction rules.

When comparing the SIZE of a quarter and a half as portions, compare them of the SAME whole — of that same whole a quarter is smaller than a half; as numbers, fractions remain comparable and a quarter is always less than a half.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a conversation artefact 'poor' ('built through folding and sharing, not dialogue, at this age') and a 3D artefact 'poor' ('planar partitioning; 3D adds nothing'). These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and are not asserted here as universal claims. Talk/naming remains valuable alongside hands-on work, and planar partitioning is the most natural model, not proof that other media add nothing.

Self-audit: a quarter of 12 is 3 (12 shared into four equal groups); making groups OF four instead yields three groups — these are different operations, correctly distinguished in the activities. A quarter is smaller than a half of the SAME whole; the 'four is more than two' reasoning is explicitly corrected rather than propagated.

Fraction-of-area idealisation assumes exactly equal parts; paper/card folds have slight thickness and real folds are approximate, so 'matching/overlaying' is a practical equality check (stated in the folding activity and constraint), not an exact proof.

The 'snap green when parts match' and 'refuse done until groups are equal' behaviours are retained as optional feedback mechanisms that make equality visible; they are examples, not mandatory tooling.

probeDeeper: How many quarters make one whole?
Is a quarter bigger or smaller than a half of the same shape - how do you know?
Show me a quarter of these 12 counters - how did you split them?
If I fold the paper in half and then in half again, what have I made?
assess.correctAnswer: No - the pieces are not equal, so they are not quarters. Quarters are four EQUAL parts; fold in half and then in half again (or divide into four equal parts) so all four match. Four equal quarters make the whole square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any four pieces are quarters - 'there are four pieces, so they're quarters' - equal-size ignored
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold two identical squares, one into equal quarters and one unequally, and overlay to show only equal parts match.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes - there are four pieces, so they're quarters
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says each piece of the unequal four-way cut is a quarter

errorPatterns.pattern: Muddles the fraction names - calls a quarter 'a half' or a half 'a quarter'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the equal parts aloud and attach the name to the count (two equal parts = halves; four = quarters); halve-then-halve to link them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses the wrong name for a correctly-made part

errorPatterns.pattern: A quarter of a set found by making groups OF four, not four equal groups
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise the 4 means FOUR equal groups; share all 12 into four hoops and take one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a quarter of 12, makes groups of four (getting three groups) or hands over four objects

responseLevels.gap: Counts four pieces as quarters regardless of equality, or confuses the name with 'half'.
responseLevels.full: States a quarter is one of FOUR EQUAL parts, makes them by halving twice, knows four quarters make a whole (and two make a half), and finds a quarter of a set by sharing into four equal groups.
responseLevels.partial: Knows quarters must be equal for a shape but cannot find a quarter of a set, or cannot reliably make four equal parts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a square divided into four pieces that are clearly different sizes. Ask: 'Is each of these pieces a quarter of the square? How do you know?' Then ask: 'How could you fold a square to be sure of making four quarters, and how many quarters make the whole square?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The right NUMBER of pieces (four) with unequal sizes separates children who count pieces from children who require equal parts. Tier 2 checks they can generate quarters (via halving) and know four quarters make the whole - not just recognise a picture.

sources.source: IES/WWC Fractions Practice Guide (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039), Recommendation 1

sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, Mathematics Programmes of Study, Year 1 fractions

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: What Is a Half?
topic.description: Recognise, find, and name a half as one of two equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
evidence: Fold a shape into two equal parts and identify each as 'a half'
Find half of 8 objects by sharing into 2 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into halves or not (equal vs unequal parts)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is helping share a sandwich equally between two people, can they cut it so both pieces are the same size — and tell you each piece is called a half?

pedagogy.summary: A half is ONE OF TWO EQUAL parts of a whole — the equality is the whole idea, not merely 'two pieces'. Build directly on children's informal fair-sharing intuition (share between two so it's fair). Halving applies to single objects (fold/cut a shape), to lengths, and to quantities/sets (share a set of objects into two equal groups). Two halves recompose the whole, and 'half of' a quantity is found by sharing equally into two.
bestPractices: Build on the informal halving/fair-share strategy children already bring; begin by sharing a SET of objects evenly between two before partitioning a single object (IES progression)
Make 'equal' the explicit criterion — use fair-sharing language ('would that be fair?') and check by matching/overlaying the parts
Accept approximately-drawn parts as long as the child treats them as equal (IES roadblock guidance)
Name the parts and the whole: 'a half', 'the other half', 'two halves make one whole'
Use both continuous (folded shapes, strips) and discrete (sharing counters) models so 'half' is not tied to one picture
keyRepresentations: Folded/cut shapes (circle, rectangle, strip) into two matching parts
A bar or length split at the midpoint
A set of counters shared into two equal groups
Two halves clicking back together to make the whole
commonMisconceptions: Any two pieces count as 'halves' regardless of size — the equal-parts requirement is missing
A half is only the one piece you take, not seeing that both parts are halves and together make the whole
Calling any fractional part 'a half' (a documented early error — IES)
Sharing a set by equal NUMBER of items rather than equal AMOUNT when items differ in size (number-vs-quantity confusion)

learn.summary: Teach 'a half' as ONE OF TWO EQUAL parts of a whole, where the equality — not merely having two pieces — is the defining idea. Build on children's informal fair-sharing intuition, starting by sharing a set of objects evenly between two before partitioning a single object. Cover halving of single objects (fold/cut a shape), lengths (split a strip at the midpoint), and quantities/sets (share counters into two equal groups). Reinforce that two halves recompose the whole, and that 'half of' a quantity is found by sharing equally into two. For ages 5–6.

activities.title: The halving bench: make it fair
feedback: If the cut is off-centre: 'Would that be fair? The two parts are not the same size, so neither one is a half. Slide the cut until both parts match.'
When equal: 'Now both parts are the same — these are two equal halves, and together they make the whole bar.'
For the set mode with equal counts but unequal item sizes: ask 'Same number, or same amount?' to separate quantity from count.
activities.rationale: Halving is an action on a whole; letting the child physically cut/fold or share and then check equality makes 'two equal parts' felt rather than told. Live equality feedback (recolouring, snapping, refusing 'done' until amounts match) makes the fairness criterion concrete. These interactions are illustrative examples of the mechanism, not required technology, and their effectiveness relative to other media is untested.
sourceClaims: Instruction should build on children's informal equal-sharing intuition, starting by sharing a set of objects evenly before partitioning a single object, grounded in the halving strategy; some children think all fractional parts are called 'one-half'
Children confuse the NUMBER of things shared with the QUANTITY shared, and may not create equal shares; addressable with colour cues and fair-sharing discussion (Roadblocks 1.2, 1.3)
Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a half as one of two equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Drag a cutting line across a rectangular chocolate bar (cutting straight across its length); when the cut is off-centre, note that the two parts are unequal (e.g. they glow red / are labelled 'not halves – not fair') and when at the midpoint the two parts are equal (snap green / labelled 'two equal halves').
Slide the two equal halves back together to remake the whole bar, saying 'two halves make one whole'.
Switch to a set mode: share a plate of biscuits (or counters) into two hoops, and only accept it as 'done' when the two amounts match.
Check equality by matching or overlaying the parts, and describe each as 'a half' and 'the other half'.
activities.intendedInsight: A half requires two EQUAL parts; the count of two pieces alone does not make halves. Both parts are halves, and together they rebuild the whole.

activities.title: Share the set first
feedback: 'You gave each person the same number — but are the amounts the same? Look at the sizes.'
Use colour cues to separate quantity from count, and ask 'same number, or same amount?'
Confirm: 'When both sides have the same amount, each side is half of the whole set.'
activities.rationale: The IES progression recommends starting from sharing a set evenly before partitioning a single object, building on the halving strategy children already bring. Discrete sharing also surfaces the number-versus-quantity confusion directly. The sequence is a recommended progression, not proven more effective than alternatives.
sourceClaims: Instruction should build on children's informal equal-sharing intuition, starting by sharing a set of objects evenly before partitioning a single object, grounded in the halving strategy; some children think all fractional parts are called 'one-half'
Children confuse the NUMBER of things shared with the QUANTITY shared, and may not create equal shares; addressable with colour cues and fair-sharing discussion (Roadblocks 1.2, 1.3)
learnerActions: Share a set of objects (for example, 8 counters, or 6 sweets) evenly between two people, giving one each in turn until the pile is gone.
State how many each person gets and, when all the objects are the same size, that each group is 'half of' the set.
With objects of different sizes (big and small sweets), check whether equal COUNT gives equal AMOUNT, and discuss which sharing is fair.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Half of' a quantity is found by sharing equally into two groups; fairness means equal amount, which may differ from equal number when items vary in size.

activities.title: Halved or not? Sort and choose
feedback: If an unequal-cut option is chosen as 'a half': 'Count — yes, two pieces — but are they the same size? If not, they are not halves.'
Reinforce that the correct answer is justified by equality, not by there being two pieces.
activities.rationale: Recognition and categorisation consolidate the equal-parts criterion and may reveal the 'any two pieces are halves' misconception. A sort can check discrimination but does not itself elicit the physical construction of halves or an explanation, so pair it with the hands-on sharing/cutting activities and the 'what would make it a half?' prompt so children also build and reason, not only identify.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a half as one of two equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Sort pictures of shapes and sets into 'halved' (two equal parts) versus 'not halved' (unequal parts).
Choose which picture shows a half when one option has an unequal cut as a tempting wrong choice.
For each 'not halved' example, say what is wrong and what would make it a half.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising halves means checking for two EQUAL parts, so an unequal split is not halves even though it has two pieces.

activities.title: Reference display: name the parts
feedback: Prompt: 'If I put the two halves back together, what do I get?' — answer: the whole.
Encourage naming both parts, not just the one taken.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference supports vocabulary and the 'both parts are halves / two halves make the whole' idea. As a reveal-only reference it supports naming but does not let the child test equality by doing, so use it alongside active cutting/sharing.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a half as one of two equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Tap or point to each half of a halved object to highlight it, then name it 'a half' and 'the other half'.
Read or say 'two halves make one whole' while watching the parts combine.
activities.intendedInsight: Both parts of a fairly divided whole are halves, and the two halves together make one whole.

constraints: Make 'equal' the explicit criterion throughout — use fair-sharing language ('would that be fair?') and check by matching or overlaying parts.
Accept approximately-drawn parts as long as the child treats them as equal (IES roadblock guidance); the concept is the equal-parts intention, not precise drawing.
Use both continuous (folded shapes, strips, bars split at the midpoint) and discrete (sharing counters) models so 'half' is not tied to a single picture.
Name the parts and the whole explicitly: 'a half', 'the other half', 'two halves make one whole'.

Recognition/sorting tasks check discrimination but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of halves; include hands-on or interactive cutting, folding and sharing so children also build halves themselves.
Reference displays support vocabulary but do not let the child test equality by acting; treat them as scaffolds rather than the main activity.
Include an unequal-cut option among the choices so that a child cannot answer correctly merely by noting there are two pieces.

Physical card/paper cutouts have slight thickness and approximate the ideal flat mathematical region; this is acceptable at this age, but keep the focus on the mathematical half represented, not the physical object.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The IES equal-sharing recommendation (Recommendation 1) carries a MINIMAL evidence rating per the source: it rests on developmental research and expert judgement, not rigorous causal evidence on instruction. Do not treat the sharing-first sequence as proven more effective.

The original row's claims that a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that spoken discussion is unsuitable/'adds little' reflect catalog fit rankings, not established pedagogical facts; these have been reframed. Discussion and spoken fair-sharing language can genuinely support ages 5–6, and alternative media may suit some learners. No universal necessity of the interactive bench is asserted.

Physical cut/folded shapes have thickness and are approximations of the ideal mathematical division; this is acceptable at this age but note the distinction between the represented region and the physical cutout.

Test-design wording from the original assessment framing was reframed into plain learner-facing language; the underlying intent (include an unequal option so two pieces alone cannot be the answer) is preserved.

probeDeeper: If I put the two pieces back together, what do I get?
Can one half ever be bigger than the other half of the same bar? Why not?
Here are 6 sweets - show me half of them. How did you decide?
If I share 6 big sweets and 6 tiny sweets by giving each of us 6, do we have the same AMOUNT?
assess.correctAnswer: No - the two pieces are not equal, so neither is a half. Halves must be two EQUAL parts; you would have to break the bar so both pieces are the same size. Two equal halves put back together make the whole bar.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any two pieces are halves - 'there are two bits, so they're halves' - the equal-size requirement is missing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cut two identical wholes, one fairly and one unfairly, and overlay the parts to show only equal parts match; use fair-share language ('is that fair?').
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, it's a half - there are two pieces
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the big piece (or either piece) of the unequal bar is a half

errorPatterns.pattern: A half is just the one piece you take - does not see that BOTH parts are halves or that two halves make the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically reassemble the two halves into the whole; rehearse 'two halves make one whole'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only one piece 'the half'; cannot say the other piece is also a half or what the two make together

errorPatterns.pattern: Calls any fractional part 'a half' regardless of how many parts there are
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a half (two equal parts) with more parts; name each explicitly and count the equal parts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels a quarter, or any share, as 'a half'

errorPatterns.pattern: Halving a set by equal NUMBER of items, not equal AMOUNT, when items differ in size
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use colour cues to separate quantity from count (IES); ask 'same number, or same amount?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Given big and small items, gives each side the same COUNT even though the amounts differ

responseLevels.gap: Counts any two pieces as halves regardless of size, or calls any part 'a half'.
responseLevels.full: States a half is one of TWO EQUAL parts, checks equality by matching, knows two halves make the whole, and halves a set by equal amount (not just equal count).
responseLevels.partial: Says halves must be equal for a simple shape but does not apply it to a set/quantity, or names one piece 'the half' without seeing both are halves; cannot transfer to the unequal-cut or the big/small set.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a chocolate bar snapped into two pieces - one big, one small. Ask: 'Is one of these pieces a half of the bar? How do you know?' Then ask: 'What would I have to do to make two halves - and if I put the two halves back together, what do I get?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'two pieces means halves' says yes to the unequal cut; a child who holds the equal-parts meaning says no and names equality as the reason. Because the pieces are visibly unequal, you cannot answer correctly just by counting two pieces - the equal-parts criterion is forced into the open, and tier 2 checks that the child also sees two halves recompose the whole.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Decomposing a shape into more equal shares
topic.description: Understand that decomposing a shape into more equal shares creates smaller shares
evidence: Explain that a quarter of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza
Demonstrate that fourths are smaller pieces than halves
Compare the size of halves and quarters of the same shape
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a pizza is shared between 2 people and then the same pizza is shared between 8 people, can {{name}} explain why each slice is smaller when more people share it?

pedagogy.summary: The inverse-size relationship: cutting a whole into MORE equal shares makes each share SMALLER. A quarter of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza, and an eighth smaller still. This directly confronts the whole-number bias by which children read a bigger denominator as a bigger amount ('4 > 2 so a quarter is bigger'). It rests on comparing unit fractions of the SAME whole, and is the seed of later fraction comparison (1/3 > 1/4).
bestPractices: Compare unit fractions of IDENTICAL wholes (same pizza, same bar) so the only thing changing is the number of shares
Use predict-then-check: ask which piece is bigger before cutting, then overlay to test (surfaces the whole-number-bias reason)
Increase the number of sharers and have children watch each share shrink (IES: link to names, 1/3 of it > 1/4 of it)
Name the pattern explicitly: more equal shares of the same whole = smaller pieces
Stress that the comparison only holds when the wholes are the same size
keyRepresentations: Two identical circles/bars, one halved and one quartered, pieces overlaid
A share-counter with a slider for number of shares, one piece highlighted shrinking
A fraction wall (1 whole, halves, quarters, eighths) aligned to the same length
commonMisconceptions: Larger denominator = larger fraction / whole-number bias ('a quarter is bigger than a half because 4 is more than 2'; 1/8 > 1/3) - documented in IES
Comparing fractions of DIFFERENT-sized wholes without noticing the whole matters
Confusing the number of pieces with the amount in one piece ('4 pieces is more than 2 pieces')

learn.summary: Help 6-7 year olds grasp the inverse-size relationship: cutting the SAME whole into more equal shares makes each share smaller. A quarter of a pizza is a smaller amount than a half of the same pizza, and an eighth smaller still. This directly confronts the whole-number bias by which children read a bigger denominator as a bigger amount ('4 > 2 so a quarter is bigger'). When comparing the actual amounts, the comparison relies on the wholes being identical, and it seeds later unit-fraction comparison (1/3 > 1/4).

activities.title: Predict-then-check with two identical pizzas
feedback: If the child predicts the quarter is bigger 'because 4 is more than 2', let the overlay settle it: the half visibly covers the quarter and more, so the bigger denominator did NOT make the bigger piece.
If the child says the 4-piece pizza has 'more' because it has more pieces, refocus on one single slice versus one single slice, not the count of pieces.
When they state the pattern themselves after watching the shrink, confirm it and restate: sharing one whole among more people gives each person less.
Keep attention on the amount of pizza each piece represents; the paper is just a model of the flat region being shared.
activities.rationale: Predicting before overlaying surfaces the whole-number-bias reasoning out loud, then the physical overlay of identical wholes contradicts it, so the correction is something the child sees happen rather than a rule they are told. Keeping the wholes identical means the number of shares is the only variable.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Children commonly view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. they think 1/8 > 1/3) - the whole-number bias
Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Give the child two identical paper 'pizzas' of exactly the same size (the paper stands in for the flat region being shared - what matters is the amount each piece represents, not the paper itself).
Before cutting, ask them to predict: if one pizza is cut into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4 equal pieces, whose single piece will be bigger, and why? Record the stated reason.
Cut both pizzas and lay one half on top of one quarter so the child can see the half blankets the quarter with room to spare.
Then cut (or imagine cutting) the same-size whole into 8, then more, and have the child watch a single piece keep getting smaller.
Name the pattern out loud together: 'more equal shares of the same whole means smaller pieces.'
activities.intendedInsight: A single share gets smaller as the same whole is split among more sharers, so a half of a pizza is a bigger amount than a quarter of the same pizza even though 4 is more than 2.

activities.title: Live share-slider: watch one piece shrink
feedback: If the child expects the piece to grow as shares increase, let them watch the highlighted slice shrink and ask them to revise their prediction.
Prompt them to connect the moving slider to the earlier paper activity: more equal shares of the same whole, smaller piece, every time.
activities.rationale: A live, adjustable number of shares with one highlighted piece lets the child generate the shrink and overlay to test a prediction, which a fixed diagram cannot be manipulated to do. An interactive model is offered as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible; it is not the only route and complements the physical paper work.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Children commonly view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. they think 1/8 > 1/3) - the whole-number bias
learnerActions: Show two identical circular pizzas side by side, each with a control that sets the number of equal shares.
Have the child set one pizza to 2 shares and the other to 4, highlight one piece on each, then drag the highlighted pieces together to overlay them.
Ask the child to describe what happens to the overlapped pieces: the half covers the quarter with space left over.
Have the child push the share control higher (8, 10, 12) on one pizza and describe how a single highlighted piece keeps shrinking.
activities.intendedInsight: As the number of equal shares rises, one share visibly shrinks, making the inverse relationship between number of shares and size of each share concrete.

activities.title: Order and compare unit fractions of the same whole
feedback: If a child orders by the denominator digit (treating 1/8 as biggest), return to overlay or the shrinking slice to re-anchor the size order.

If a child says a quarter is 'always' a smaller amount than a half regardless of the cakes, contrast a quarter of a large cake with a half of a small one to show the two wholes must be equal for that amount comparison to hold.
Reward reasoning that names that the wholes must be the same AND that more shares means each piece is smaller.
activities.rationale: Ordering and choosing between unit fractions of the same whole consolidates the pattern and lets you check whether the child reasons from piece size or reverts to the digit. The explicit 'different-sized wholes' question guards against over-generalising the amount comparison, and the 'biggest number on the bottom' prompt confronts the whole-number bias by name.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Show pictures of 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/8 of the SAME cake and ask the child to order them largest to smallest.
Ask the child to explain why the order goes that way in terms of sharing.
Ask the child directly: 'Why doesn't the biggest number on the bottom mean the biggest piece?'
Pose a comparison question such as: 'Who has more, someone with a half of a cake or someone with a quarter of the same cake?' and ask for the reason.
Ask the trap question: 'Could a quarter ever be a bigger amount than a half? What would have to be true about the two cakes?'
activities.intendedInsight: Unit fractions of the same whole can be ordered by size (1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/8); when comparing the actual amounts in the pieces, the comparison relies on the wholes being the same size.

activities.title: Aligned fraction wall as a reference
feedback: If the child cannot see the comparison, draw attention to one tile per row rather than the whole row.
Note that this wall shows the sizes but does not let them generate the shrink themselves; pair it with the paper or slider activity for the 'why'.
activities.rationale: A static aligned wall is a useful reference for the size order of halves, quarters and eighths, but it shows the result rather than letting the child produce the shrink or test their own prediction, so it works best as a support alongside the hands-on comparisons.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Show a fraction wall with rows for 1 whole, halves, quarters and eighths, all aligned to the same total length.
Have the child point to and compare a single tile in each row against the whole and against each other.
Ask them to find which single tile is biggest and which is smallest, and to say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A single piece gets shorter as the whole is divided into more equal parts, shown against a common length.

constraints: When comparing the actual amount in a piece, use IDENTICAL wholes (same pizza, same bar) so the only thing changing is the number of shares. This is a requirement for comparing represented portions; it is NOT a claim that fractions as numbers are incomparable (as numbers, 1/2 is always greater than 1/4).

Stress that 'a quarter is a smaller amount than a half' is guaranteed only when the two physical wholes are the same size; with different-sized wholes it can go either way, for example a quarter of a large whole can be a larger amount than a half of a small whole.

The aligned fraction wall and other fixed diagrams show the size order but do not let the child generate the shrink or test a prediction; use them as supports, not as the main mechanism for confronting the misconception.

Ordering/multiple-choice tasks can check whether the child selects the right size order, but selection alone does not show the child constructing the reasoning, so pair selection tasks with 'explain why' prompts.
Keep the focus on the amount in ONE single piece, not the number of pieces, when confronting the 'more pieces = more to eat' confusion.
Paper pizzas and cards are physical stand-ins for the ideal flat regions being shared; compare the amounts they represent rather than any property of the paper itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source rated a 3D manipulation as adding 'nothing' and plain conversation as 'poor' because the misconception 'yields to physical comparison, not to talk'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established facts; they have been softened. Physical comparison is well suited here, but talk and discussion can still support reasoning, and this rewrite does not assert any format is universally useless or uniquely necessary.

The claim that an interactive slider is uniquely able to teach the inverse relationship was softened: a fixed diagram cannot be manipulated, but can still support learning; the slider is presented as one concrete option.
The 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/8 size ordering, the overlay demonstration, and the whole-number-bias description are internally consistent and arithmetically sound.

The common-whole requirement is scoped to comparing the represented amounts; as numbers, fractions remain comparable (1/2 > 1/4 always), which is a nuance beyond the explicit scope of the cited sources for this age.

assess.poeTask: Give the child two identical paper 'pizzas'. BEFORE cutting, ask them to predict: if one is cut into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4, whose single piece will be bigger, and WHY - record the reason. Then cut both and lay one half on top of one quarter. Observe the half covers the quarter and more. The pre-cut REASON is the diagnostic part: a '4 is bigger than 2' justification reveals whole-number bias, which the overlay then contradicts.
probeDeeper: If Bea cut hers into 8 pieces instead, would her piece be bigger or smaller than a quarter?
Could a quarter ever be bigger than a half? What would have to be true about the two pizzas?
Order these for size: a half, a third, and a quarter of the same cake.
Why doesn't the biggest number on the bottom mean the biggest piece?
assess.correctAnswer: Ali has more - a half is bigger than a quarter of the same pizza. Cutting the same whole into more equal pieces makes each piece smaller, because one whole is being shared among more parts. (Tier 2: the more sharers, the less each one gets.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Larger denominator means larger fraction - 'a quarter is bigger because 4 is more than 2' (whole-number bias)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Predict-then-overlay two identical wholes (see poeTask); name the pattern 'more shares = smaller piece'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Bea - a quarter is bigger because 4 is more than 2
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Bea and justifies with the size of the denominator digit

errorPatterns.pattern: More pieces means more to eat - confuses the NUMBER of pieces with the AMOUNT in one piece
errorPatterns.nextMove: Focus on the size of a single piece; overlay one slice on one slice.
errorPatterns.distractor: Bea - she cut hers into more pieces, so she has more
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Bea 'because she has 4 pieces and Ali only has 2', even though each eats one piece

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores that the wholes must be the same size to compare
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast 1/4 of a large pizza with 1/2 of a small one; the whole must be equal for the rule to hold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Later claims 'a quarter is always smaller than a half' regardless, or cannot see why 'same size pizza' was stated

responseLevels.gap: Picks the larger-denominator fraction as bigger and reasons from the digits ('4>2').
responseLevels.full: States that more equal shares of the same whole means smaller shares, orders 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 and explains why, recognises the wholes must be identical, and transfers to 1/8.
responseLevels.partial: Orders unit fractions of the same whole correctly when shown a picture, but reverts to 'bigger number = bigger' without the model, or overlooks that the wholes must be the same size.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two children each have a whole pizza, exactly the same size. Ali cuts hers into 2 equal pieces and takes one piece. Bea cuts hers into 4 equal pieces and takes one piece. Ask: 'Who has more pizza to eat - and how do you know?' Then ask: 'Why does cutting the same pizza into MORE pieces make each piece smaller?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-bias child reasons '4 is more than 2, so Bea's quarter is bigger' and gives the wrong answer with a confident, articulable wrong reason - exactly the tell we want. A child who understands sharing picks Ali and explains that more pieces from the same whole means smaller pieces. Identical pizzas remove the 'it depends on the pizza' escape, so the denominator size is the only thing in play.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Halves & Quarters of Shapes
topic.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares and describe them using the words halves, fourths, and quarters
evidence: Divide a circle into two equal halves
Divide a rectangle into four equal quarters
Describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a round pizza or a rectangular chocolate bar, can they divide it into four equal pieces and tell you each piece is called a quarter or a fourth?

pedagogy.summary: Partitioning continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, naming them halves and quarters, and describing the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The emphasis is on equal parts and on the part-whole relationship: the equal parts together reconstitute the whole. Children meet that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way, provided the parts are equal.
bestPractices: Partition by folding and cutting so equality is physical; verify by overlaying parts
Show more than one correct way to halve/quarter the same shape (e.g. a rectangle split vertically or horizontally) so 'halves' is not tied to one cut
Always recompose: 'two halves make the whole', 'four quarters make the whole'
Count the resulting PARTS (regions), not the cuts
Name as you go and have children label their partitions
keyRepresentations: Circles partitioned into 2 and 4 equal sectors
Rectangles partitioned into 2 and 4 equal parts (different orientations)
Overlay/rotation to check parts are equal
Parts reassembling into the whole shape
commonMisconceptions: Accepting unequal parts as halves/quarters because the number of pieces is right
Thinking a shape can only be partitioned one 'correct' way (rejecting valid alternative cuts)
Confusing the number of CUTS with the number of PARTS
Not seeing the whole as composed of its equal parts (cannot say two halves/four quarters make the whole)

learn.summary: Children partition continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, name them halves and quarters, and describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The core ideas are equality of parts (equal in size, not necessarily the same shape), the part-whole relationship (equal parts recompose the whole), and that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way as long as the parts are equal.

activities.title: Cut it, check it, rebuild it
feedback: If parts don't match when overlaid, even after rotating or flipping them, they are not the same shape and size. For the strip, grid and straight-cut halves in this activity, that means they are not equal, so they are not halves/quarters even if the number of pieces looks right. (Pieces with equal area but different shapes, like the diagonal triangles below, need a different check.)
When a horizontal, vertical, or single-diagonal cut each produce two equal parts, each is a valid way to make halves: there is no single 'right' cut, only the equal-parts rule.

A rectangle can be quartered in more than one way too (four equal strips, or a 2x2 grid). Drawing BOTH diagonals also gives four triangles that each have one quarter of the AREA, but in a non-square rectangle they are different shapes and will not match when overlaid, so use strips or a 2x2 grid when you want quarters you can check by overlaying. Remember that equal parts must be the same SIZE, not necessarily the same shape.
After rebuilding, prompt: 'Two halves make what? Four quarters make what?' to rehearse the whole as composed of its equal parts.
Count the regions you ended up with, not the lines you drew: one cut through a shape makes two parts.
Real paper has slight thickness and cuts are never perfectly clean, so overlaying is a practical equality check; the cutouts stand for idealised flat shapes with zero thickness.
activities.rationale: Partitioning is a physical cutting/folding action; folding and overlaying makes equality concrete, showing several valid cuts confronts the 'only one correct way' misconception, and recomposing rehearses the part-whole relationship. Early fraction work centres on partitioning single objects into equal parts, naming them, and reconstituting the whole.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
Year 2 pupils recognise, name, and write fractions and can partition shapes; equal shares of identical wholes are emphasised
learnerActions: Take a paper circle and a paper rectangle and fold or draw a line to make two parts.
Overlay or rotate the two parts on top of each other to check they match exactly (equal).

On fresh copies of the same rectangle, make two halves a DIFFERENT way (e.g. vertically, then horizontally, then a single diagonal through opposite corners) and check equality again. For the diagonal, cut along it and turn one triangle half a turn to lay it on the other, because folding a non-square rectangle along its diagonal will not make the halves line up.
Now partition a circle and a rectangle into four equal parts (e.g. the rectangle as four equal strips or a 2x2 grid) and check all four match.
Slide or stick the parts back together to rebuild the whole, saying aloud 'two halves make the whole' and 'four quarters make the whole'.
Label each partition with 'halves' or 'quarters' and count the PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
activities.intendedInsight: Halves are two equal parts and quarters are four equal parts; the equal parts together rebuild the whole, and the same shape can be halved or quartered in more than one correct way provided the parts are equal in size.

activities.title: Halves, quarters, or neither?
feedback: A shape with two parts is only 'halves' if the two parts are equal: two unequal parts belong in 'neither'.
A rectangle cut by a single diagonal, or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre, is still valid halves because the parts are equal.
Watch for judging by appearance of a usual cut: check equality directly by comparing part sizes.
A sorting task can check and teach how you classify partitions, but it does not itself give the experience of producing a partition; pair it with the cutting/folding activity.
activities.rationale: Categorising and matching partitions to names lets children apply the equal-parts rule and surfaces both the 'count the pieces' and 'only one correct cut' misconceptions through deliberate distractors. This is recognition practice that complements, rather than replaces, hands-on partitioning.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
learnerActions: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into three groups: 'halves', 'quarters', and 'neither'.
Include a shape split into two UNEQUAL parts (right number of pieces, wrong equality) to place in 'neither'.
Include a non-standard but valid cut (e.g. a diagonally-halved rectangle or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre) to place in 'halves'.
For each decision, explain how you know, e.g. 'the parts are equal' or 'the parts are not the same size'.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding whether a partition shows halves or quarters depends on whether the parts are equal in size, not on the number of pieces or on a familiar orientation.

activities.title: Diagnostic: unequal pieces with the right count
feedback: Neither shape is correctly cut: in each, the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (for example, a straight line through the centre of a circle or rectangle); quarters are four equal parts.
Put back together, the four parts still make the whole rectangle, but because they are not equal they are not quarters; four equal quarters would also rebuild the whole rectangle.
A circle can be halved by any line through its centre, so there is more than one correct way.
If a child says 'yes, there are two parts so they are halves', overlay or rotate the parts to test equality and contrast an equal with an unequal partition of identical shapes.
activities.rationale: Both shapes have the right number of pieces but unequal sizes, so a piece-counting child says yes while a child requiring equal parts says no; the follow-up probes whether they see the parts recompose the whole and accept more than one valid partition.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
learnerActions: Look at a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large.
Answer: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?'
Then answer: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make? Is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
activities.intendedInsight: Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough; halves and quarters must be EQUAL parts, which together recompose the whole, and there can be more than one valid partition.

constraints: Emphasise EQUAL parts throughout; a partition with the correct number of pieces but unequal sizes is not halves/quarters. Equal means equal in size, not necessarily the same shape.

Show more than one correct way to halve the same shape (e.g. a rectangle split vertically, horizontally, or by a single diagonal through opposite corners) and more than one way to quarter it (e.g. four equal strips or a 2x2 grid). Both diagonals of a rectangle also make four triangles of equal AREA (each one quarter), but for a non-square rectangle these triangles are not congruent, so they cannot be confirmed by overlaying - prefer strips or a 2x2 grid when children verify quarters by overlay.
Always recompose the whole: 'two halves make the whole', 'four quarters make the whole'.
Count the resulting PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
A sorting/matching task checks and can teach recognition and classification; it does not by itself give children the experience of producing partitions, so pair it with hands-on cutting/folding.
A poster or display of partitioned shapes is a useful reference but does not let a child partition and test equality themselves; treat it as a scaffold, not the main activity.
Paper cutouts have slight thickness and imperfect cuts; use overlaying as a practical equality check and treat the paper as an approximation of the idealised flat (zero-thickness) shape.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source noted '3D adds nothing' for these planar shapes; dropped as a universal claim. These shapes are plane figures so a solid model is not needed here, but that is a scope point, not evidence that 3D can never help.

An interactive version could shade equal parts green and unequal parts red, accept several valid halving cuts, and provide a 'rebuild' button that slides parts back and labels 'two halves'/'four quarters'. These are optional feedback mechanisms that make the equality check and recomposition concrete; they are not required.

The source labelled a conversation format 'poor' because this is a hands-on skill; spoken discussion while cutting (naming parts, explaining equality) remains valuable and is retained within the activities, so the format is not treated as useless.
Description mixes 'quarters' and 'fourths'; both name four equal parts and are used interchangeably here.

Corrected an earlier geometry error: both diagonals of a rectangle produce four triangles of EQUAL AREA (each a quarter), not unequal parts; for a non-square rectangle they are not congruent and so cannot be verified by overlay. A single diagonal is presented as a halving method because its two triangles are congruent and overlay-checkable. This reinforces that equal fractional parts must be equal in size, not identical in shape.

probeDeeper: Put the four pieces back together - what do you get?
Is there more than one way to cut this square into two halves? Show me another.
How is this different from just cutting it into any two pieces?
If I cut the rectangle into four equal parts, what is each part called, and what do all four make?
assess.correctAnswer: No to both - the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (a line through the middle); quarters are four equal parts. Put back together, the four equal quarters make the whole rectangle, and a circle can be halved by any line through its centre (more than one way).

errorPatterns.pattern: The right number of pieces means the fraction - accepts unequal parts as halves/quarters
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay/rotate the parts to test equality; contrast an equal and an unequal partition of identical shapes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes - there are two parts, so they are halves
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the unequal circle shows halves, or the unequal rectangle shows quarters

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot describe the whole as composed of its equal parts (two halves / four quarters make the whole)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically reassemble the parts into the whole; rehearse 'four quarters make one whole'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot answer what the parts make when reassembled

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a shape can be partitioned only one 'correct' way (rejects a valid alternative cut)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show several equal partitions of the same shape side by side; the rule is equal parts, not a fixed cut.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a horizontally- or diagonally-halved rectangle is 'wrong' because it isn't the usual vertical cut

responseLevels.gap: Accepts unequal parts as halves/quarters; counts pieces only.
responseLevels.full: Partitions circles and rectangles into equal halves and quarters, recognises different equal partitions are all valid, and describes the whole as composed of its equal parts.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies equal halves/quarters in the standard orientation but rejects valid alternative cuts, or cannot describe the whole as two halves / four quarters.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large. Ask: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?' Then ask: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make - and is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both shapes have the RIGHT NUMBER of pieces but UNEQUAL sizes, so a child who counts pieces says yes while a child who requires equal parts says no. Tier 2 exposes whether they see the parts recompose the whole and accept more than one valid partition.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Fractions as parts of shapes
topic.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas and express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole
evidence: Partition a rectangle into 6 equal-area parts and label each 1/6
Show two different ways to partition a square into 4 equal parts
Given a pre-partitioned shape, write the unit fraction for one part
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to fold a square piece of paper into 8 equal parts, can they tell you what fraction of the whole square each part represents?

pedagogy.summary: Partitioning a shape into equal parts means parts of equal AREA — the same amount of the whole — not parts of the same SHAPE. A square can be split into 4 equal parts as four strips, four small squares, or four triangles, and each is 1/4 because the areas are equal. The denominator counts how many equal-area pieces the whole is cut into, and each piece is 1/b of the whole. Equal shares of the same whole need not look alike.
bestPractices: Define equal parts as equal AREA, and show several correct partitions of one shape that look different but cover the same amount
Contrast valid equal-area partitions with tempting invalid ones (four pieces of different sizes) so 'four pieces' does not automatically mean 'quarters'
Use overlay/rearrangement or a squared grid to check that differently-shaped parts really have equal area
When reading a pre-partitioned shape, count the equal REGIONS (not the cut lines) and check they are equal before writing 1/b
Connect to the unit-fraction meaning: each equal-area part is 1/b of the whole
keyRepresentations: A square partitioned several ways into 4 (strips, quadrants, both diagonals)
Squared/grid paper to measure and compare areas
Overlay or cut-and-rearrange to prove two differently-shaped parts are equal
Area-model rectangle labelled in unit fractions
commonMisconceptions: Believes equal parts must be the same SHAPE (rejects a valid differently-shaped 1/4)
Counts pieces without checking equal area — calls any shape cut into 4 pieces 'quarters', even unequal ones
Writes the unit fraction from the number of cut lines rather than the number of regions
Thinks only the 'standard' partition (e.g. four small squares) is correct

learn.summary: Equal parts of a shape means parts of equal AREA — the same amount of the whole — not parts of the same SHAPE. A square can be split into four equal parts as strips, as quadrants, or as four triangles (both diagonals), and each is 1/4 because the areas are equal. The denominator counts how many equal-area regions the whole is cut into, and each region is 1/b of the whole. Learners should partition shapes several ways, check equal area by cutting and rearranging or by counting grid squares, contrast valid partitions with unequal 'four-piece' traps, and read a pre-partitioned shape by counting equal regions rather than cut lines.

activities.title: Quarter a square two different ways
feedback: If the learner makes only look-alike splits, prompt: 'Can you quarter it a way that does NOT make four identical pieces?' Offer the both-diagonals triangle split.
When four triangles and four strips both read 1/4, highlight: 'These look nothing alike, yet each is one quarter — because each covers the same AREA.'

If a learner rejects the triangle-quarter, verify equal area: cut the triangle into pieces and reassemble them to fill a strip, or count grid squares, putting the half squares cut by the diagonal together, to show the triangle and the strip cover the same number of squares (for example, 4 each on a 4-by-4 grid). A bare overlay of the two different shapes does not by itself prove equal area.
activities.rationale: Producing and comparing genuinely different equal-area partitions targets the belief that equal parts must be congruent, and grounds the unit fraction in area. An interactive version where the learner draws cut lines and each region's area is reported as a fraction of the whole would make 'equal area, any shape' directly checkable; a challenge mode asking for TWO valid ways reinforces that the standard partition is not the only correct one.
sourceClaims: CCSS 2.G.A.3 requires students to 'recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.'

CCSS 3.G.A.2 requires partitioning shapes into parts with EQUAL AREAS and expressing the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole (e.g. partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area and describe each part as 1/4 of the shape's area) — grounding 'equal parts = equal area'.

NCETM lists as a common error 'children thinking that equal means they must look identical'. It teaches that a square's four parts can each have the same area (1/4 of the whole) yet be non-congruent (not look identical), and recommends starting with congruent partitions then deliberately varying examples (including non-straight cut lines, different ways to quarter a square) to expose the misconception.
A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Take a square and cut (or draw cut lines) to make 4 equal parts.
Now make 4 equal parts a DIFFERENT way — e.g. four vertical strips, then four quadrants, then four triangles using both diagonals.

For each attempt, check that every part covers the same amount: cut and rearrange the parts to see if they match, or draw the square on grid paper and count the squares (putting half squares together) in each part.
Label each part 1/4 and state in words why it is one quarter.
Compare a set of four triangles with a set of four strips: confirm both read 1/4 even though they look nothing alike.
activities.intendedInsight: Parts that look completely different can each be 1/4 as long as their AREAS are equal and together they cover the whole.

activities.title: Spot the trap: four pieces vs four equal parts
feedback: If the learner calls a shape with four unequal pieces 'quarters', compare the areas on a grid: 'These pieces are different sizes, so they can't each be one quarter.'
Reinforce: 'A quarter means one of four EQUAL parts — same amount each — not just one of four pieces.'
activities.rationale: Contrasting valid equal-area partitions with tempting unequal ones breaks the 'four pieces = quarters' shortcut and forces an area check before naming the fraction. A sorting task with distractors built from congruence-required and count-the-pieces errors makes the judgement explicit and checkable, though it rehearses the decision rather than eliciting the learner's own partitioning.
sourceClaims: CCSS 3.G.A.2 requires partitioning shapes into parts with EQUAL AREAS and expressing the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole (e.g. partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area and describe each part as 1/4 of the shape's area) — grounding 'equal parts = equal area'.
A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Look at a square cut into four pieces of clearly different sizes. Decide: is each piece a quarter? Explain.
Check by comparing the areas — on squared/grid paper, or by cutting and rearranging the pieces to see if they match.
State whether 'four pieces' is the same as 'four equal parts', and why.
Sort several partitioned shapes into 'shows quarters' and 'does not': include an equal-area-but-different-shape example (YES) and a four-unequal-pieces example (NO).
activities.intendedInsight: Counting four pieces is not enough — a quarter must be one of four EQUAL-area parts. Unequal pieces are not quarters even though there are four of them.

activities.title: Read a pre-partitioned shape: count regions, not lines
feedback: If the learner writes 1/3 for a shape with three parallel cut lines and four regions, say: 'Count the PARTS, not the lines — three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4.'
If the learner names a fraction without checking the regions are equal, prompt: 'Are all these regions the same amount? Check before you write the fraction.'
activities.rationale: Reading pre-partitioned shapes is a distinct skill from making partitions, and the off-by-one cut-line error and the skip-the-equality-check error are common. Requiring both an equality check and region-counting addresses both errors.
sourceClaims: A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Given a shape already cut into equal parts, first check the regions really are equal in area.
Count the number of equal REGIONS (the parts), not the number of cut lines.
Write the unit fraction for one part, e.g. 1/5 for one of five equal regions.
Check your reasoning on a case with three parallel cut lines: three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4 — not 1/3.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the number of equal regions the whole is cut into, so you count the parts, not the cuts; and the regions must be equal in area before you name the fraction.

activities.title: Prove two different shapes are equal area
feedback: To show a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter are the same amount, cut one into pieces and reassemble them to fill the other, or check they cover the same number of grid squares, putting the half squares cut by the diagonal together; then name it: 'Same amount, different shape — both are one quarter.' A bare overlay of two different shapes does not by itself prove equal area.
If the learner cannot justify beyond appearance, steer toward an area check: 'Cut it up and fit the pieces into the other shape, or count grid squares, to see if the amounts match.'
If using paper or card cutouts, note they are approximations of the ideal flat figure: their slight thickness is not part of the area being compared — only the flat region matters.
activities.rationale: Giving learners a concrete method to verify equal area turns the abstract claim 'equal parts = equal area' into something they can test, and supports the deeper justification tier where understanding shows rather than rote production of two partitions.
sourceClaims: NCETM lists as a common error 'children thinking that equal means they must look identical'. It teaches that a square's four parts can each have the same area (1/4 of the whole) yet be non-congruent (not look identical), and recommends starting with congruent partitions then deliberately varying examples (including non-straight cut lines, different ways to quarter a square) to expose the misconception.
CCSS 2.G.A.3 requires students to 'recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.'
learnerActions: Pick a differently-shaped candidate quarter (a triangle, an L-shape, a strip) and a square.
Use cut-and-rearrange to test whether the candidate covers the same area as a known quarter, or place both on squared/grid paper and count squares, putting any half squares together.
Decide whether the candidate really is 1/4 and justify by area.
Try the diagnostic: show two DIFFERENT ways to split a square into 4 equal parts, label each part, and explain how you know each is 1/4 even when the parts are different shapes.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal area can be verified by cutting pieces and reassembling them to fill the other shape, or by measuring on a grid — so you can confirm a differently-shaped part is genuinely 1/4.

constraints: Define equal parts as equal AREA throughout; the shape of a part may differ as long as it covers the same amount of the whole.

Start with congruent (look-alike) partitions, then deliberately vary examples — including non-straight cut lines and multiple ways to quarter a square — to expose the 'must look identical' misconception.
Require an equal-area check (cut and reassemble to fill, or count grid squares) before naming any fraction; do not let 'four pieces' or a count of cut lines determine the denominator.
A bare overlay of two differently-shaped parts does not prove equal area; use cutting-and-reassembling or grid-square counting to demonstrate it.

A static gallery of partitioned shapes with tap-to-reveal areas can illustrate the idea and serve as a reference, but it does not let the learner partition a shape or test their own cuts; use it as a scaffold, not as the main activity.

A sort or multiple-choice judgement (shows quarters vs not, 'is the triangle a quarter?') can rehearse and check the decision but does not itself elicit the learner constructing their own partitions; pair it with hands-on partitioning.
This is a 2D area idea; introducing a third dimension is unlikely to help and may distract from equal-area partitioning of a flat shape.

When using paper/card cutouts to cut, reassemble and compare, treat them as approximations of the ideal flat regions — their thickness is not part of the area being compared; state this to the learner in the activity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated conversation and 3D as 'poor' and asserted a third dimension 'confuses rather than clarifies' and that insight comes 'not from in-role dialogue'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints.

The off-by-one cut-line example is sound for parallel straight cuts: three parallel cuts producing four equal regions gives 1/4, not 1/3. No arithmetic or geometric errors were found in the source examples; the equal-area-by-decomposition reasoning is valid for the flat-figure idealisation.

Verification of equal area between a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter requires cutting one into pieces and reassembling (or grid-square counting); a single uncut piece will not coincide with a differently-shaped piece. Feedback wording was corrected accordingly.

The legacy 'area meter refuses to call them quarters' framing is an optional interactive feedback example (live area reporting, flagging unequal pieces); it is preserved as an optional mechanism, not a required one, and its learner-testing status is unknown.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a square split into 4 parts of clearly different SHAPES but equal AREA (e.g. one large right-triangle and several strips that together equal it). Before any measuring, ask: 'Are these four parts equal? Is each one a quarter?' Have them predict and say why. A child judging by appearance predicts 'no, they're different sizes'. Then check by overlaying/rearranging on a grid — the areas match — refuting the shape-based prediction and revealing that equal parts are about area, not looks.
probeDeeper: I've split this square into a big triangle and some strips — is the triangle a quarter? How could we check the areas are equal?
Here is a shape already cut into 5 equal parts — what fraction is one part, and how do you know it is 1/5?
If I cut a square into 4 pieces but they are different sizes, is each one 1/4? Why not?
Can two quarters of the same square look completely different and still both be 1/4?
assess.correctAnswer: Two distinct equal-area partitions (e.g. four vertical strips, and four triangles by both diagonals), each part labelled 1/4. Each part is 1/4 because the four parts have EQUAL AREA and together make the whole — the shape of a part can differ as long as it covers the same amount.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes equal parts must be the same shape — 'those aren't quarters because they don't look the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay or rearrange a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter to show they cover the same area; equal parts means equal amount, not identical shape.
errorPatterns.distractor: The parts must all be the same shape, or they aren't quarters
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can produce only congruent-looking splits; rejects a valid differently-shaped 1/4 (e.g. a triangle) as 'not a quarter'

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts pieces without checking equal area — 'four pieces, so each is a quarter', even when the pieces are different sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the areas on a grid; unequal pieces are not quarters. A quarter must be one of four EQUAL-area parts.
errorPatterns.distractor: Any shape split into 4 pieces shows quarters, even if the pieces are different sizes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels an unequally-cut shape as quarters; counts regions but never compares their areas

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes the unit fraction from the number of cut LINES rather than the number of regions (off by one)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the equal REGIONS, not the lines: three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a pre-partitioned shape, counts the cuts (e.g. 3 lines) and writes 1/3 for what are actually 4 regions

responseLevels.gap: Insists equal parts must be identical in shape, or labels unequal pieces as fractions by counting them; cannot produce a second valid partition.
responseLevels.full: Produces two genuinely different equal-area partitions, labels each 1/4, justifies by equal area covering the whole regardless of shape, reads a pre-partitioned shape by counting equal regions, and rejects unequal partitions.
responseLevels.partial: Produces equal-area partitions and labels 1/b, but only congruent-looking ones, or cannot articulate that equal AREA (not shape) is what matters, or is unsure about a differently-shaped quarter.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a square. Show me two DIFFERENT ways to split it into 4 equal parts, and label each part. Then tell me: how do you know each part really is 1/4, even when the parts are different shapes?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Tier 1 (produce two partitions) can be done by rote. Tier 2 — justifying that differently-shaped parts are still 1/4 because their AREAS are equal — is where understanding shows. A child judging by appearance offers only look-alike splits, rejects a valid triangle-quarter, or accepts four unequal pieces as quarters by counting them. A secure child produces genuinely different partitions and appeals to equal area.
