topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Fractions of a whole (age 8+)
topic.description: Express whole numbers as fractions (e.g. 3 = 3/1) and recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers (e.g. 4/4 = 1, 6/1 = 6)
evidence: Write 5 as 5/1 and explain why
Locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point on a number line
Identify which fractions from a list equal a whole number: 6/3, 8/4, 5/2
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to write the number 3 as a fraction, can they write 3/1 — and also tell you what fraction equals exactly 1 whole, like 4/4 or 5/5?

pedagogy.summary: Whole numbers are fractions too. Any whole number n equals n/1 (n wholes, each in one piece), and a fraction whose numerator is a multiple of its denominator equals a whole number (4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2). This grows from a/b as iteration of 1/b: b copies of 1/b make one whole (b/b = 1). The number line unifies it — 4/4 and 1 are the same point — and the idea connects to division (a/b = a ÷ b).
bestPractices: Build b/b = 1 by iterating the unit fraction b times (four quarters fill exactly one whole).
Introduce n/1 as 'n wholes, each left in one piece' — a denominator of 1 means 'not cut'.
Use the number line to land 4/4 on 1 and 8/4 on 2.
Sort fractions into 'equals a whole number' vs 'not' (6/3, 8/4 vs 5/2).
Connect informally to division: 6/3 = 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
keyRepresentations: Number line (4/4 on 1, 8/4 on 2)
Iterating unit fractions to complete a whole (b/b = 1)
Area model with the whole fully shaded
Fraction-as-division link (a ÷ b)
commonMisconceptions: 'A fraction can't be a whole number / can't equal 1' — fractions are always 'parts', always less than one
Thinking 4/4 is a little less than 1, or reading it as 'four'
n/1 puzzling — treating a denominator of 1 as meaningless or as zero
Reading 8/4 as separate digits rather than as 2

learn.summary: Helps 8–9 year-olds see that whole numbers are fractions too: any whole number n equals n/1, and a fraction whose numerator is a multiple of its denominator equals a whole number (4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2, 6/1 = 6). The core insight grows from iterating a unit fraction — b copies of 1/b make one whole, so b/b = 1 — and is unified on the number line, where 4/4 and 1 sit at the same point. The idea connects informally to division (a/b = a ÷ b). It is designed to address the misconception that fractions are always 'parts' less than one.

activities.title: Iterate quarters until a fraction lands on a whole number
feedback: If the marker is placed short of 1 for 4/4: lay the four quarter pieces end to end — they fill exactly one whole with nothing missing and nothing left over, so 4/4 sits exactly on 1, not before it.
If 8/4 is read as 'eight' or as separate digits: count the quarters as you stack — it takes four to reach 1 and four more to reach 2, so 8/4 lands on 2.
Prompt: 'How many quarters do you need to make exactly one whole? What fraction is that?' to reinforce b/b = 1.
activities.rationale: b copies of the unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built by iterating 1/b; placing whole numbers and fractions on the same number line lets 4/4 and 1 be seen as the same point, countering the idea that fractions are always less than one. Live iteration makes the moment of completion visible; a static families chart or an area model can also show b/b = 1 for recall but do not show the completion unfolding.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Starting from 0 on a number line, add one quarter piece at a time and read the running total: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 …
As the fourth quarter is added, check where the marker lands and name the fraction there (4/4) and the whole number at that point (1).
Keep stacking quarters past one whole and find where 8/4 lands (on 2), noticing it took eight quarters — two full wholes' worth.
Say in your own words how many quarters make exactly one whole, and complete b/b = 1 for quarters (4/4 = 1).
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction can land exactly on a whole number: four quarters compose one whole, so 4/4 IS 1, and 8/4 IS 2. This happens whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator.

activities.title: A denominator of 1 means 'not cut': writing whole numbers as fractions
feedback: If a denominator of 1 seems meaningless or like zero: a cut into 1 piece leaves the whole intact, so 5/1 is five whole, uncut bars — not nothing.
If the child cannot write 5 as a fraction: ask how many pieces each whole is cut into when it is left whole (one), then the numerator counts the wholes: 5/1.
Check placement: 5/1 should sit on the 5 mark, confirming 5/1 = 5.
activities.rationale: Expressing whole numbers as fractions (3 = 3/1) and recognising fractions equivalent to whole numbers are stated Year 3 expectations in the cited curriculum; framing a denominator of 1 as 'in one piece' addresses the specific n/1 confusion where a denominator of 1 seems meaningless.
sourceClaims: In Year 3 (age 8–9) pupils recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers and begin to express whole numbers as fractions.
learnerActions: Work with whole, uncut bars and read a denominator of 1 as 'the whole is left in one piece'.
Write the number 5 as a fraction (5/1) and explain that it means five wholes, each uncut.
Place 5/1 on a number line at 5, and 3/1 at 3, checking they land on the whole-number marks.
Explain what the bottom number 1 is telling you when you write 3 = 3/1.
activities.intendedInsight: A denominator of 1 is meaningful: it says the whole has not been cut, so n/1 is simply n wholes. Every whole number can be written as a fraction.

activities.title: Sort fractions: whole number or not?
feedback: If 5/2 is called a whole number 'because 5 and 2 are both whole numbers': 5 ÷ 2 is not exact — 5 is not a multiple of 2 — so 5/2 lands at 2½, between the whole numbers, not on one.
If 6/3 is mishandled: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 exactly, and three thirds make one whole so six thirds make two wholes; 6/3 lands on 2.
Prompt: 'Is 5/2 a whole number? Where does it land, and what does that tell you?'
activities.rationale: Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception; relating a/b to a ÷ b and testing the multiple relationship generalises beyond the single case b/b = 1 to a·b/b. Sorting and matching tasks are suited to checking and consolidating classification once the completion idea has been built; a sort by itself does not elicit the child building a whole or explaining why.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Decide for each of 6/3, 8/4 and 5/2 whether it equals a whole number, and sort them into 'equals a whole number' vs 'not'.
For each, test whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, using division: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 5 ÷ 2 is not a whole number.
Place 5/2 on a number line to show it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3.
Match 8/4 to the whole number 2 and explain how you knew.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction equals a whole number exactly when the numerator is a multiple of the denominator; a/b can be read as a ÷ b. Having both digits be whole numbers (as in 5/2) does not make the fraction a whole number.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: where does 4/4 land?
feedback: If the prediction was 'before 1' because 'a fraction is always less than one': the four quarters fill exactly one whole with nothing left over, landing on 1 — so a fraction CAN equal a whole number.
Confirm the generalisation: this works whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator (4/4, 8/4, 6/3), not just for this one case.
If the reason given before observing was correct, ask the child to predict where 8/4 lands to extend the rule.
activities.rationale: The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part: a child who thinks fractions are always parts less than one predicts before 1, and iterating the quarters directly contradicts that belief by landing exactly on 1. Predict-then-check with a reason is proposed to surface the misconception rather than only assess the answer.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Before doing anything, PREDICT with a reason whether 4/4 lands before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 on a number line, and state your reason out loud or in writing first.
Then iterate four 1/4-jumps from 0 (or build four quarters) and observe where you land.
Compare what happened to your prediction, and revise your reason if needed.
State the general rule you now believe about whether a fraction can equal a whole number.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before observing surfaces the belief 'fractions are always parts less than one'; building four quarters that fill exactly one whole and land on 1 contradicts it.

constraints: Multiple-choice, matching and slider tasks (e.g. 'which equal whole numbers: 6/3, 8/4, 5/2?', matching 8/4 → 2, placing 4/4 on a line, filling in 5 = ?/1) are suited to classifying and recall once the idea is built, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit the child constructing the whole by iteration or explaining why; pair them with building or explanation.

A static reference (tap 4/4 → 'four quarters = one whole = 1', flip-to-reveal 8/4 = 2) can support recall of b/b = 1 families but does not show the completion of a whole unfolding; use it as a reference alongside the iteration activity, not as a replacement.

An area model with the whole fully shaded (e.g. four shaded quarters filling one square) is another valid representation of b/b = 1 alongside the number line and the stacked/length model; use whichever makes 'four quarters compose one whole' concrete for the child.

Paper or card quarter pieces have slight real thickness and are a physical model of the ideal mathematical idea; treat the stacked pieces as a way of composing one whole, and keep the exact number-line point as the mathematical meaning.
Ensure the child generalises beyond the single memorised case b/b = 1 to a·b/b (e.g. 8/4, 6/3); accepting 4/4 = 1 alone is partial understanding.
Use the fraction-as-division link (a/b = a ÷ b) informally at this age, as a test for whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, not as a formal algorithm.
Treat fractions as numbers that share one number line with the whole numbers; the task is to compare and place their values, not to require redrawing a common whole.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The first listed source (IES/WWC Practice Guide) is marked verified:true in the row; the second (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false. The Year 3 curriculum claim used in activity 2 should be treated as unconfirmed in this rewrite.

The predict-then-check routine in activity 4 is a design proposal; the cited sources support that iteration on a number line refutes the 'less than one' belief, but do not establish the comparative effectiveness of reason-before-observing.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2, 6/1 = 6, and 5/2 = 2½ (between 2 and 3) are all correct and retained. No arithmetic errors found.
The area model representation listed in the source's key representations is carried as an alternative representation constraint alongside the number line and length model.

The non-preferred 3D-interactive and conversation catalog entries were dropped as ranking judgements, not pedagogical laws; a denominator of 1 and the fraction-as-division idea could in principle also be discussed verbally as support, so no categorical 'only building teaches' claim is asserted.

Independent re-audit confirms no 'denominator flips' comparison, no categorical modality claim, and that the physical-cutout thickness/ideal-figure distinction is stated in the activity-facing constraints, not only in a reviewer note.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT, with a reason, whether 4/4 lands before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 on a number line. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part — a child who thinks fractions are always 'parts less than one' predicts before 1. Then iterate four 1/4-jumps from 0 (or build four quarters): they fill exactly one whole and land on 1, refuting 'a fraction must be less than 1'.
probeDeeper: How many quarters do you need to make exactly one whole? What fraction is that?
Where does 8/4 go on the line — and why is it the same place as 2?
Is 5/2 a whole number? Where does it land, and what does that tell you?
Write the number 3 as a fraction. What does the bottom number 1 mean?
assess.correctAnswer: 4/4 = 1 — four quarters make one whole, so it lands exactly on 1. Whole numbers: 6/3 = 2 and 8/4 = 2 (the numerator is a multiple of the denominator: 6÷3 = 2, 8÷4 = 2). 5/2 is not a whole number (5 is not a multiple of 2; it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Fractions are always parts / always less than 1 — '4/4 is a bit less than 1, it's still a fraction'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate four quarters to fill exactly one whole; land 4/4 on the 1 mark; name b/b = 1
errorPatterns.distractor: 4/4 is a little less than 1 — it's a fraction, not a whole number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 4/4 short of 1; denies a fraction can equal a whole number

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — 'if both digits are whole numbers the fraction is a whole number', so 5/2 counts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Relate a/b to a ÷ b and to iterating on the line; test whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator
errorPatterns.distractor: 5/2 is a whole number because 5 and 2 are both whole numbers
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls 5/2 a whole number, or cannot see 8/4 = 2

errorPatterns.pattern: n/1 confusion — a denominator of 1 seems meaningless, so cannot write 5 as 5/1
errorPatterns.nextMove: A denominator of 1 means the whole is in one piece, so 5/1 is five wholes; place 5/1 on the line at 5
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot express a whole number as a fraction, or misreads 5/1

responseLevels.gap: Believes fractions are always less than 1; places 4/4 before 1; reads 8/4 and 5/2 by their separate digits.
responseLevels.full: Places 4/4 on 1 and explains b copies of 1/b make a whole; identifies 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers (numerator a multiple of the denominator / a ÷ b) and 5/2 as not; writes a whole number as n/1.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts 4/4 = 1 but cannot reliably identify 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers or explain n/1 — knows the single case b/b = 1 without generalising to a·b/b.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 4/4 equal to 1, or less than 1? Put a dot where 4/4 goes on this 0-to-2 number line and explain why it lands there. Then: which of these are whole numbers — 6/3, 8/4, 5/2 — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands b/b = 1 and a/b as iteration places 4/4 on 1 and identifies 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers. A child who believes fractions are always less than 1 puts 4/4 short of 1; a whole-number-bias child mishandles 6/3 or calls 5/2 a whole number by reading the digits separately.

topic.assessmentPrompt: If each section of a garden uses 3/4 of a bag of compost and there are 4 sections, can {{name}} work out how many bags are needed in total?

pedagogy.summary: These word problems apply multiplication of a fraction by a whole number in context — 5 people each eating 3/8 of a pizza, four 2/3-metre ribbon pieces. The core idea is a/b × n as n copies of a/b (repeated addition of a unit-fraction multiple), and the practical twist is interpreting an improper-fraction product back in context: 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 pizzas eaten, but you must BUY 2 whole pizzas. Teach it as repeated groups on a bar or number line, estimate between whole numbers (6 × 3/4 lies between 4 and 5), convert the improper result to a mixed number, and round or interpret according to the situation.
bestPractices: Model as repeated equal groups — n copies of a/b — accumulating on a bar or number line so the product is built, not just computed
Multiply only the numerator by the whole number (n × a/b = na/b); keep the denominator as the unchanged unit
Estimate between which whole numbers the product lies before computing (6 × 3/4 is between 4 and 5)
Convert the improper product to a mixed number and INTERPRET it in context (round pizzas needed up to a whole)
Distinguish 'how much is eaten' (exact mixed number) from 'how many must be bought' (rounded up)
keyRepresentations: Number line with repeated fraction jumps of a/b
Repeated-groups bar (n copies of the fraction) accumulating past wholes
Improper → mixed conversion of the product
Context interpretation card (eaten vs needed)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies the denominator too (4 × 2/3 → 8/12), scaling the unit as well as the count
Adds the whole number to the fraction instead of multiplying (3/8 + 5)
Leaves the answer as an improper fraction with no contextual meaning, or fails to round 'pizzas needed' up
Chooses the wrong operation because the repeated-groups structure is not read

learn.summary: Learners solve word problems that multiply a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) by treating the product as n copies of the unit-fraction multiple, accumulating them on a bar or number line, converting the improper result to a mixed number, and interpreting that result in context — distinguishing exactly how much is used (e.g. 1 7/8 pizzas eaten) from how many whole units must be bought (2 pizzas). Core examples: 5 people each eating 3/8 of a pizza; four ribbon pieces of 2/3 metre; estimating that 6 × 3/4 lies between 4 and 5.

activities.title: Build the product by stacking repeated fraction groups
feedback: If the denominator changed (e.g. 4 × 2/3 written as 8/12), return to the groups: 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 — only the number of thirds grows, each piece is still a third.
If the whole number was added instead (3/8 + 5), redraw the five groups of 3/8 and name it aloud as 'five lots of 3/8' before writing ×.
If the answer was left improper, prompt: how many whole bars and how much extra does 15/8 make?
activities.rationale: Modelling multiplication as accumulating repeated groups on a visual model builds na/b concretely and confronts the documented error of scaling the denominator; keeping the denominator fixed shows the unit is unchanged.
sourceClaims: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
learnerActions: Take a catering problem: 5 friends, each eats 3/8 of a pizza — work out the total eaten by building copies, not by jumping to a rule.
Stack five copies of a 3/8 bar (or draw five jumps of 3/8 on a number line) and track the running total: 3/8, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8, 15/8, noting when the total crosses a whole.
Record the result as the improper fraction 15/8 and convert it to the mixed number 1 7/8.
State in words: the top number (count of eighths) grows while the denominator stays eighths — the unit does not change.
Repeat the build for 4 × 2/3 (thirds accumulating to 8/3 = 2 2/3) to generalise.
If a live builder is available, set the fraction and the count and watch copies stack with a running total snapping the whole-number boundaries; otherwise draw each jump by hand.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is repeatedly adding that fraction: n copies of a/b accumulate to na/b, so only the numerator (count of unit fractions) grows while the denominator stays the fixed unit.

activities.title: Interpret the result: eaten versus bought
feedback: If 15/8 or 1 7/8 is given as the number to buy, ask: 'You can't buy 7/8 of a pizza — how many whole ones cover 1 7/8?' The multiplication is correct; only the interpretation is missing.
If rounding is applied where it isn't needed (ribbon length), point out that 2 2/3 metres is a valid measurement — rounding depends on whether the unit can be partial.
Reinforce estimating first: if 6 × 3/4 was expected to be a whole number, note that 18/4 = 4 1/2 lies between 4 and 5, as the estimate predicts, so the product is not a whole number.
activities.rationale: Interpreting the improper product in context — distinguishing the exact amount from the whole quantity a situation demands — is the real purpose of the word problem; estimating between whole numbers provides a reasonableness check.
sourceClaims: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
learnerActions: Using the computed total 1 7/8 pizzas eaten, decide how many whole pizzas must be ordered, given you cannot buy part of a pizza.
Explain why 1 7/8 rounds UP to 2 here, and why the question 'how much is eaten' keeps the exact 1 7/8.
Answer a contrast pair: 'How much pizza is eaten?' (1 7/8, exact) and 'How many whole pizzas must be bought?' (2, rounded up).
For the ribbon problem, state 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 metres and decide whether rounding is needed (it is not — a length can be a mixed number).
Before computing another problem, estimate between which two whole numbers the product lies, e.g. 6 × 3/4 is between 4 and 5.
activities.intendedInsight: An improper-fraction product must be read back into the situation: the exact mixed number answers 'how much', but 'how many whole units are needed' may require rounding up — and some quantities (like length) sensibly stay as mixed numbers.

activities.title: Check and consolidate with targeted questions
feedback: A product with a changed denominator (8/12), often then 'simplified' to 2/3, reveals the denominator-scaling error — reteach via repeated groups.
A correct computation but a fractional buy-quantity shows a missing interpretation step, not a broken method.
An answer near 5 3/8 or an addition of whole and fraction signals the wrong operation was chosen — redraw the groups and name them before writing ×.
activities.rationale: A short set of discriminating items separates computational slips, the denominator misconception, and interpretation gaps, and checks transfer to a new context. Recognition items check reasoning but do not by themselves show independent construction, so pair them with an end-to-end solve.
sourceClaims: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
learnerActions: Answer: 4 × 2/3 = ? Choose and justify from 8/12, 8/3, 2 2/3, explaining why 8/12 is wrong (denominator scaled) and showing that 8/3 and 2 2/3 are the same value.
Fill in the blank: n × a/b = __/b, stating the rule in your own words.
Estimate on a scale 'between which two whole numbers is 6 × 3/4?' and place it.
Solve a fresh word problem (e.g. a new fraction × whole context) end to end: build, compute na/b, convert, and interpret whether to round.
Explain in a sentence what a party host should order for a group, separating 'eaten' from 'bought'.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent learners compute na/b (numerator only), convert to a mixed number, interpret in context, estimate between whole numbers, and transfer the method to a new word problem.

constraints: Enforce or emphasise numerator-only scaling: when multiplying, the denominator (unit) stays fixed; a builder that makes multiplying the denominator impossible is a scaffold, but learners must also be able to state and apply the rule without the tool.

Recognition/multiple-choice items (e.g. choosing 8/3 over 8/12) check whether the learner can judge answers but do not on their own demonstrate independent construction; include at least one full build-and-interpret task.
A tap-to-reveal static worked pair illustrates the accumulation and interpretation but cannot let the learner vary the count — use it as an example, not as the main practice where varying n matters.
Rounding up applies to quantities that must be whole (pizzas to buy); it is not universal — lengths and similar measures can remain mixed numbers. Always tie rounding to the situation.
A conversational/role-play framing (party-planning host) can pose the 'eaten vs bought' question well, but the accumulation itself benefits from a visual surface (bar or number line).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic audit (independently re-checked): 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8; 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3; 6 × 3/4 = 18/4 = 4 1/2, which lies between 4 and 5. The original candidate draft had written '18/4 = 4 2/3' in the interpret activity's estimation feedback; this is incorrect and now reads 4 1/2 at every occurrence.

The source row rated a 3D/physical representation as a 'poor fit' with the claim that '3D adds nothing' for planar repeated groups; this categorical modality claim is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped. A 3D or physical representation is simply a different, non-required experience, not evidence that one medium is superior.

CCSS source is marked verified:false in the row; no new verification was performed. The IES/WWC source is marked verified:true in the row — this reflects legacy metadata, not a re-check during this rewrite.

probeDeeper: In (a), 15/8 pizzas are eaten — can you buy 15/8 of a pizza? How many whole ones do you need?
Between which two whole numbers does 6 × 3/4 lie, without computing exactly?
Show 4 × 2/3 as jumps on a number line — how many thirds altogether?
Estimate (b) — more or less than 2 metres? more or less than 3?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 pizzas eaten; you must buy 2 whole pizzas. (b) 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 metres.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the denominator as well: 4 × 2/3 → 8/12 (scales the unit along with the count)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to repeated groups — four lots of 2/3 is 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 — on a number line so only the count of thirds grows; the third stays the unit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product has a changed denominator (8/12 rather than 8/3); often then 'simplified' to 2/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the answer as an improper fraction with no contextual meaning, or fails to round 'pizzas needed' up: reports 15/8 or 1 7/8 as the number to buy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'you can't buy part of a pizza; how many whole ones cover 1 7/8?' — the multiplication is sound, only the interpretation is missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computation correct but the buy-quantity is given as a fraction/mixed number rather than 2 whole pizzas

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds instead of multiplies, or chooses the wrong operation: 3/8 + 5, because the repeated-groups structure is not read
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the groups first — 5 people each with 3/8 — and name it as 5 lots of 3/8 before writing ×
errorPatterns.revealedBy: An addition of the whole and the fraction, or an answer near 5 3/8; no repeated-groups working

responseLevels.gap: Multiplies the denominator, or adds instead of multiplies; no repeated-groups model.
responseLevels.full: Multiplies correctly (numerator only), converts to a mixed number, interprets in context (rounds pizzas needed up to 2), estimates between whole numbers, and transfers to a new fraction × whole word problem.
responseLevels.partial: Computes na/b correctly (15/8, 8/3) but cannot convert/interpret the improper result in context — leaves it improper or fails to round the buy-quantity up.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these, showing your working: (a) Each person eats 3/8 of a pizza and there are 5 people — how much pizza is eaten in total, and how many whole pizzas must be bought? (b) A ribbon is cut into pieces each 2/3 of a metre long — how long are 4 pieces altogether?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the method catches the two faults a bare answer hides: whether the denominator was wrongly scaled (4 × 2/3 → 8/12 instead of 8/3) and whether the improper product was interpreted in context. Part (a) is engineered to separate 'how much is eaten' (1 7/8, exact) from 'how many to buy' (2, rounded up) — a child who reports 1 7/8 pizzas to buy has computed correctly but not interpreted. A child who multiplies the denominator, or adds instead, reveals a broken model of a/b × n.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Fractions of a whole (age 10+)
topic.description: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b); solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to fractional or mixed-number answers
evidence: Explain that 3/4 means 3 ÷ 4 and verify by showing 3/4 × 4 = 3
Solve: '9 people share a 50-pound sack equally — how many pounds each?' and express the answer as 5 5/9
Use a visual model to show that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each person 3/4
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} shares 3 pizzas equally among 4 friends, can they work out what fraction each person gets — and explain why 3 ÷ 4 gives the same answer as 3/4?

pedagogy.summary: A fraction a/b means a ÷ b — the fraction bar IS a division sign. 3/4 is what each person gets when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4, and that is exactly 3 ÷ 4. This unifies fractions and division: every division has an exact answer even when the dividend is smaller than the divisor (3 ÷ 4 = 3/4), and any whole-number division with a remainder can be written as a mixed number (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, the leftover 5 shared among 9). The inverse check 3/4 × 4 = 3 confirms the meaning.
bestPractices: Derive it from equal-sharing of SEVERAL wholes: share 3 bars among 4 by cutting each bar into quarters — each person collects 3 quarters, so 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4
Make the bar-as-division-sign explicit and verify every result with the inverse multiplication (3/4 × 4 = 3)
Connect remainders to fractional parts: 50 ÷ 9 gives 5 each with 5 left, and the 5 shared among 9 is 5/9, so 5 5/9
Contrast a ÷ b with b ÷ a (3 ÷ 4 vs 4 ÷ 3) so the direction of division carries meaning, heading off the 'always divide the bigger by the smaller' habit
Use the sharing model to show that a ÷ b is defined and exact even when a < b
keyRepresentations: Equal-sharing / partition diagram (3 bars each cut into 4, one quarter to each person)
Number line locating 3/4 and 3 ÷ 4 at the same point
The ÷ ↔ fraction-bar equivalence written side by side
Long division producing a fractional (not just whole + remainder) answer
commonMisconceptions: 'You can't divide a smaller number by a larger one', so 3 ÷ 4 is declared impossible or flipped to 4 ÷ 3
Reverses to bigger ÷ smaller (computes 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3)
Stops at a whole-number remainder ('5 remainder 5') instead of expressing it as 5 5/9
Treats 3/4 as only '3 out of 4 parts', unconnected to the division 3 ÷ 4

learn.summary: Teach a/b as a ÷ b — the fraction bar means divide — by having learners share several wholes equally among more people than there are wholes. Sharing 3 bars among 4 children gives each 3/4, making 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 a result learners produce and see, not a rule to memorise. Verify with the inverse (3/4 × 4 = 3) and extend to division with remainders expressed as mixed numbers (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, the leftover 5 shared among 9). Directly contrasting a÷b with b÷a keeps the direction of division meaningful.

activities.title: Share the bars: discover 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4
feedback: If a learner predicts it is impossible, don't correct the prediction — proceed to cut and deal, then revisit: everyone got 3 quarters, so 3 ÷ 4 is defined and equals 3/4.
If a learner flips to 4 ÷ 3, share 4 bars among 3 separately and place the two results side by side so the different answers show the direction of division carries meaning.
Confirm the inverse check out loud: four lots of 3/4 reassemble the original 3 bars, so 3/4 must be the right share.
activities.rationale: Equal-partitioning/sharing is a well-documented foundation for understanding a fraction as a quotient. Performing the share is intended to help resolve the 'you can't divide a smaller number by a larger' belief through a concrete action, and predicting before cutting is meant to surface that belief so the observed 3/4 can confront it. Contrasting a÷b with b÷a is aimed at heading off the 'always divide the bigger by the smaller' habit. These are research-informed proposals, not tested interventions.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.NF.B.3: interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). It gives the exact examples this record uses: interpret 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4, noting 3/4 × 4 = 3 and that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each 3/4; and 'if 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds each?' (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, between 5 and 6). Answers to whole-number division can be fractions or mixed numbers.
Fractions arise from equal partitioning/sharing and are numbers in their own right; the equal-sharing interpretation underpins understanding a fraction as a quotient.

Üzel (2018), a peer-reviewed study of 84 eighth-graders, lists among documented division-of-fractions misconceptions 'Dividend must be bigger than divisor', 'Result must be bigger than 1' and 'Results must be integer number', tracing them to over-generalising whole-number reasoning ('multiplication enlarges; division reduces'); students over-apply memorised rules rather than reasoning about the quantities.
learnerActions: Set up the problem: 3 identical chocolate bars to share equally among 4 children.
BEFORE cutting, predict and give a reason: can everyone get the same, and if so how much each? Sit with the 'there aren't enough bars' feeling if it arises.
Cut each bar into 4 equal quarters.
Deal one quarter from every bar to each child, then count what ends up on each plate (3 quarters).
Write the result as a division: 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4.
Check in reverse: show that 3/4 × 4 rebuilds the 3 whole bars.
Compare directions: share 4 bars among 3 children and work out 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3; note that 3 ÷ 4 and 4 ÷ 3 give different answers.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction a/b is exactly the quotient a ÷ b; you can divide a smaller number by a larger one and the answer is a fraction. The order of division matters, so 3 ÷ 4 ≠ 4 ÷ 3.

activities.title: Remainders are divisions too: 50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9
feedback: If a learner writes '5 r5' (leaving the remainder unshared) or '5.5' (mis-reading remainder 5 as a half — note 50 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.56, not 5.5), both are incomplete or incorrect: return to the sack and share the 5 leftover pounds among the same 9 people, giving 5/9 each, so 5 5/9.

Reinforce that in this rice problem '5 remainder 5' is an unfinished answer: rice can be split, so the leftover 5 pounds can be divided further by the same divisor, 9. (With things that can't be split, like people or cars, a whole-number answer with a remainder can be the right answer.)
activities.rationale: Connecting remainders to fractional parts extends the fraction-as-division idea to a new case and is intended to counter the 'results must be an integer' / stop-at-remainder error. Transferring to a different context (rice, not bars) is intended to probe genuine understanding rather than a memorised bar routine. Proposed activity, not an evaluated one.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.NF.B.3: interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). It gives the exact examples this record uses: interpret 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4, noting 3/4 × 4 = 3 and that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each 3/4; and 'if 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds each?' (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, between 5 and 6). Answers to whole-number division can be fractions or mixed numbers.

Üzel (2018), a peer-reviewed study of 84 eighth-graders, lists among documented division-of-fractions misconceptions 'Dividend must be bigger than divisor', 'Result must be bigger than 1' and 'Results must be integer number', tracing them to over-generalising whole-number reasoning ('multiplication enlarges; division reduces'); students over-apply memorised rules rather than reasoning about the quantities.
learnerActions: Pose: 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight — how many pounds each?
Give out whole pounds first: 5 each uses 45 pounds, leaving 5 pounds.
Decide what to do with the leftover 5 pounds: share those 5 among the 9 people too.
Express that leftover share as a fraction: 5 ÷ 9 = 5/9.
Combine to the mixed number: 5 5/9 pounds each.
Sanity-check the size: the answer lies between 5 and 6.
activities.intendedInsight: A whole-number division with a remainder has an exact answer as a mixed number; the remainder is itself a division (the leftover shared among the same group).

activities.title: Check and discriminate: name the division and verify
feedback: If a learner answers 3/4 but calls it only 'three shaded of four' with no link to division, show the share and the division produce the SAME 3/4, then verify 3/4 × 4 = 3 to connect the two views.
If a learner flips to 4 ÷ 3, deal 4 bars among 3 to show 4 ÷ 3 is a different question with a different answer.
Treat a correct 'how much each' answer given with only a part-of-whole reason as partial: prompt for the division name and the inverse check before counting it as full understanding.
activities.rationale: Checkable items with carefully chosen wrong-answer options are intended to surface the reversal (computing 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3), the 'impossible' belief, and the stop-at-remainder error. Requiring both the answer and its division name with an inverse check is intended to distinguish rote part-of-whole reading from quotient understanding. Recognition and fill-in items can assess and rehearse the link but do not by themselves require the learner to perform and feel the share, so pair them with the sharing activity.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.NF.B.3: interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). It gives the exact examples this record uses: interpret 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4, noting 3/4 × 4 = 3 and that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each 3/4; and 'if 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds each?' (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, between 5 and 6). Answers to whole-number division can be fractions or mixed numbers.

Üzel (2018), a peer-reviewed study of 84 eighth-graders, lists among documented division-of-fractions misconceptions 'Dividend must be bigger than divisor', 'Result must be bigger than 1' and 'Results must be integer number', tracing them to over-generalising whole-number reasoning ('multiplication enlarges; division reduces'); students over-apply memorised rules rather than reasoning about the quantities.
learnerActions: Given a sharing situation (e.g. 3 bars among 4 children), state how much each gets AND which division it represents.
Explain how to check the answer using inverse multiplication (3/4 × 4 = 3).

Answer a short set of linked items: 3 ÷ 4 = ? (compare against the tempting wrong answers 1 1/3 (which comes from working out 4 ÷ 3 instead) and 'impossible', both labelled as incorrect answers to 3 ÷ 4); fill in 50 ÷ 9 = 5 __/9; match each division to its fraction or mixed-number result.
Say in your own words why a share of 3 bars among 4 is less than one whole each.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to name 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4 and verify it with ×4 — not just read it as 'three out of four parts' — is what shows the division meaning has been grasped.

constraints: Target age 10–11; conceptual objective: interpret a/b as a ÷ b and solve whole-number division problems with fractional/mixed-number answers.
Derive the result from equal-sharing of SEVERAL wholes (not one whole cut up), so the smaller-divided-by-larger case is genuinely enacted.
Let the learner attempt to share before cutting so the 'not enough bars' impasse is felt before it is resolved; keep the prediction uncorrected until the share is performed.
Always close the loop with the inverse check (3/4 × 4 = 3) — naming the division alone is not sufficient evidence of understanding.

A static picture of finished shares (e.g. tap a plate to reveal '3 quarters = 3 ÷ 4') can illustrate the result and serve as a reference, but does not let the learner perform the share or experience the initial impasse; use it as a scaffold or companion, not as the main activity.

Checkable fill-in/matching items rehearse and assess the link and surface the reversal and stop-at-remainder errors, but recognition-only responses do not require independent construction of the share; pair them with hands-on sharing.

Represent the quotient in more than one way where possible (sharing diagram, number line placing 3/4 and 3 ÷ 4 at the same point, long division yielding a fractional answer) rather than relying on a single model.

Present reversal (giving 1 1/3, the value of 4 ÷ 3, as the answer to 3 ÷ 4; computing 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3) and 'impossible' only as labelled wrong-answer options to confront, never as valid methods. 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3 is itself true and may be worked out as a separate comparison question.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit (all confirmed): 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4; 3/4 × 4 = 3; 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3; 50 ÷ 9: 9×5 = 45, remainder 5, 5/9 each, so 5 5/9, which lies between 5 and 6 (decimal ≈ 5.56). No errors found; the reversal, 'impossible', '5 r5' and '5.5' are presented only as labelled wrong answers, never as valid answers.

The source listed two distinct 'bigger ÷ smaller' examples — the reversal of 3 ÷ 4 to 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3, and computing 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3. Both are preserved as misconception/wrong-answer patterns, not as correct methods.

The Üzel (2018) study concerns division OF fractions among eighth-graders; it documents the relevant 'dividend must be bigger', 'result must be >1', 'result must be integer' misconceptions but is not direct evidence about teaching a/b = a ÷ b to 10–11 year-olds. Treat its citation as support for the existence of the misconceptions, not for the efficacy of these activities.

Non-preferred artefact judgements from the source ('3D depth adds nothing', 'dialogue cannot teach this', static image 'cannot let the child perform the sharing') are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; recast as narrow scaffold limits in constraints without asserting universal necessity of any medium.
Source confidence was labelled 'high' and claims 'verified:true'; this rewrite does not independently upgrade or re-verify those ratings.

assess.poeTask: Before any cutting, ask: 'Can we share these 3 bars equally among 4 children so everyone gets the same, and if so how much each?' Have the child PREDICT and give a reason. Many predict it is impossible, or that each gets 'less than one but I can't say how much'. Then share for real — cut each bar into quarters and deal them out — and each child holds 3/4. The pre-cut reason is the diagnostic: a child expecting 'impossible' reveals the 'can't divide smaller by larger' belief, which the observed 3/4 directly refutes.
probeDeeper: 9 people share a 50-pound sack equally — how many pounds each? What do you do with the 5 pounds left after everyone has 5?
How could you check that 3/4 is the right share — what is 3/4 × 4?
Is 3 ÷ 4 the same as 4 ÷ 3? Share 4 bars among 3 children and compare the two answers.
If each bar is one whole, why is each child's share less than a whole here?
assess.correctAnswer: Each child gets 3/4 of a bar. This represents 3 ÷ 4 (the fraction bar means divide), and it checks because 3/4 × 4 = 3 — the three original bars.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can't share 3 among 4 — there aren't enough bars', so declares it impossible or flips it to 4 ÷ 3 = 1⅓
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the sharing engine: cut each of the 3 bars into 4 and deal them out; everyone gets 3 quarters, so 3 ÷ 4 is defined and equals 3/4. Contrast with 4 ÷ 3 to show direction matters.
errorPatterns.distractor: 3 ÷ 4 can't be done because 3 is smaller than 4
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 3 ÷ 4 can't be done, or gives 1⅓ by dividing the larger by the smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives 3/4 but cannot connect it to division — 'it just means 3 parts out of 4', with no link to 3 ÷ 4 and no way to check
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the sharing produces the SAME 3/4 as the division; verify 3/4 × 4 = 3 to link the two views.
errorPatterns.distractor: 3/4 just means 3 parts out of 4 — it has nothing to do with dividing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct tier-1 answer, but tier-2 reason is 'three shaded of four' and the child cannot say it is 3 ÷ 4 or verify with × 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops at a whole-number remainder for the sack problem — '5 remainder 5' — and cannot express the leftover as 5/9
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share the leftover 5 pounds among the 9 people: that is 5/9 each, so 5 5/9. The remainder is itself a division.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 50 ÷ 9 probe, writes '5 r5' or '5.5' and treats the remainder as un-shareable

responseLevels.gap: Declares 3 ÷ 4 impossible or reverses it to 4 ÷ 3; stops at '5 remainder 5'; treats 3/4 as parts with no division meaning.
responseLevels.full: States each gets 3/4 = 3 ÷ 4, justifies by sharing, verifies 3/4 × 4 = 3, and solves 50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9 by sharing the remainder — transferring the bar-as-division idea to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Gets 3/4 each and can say it is 3 ÷ 4 in the sharing case, but cannot verify with the inverse (× 4) or extend to 50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 3 identical chocolate bars to share equally among 4 children. How much does each child get? Then tell me: what division does this sharing represent, and how could you check your answer is right?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The first tier (how much each gets) can be answered '3/4' from part-of-whole habit. The second tier — naming it as 3 ÷ 4 AND checking with the inverse × 4 — is where understanding shows. A child who holds 'you can't divide a smaller number by a larger' declares the share impossible or flips to 4 ÷ 3; a child who sees 3/4 only as 'three out of four' cannot connect it to a division or verify it. Reasoning correctly and reasoning wrongly produce visibly different tier-2 answers.

sources.claim: CCSS 5.NF.B.3: interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). It gives the exact examples this record uses: interpret 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4, noting 3/4 × 4 = 3 and that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each 3/4; and 'if 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds each?' (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, between 5 and 6). Answers to whole-number division can be fractions or mixed numbers.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 5 Number & Operations—Fractions (5.NF.B.3)

sources.claim: Üzel (2018), a peer-reviewed study of 84 eighth-graders, lists among documented division-of-fractions misconceptions 'Dividend must be bigger than divisor', 'Result must be bigger than 1' and 'Results must be integer number', tracing them to over-generalising whole-number reasoning ('multiplication enlarges; division reduces'); students over-apply memorised rules rather than reasoning about the quantities.
sources.source: Üzel, D. (2018), Investigation of Misconceptions and Errors about Division Operation in Fractions, Universal Journal of Educational Research 6(11):2656–2662 (ERIC EJ1195709)

sources.claim: Fractions arise from equal partitioning/sharing and are numbers in their own right; the equal-sharing interpretation underpins understanding a fraction as a quotient.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction (Recommendation 1)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Fractions of amounts (harder)
topic.description: Solve problems involving increasingly harder fractions to calculate quantities, including non-unit fractions where the answer is a whole number
evidence: Find 3/5 of 20
Calculate 2/3 of 18 and explain the two-step process (divide then multiply)
Solve: A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red — how many red sweets?
topic.assessmentPrompt: If 3/4 of a class of 28 pupils brought their homework in, can {{name}} work out exactly how many pupils that is?

pedagogy.summary: Finding a non-unit fraction of a quantity is a two-step operator procedure: divide the whole by the denominator to find one equal part (the unit fraction), then multiply that part by the numerator. The teaching goal at age 8-9 is fluency and reliable structure — children already know unit fractions of sets, so the new work is coordinating the divide-then-multiply sequence and interpreting worded problems ("3/8 of 24 sweets") into that structure. Best taught by making the two steps explicit and visible before compressing them, and by grounding the procedure in the meaning of the denominator (how many equal shares) and numerator (how many shares we take).
bestPractices: Make the two steps explicit: ring-fence 'divide by the denominator to get one part' as step 1, then 'multiply by the numerator' as step 2, before letting children compress it — many errors are a collapsed or reversed sequence, not arithmetic slips.

Anchor the procedure in the fraction-as-operator meaning: the denominator says how many equal groups to split into, the numerator says how many of those groups to take. This lets children self-check which number divides and which multiplies.

Use bar models / arrays: draw the whole as a bar, partition into 'denominator' equal parts, shade 'numerator' of them, and read off the total — the model makes the divide-then-multiply visible and catches the 'divide by numerator' error.
Sequence from unit to non-unit: confirm 1/8 of 24 = 3 first, then 3/8 = 3 x 3 = 9, so the new step (multiply by numerator) is isolated against secure ground.
Include a plausibility check: a proper fraction of a quantity must be smaller than the whole (9 red sweets out of 24), which catches multiply-the-whole errors.
Vary the worded contexts (sweets, money, measures, sets of people) so children practise translating language into the divide-then-multiply structure rather than pattern-matching one phrasing.
keyRepresentations: Bar model partitioned into denominator equal parts with numerator shaded (whole labelled, one part labelled)
Array / equal groups (24 counters in 8 groups of 3; take 3 groups)
Double number line: 0 ... whole on top, 0 ... fraction on bottom, marking one part then stepping along
Written two-step record: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, then 3 × 3 = 9
commonMisconceptions: Divides by the numerator instead of the denominator (3/8 of 24 read as 24 ÷ 3)
Stops after one step — finds the unit fraction (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and gives that as the answer without multiplying by the numerator
Multiplies the whole by the numerator (24 × 3) giving an answer larger than the whole
Multiplies numerator and denominator into the whole in the wrong order or muddles which is which under worded-problem load

learn.summary: Finding a non-unit fraction of a quantity (e.g. 3/8 of 24) is a two-step operator procedure for 8-9 year olds: divide the whole by the denominator to find one equal part, then multiply that part by the numerator. Children already know unit fractions of sets, so the new work is coordinating the divide-then-multiply sequence, grounding it in the meaning of numerator and denominator, and translating worded problems into that structure. Make the two steps explicit and visible before compressing them.

activities.title: The fraction-of machine: divide to build parts, then take them
feedback: If a learner takes 3 single sweets rather than 3 groups, pause: '3/8 means 8 equal shares - how many shares do you take, and how big is each share?' This shows the learner is treating the numerator as a number of single items and ignoring the denominator. Note that the answer (3) matches the size of one share here, so watch the action, not just the answer.

If a learner tries to make 3 groups instead of 8, use a meaning-based prompt (24 does divide evenly by 3, so the partition alone will not flag the error): 'Does the bottom number tell how many groups, or the top? /8 means 8 equal groups.'
If a learner stops after making 8 groups of 3 and reports '3', prompt: 'That is 1/8. The question asks for 3/8 - how many of those groups do we take?'

If a learner produces a number bigger than 24, ask the plausibility check: 'Can 3/8 of 24 be more than 24? A proper fraction of an amount is smaller than the whole.' Then rebuild the divide-first step.
When correct, confirm: dividing built the parts (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and selecting took 3 of them (3 × 3 = 9).
activities.rationale: Letting the child perform and see both steps, with a bar model shown alongside tying the actions to the written record, isolates the load-bearing skill (the sequence) and surfaces the two canonical errors in the action itself. Live partitioning, selecting groups, and a running total are optional interaction examples that make the divide-then-multiply mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: Set up the problem '3/8 of 24 sweets': start with 24 sweets to share.
Split the 24 sweets into equal groups, where the number of groups is fixed by the denominator (8 groups of 3).
Now take the numerator's worth of those groups: take 3 of the 8 groups and count the total (9).
Record the two steps in writing alongside the action: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, then 3 × 3 = 9.
Repeat with new fractions and new contexts (e.g. 3/5 of 20 pounds, 2/3 of 18 people) so the structure, not one phrasing, is practised.
activities.intendedInsight: The procedure is two distinct actions with two distinct results: dividing by the denominator builds the equal parts, and multiplying by the numerator (selecting that many groups) takes them. Children can self-check which number divides (how many equal shares) and which multiplies (how many shares to take).

activities.title: Isolate the new step: from unit fraction to non-unit fraction
feedback: If the learner re-divides when the numerator changes, point out the groups of 3 already exist - only the number of groups taken changes.
If the learner can do 3/8 but stalls on 5/8, they may be pattern-matching the last answer rather than using the structure; walk back to 'how big is one group?'
Praise explanations that reference meaning ('8 says make 8 equal shares, 3 says take 3 of them') over recited rules.
activities.rationale: Sequencing from unit to non-unit isolates the new multiply step against secure ground and builds the fraction-as-operator meaning rather than a rote rule.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: First confirm the unit fraction on secure ground: find 1/8 of 24 (= 3).
Then isolate the new step: 'That is one group. For 3/8, how many groups do we take?' Take 3 groups to get 9.
Try the same whole with a different numerator: 5/8 of 24 re-uses the groups of 3 and takes 5 (= 15); notice you do NOT re-divide.
Explain in your own words why the denominator divides and the numerator multiplies.
activities.intendedInsight: The division step is shared across all eighths of 24; only the numerator (how many groups to take) changes. This separates the secure prior skill from the genuinely new multiply-by-numerator step.

activities.title: Bar models and arrays: making divide-then-multiply visible
feedback: If a learner partitions into the numerator's parts, compare: 'Which number tells how many equal parts to cut? The bottom (denominator).'
If a learner shades all parts or more than the whole, revisit: the shaded amount is part of the bar, so it cannot exceed 24.

A tap-to-reveal worked example (reveal the partition, then reveal which parts are taken and the total) can serve as a pre-teach, but it shows one case and does not let the child perform the procedure across varied quantities, which fluency requires.
activities.rationale: Bar models, arrays and number lines represent the operator structure concretely and catch the characteristic errors; a single revealed worked example is a useful scaffold but limited to one case.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
learnerActions: Draw the whole as a bar labelled 24; partition it into the denominator's number of equal parts (8 parts), label one part (3).
Shade the numerator's number of parts (3 parts) and read off the shaded total (9).
Build the same with counters: arrange 24 counters as 8 groups of 3, then ring 3 groups.
Use a double number line: amount (0 to 24) on top and fraction (0 to 1, marked in eighths) on the bottom, so 1/8 lines up with 3 and 8/8 lines up with 24. Mark one part, then step along to 3/8 (9).
activities.intendedInsight: The model makes the divide-then-multiply structure visible: partitioning is the division, shading/selecting is the multiplication. Reading the total off the model catches the divide-by-numerator error (wrong number of parts) and the multiply-the-whole error (answer must fit inside the bar).

activities.title: Varied worded problems and plausibility checking
feedback: If a learner computes 24 x 3 = 72, ask 'Can part of 24 be bigger than 24?' before rebuilding the divide-first step.
If a learner solves sweets but stalls on money, highlight that the structure is identical: divide the amount by the denominator, multiply by the numerator.

Scored practice can check fluency and capture the two-step structure: on a 0-24 slider an answer of 3 (stopping after one step) is a selectable error, while a free-entry answer can additionally surface an answer of 72 (multiplying the whole), and a fill-in-the-blanks format (24 ÷ ☐ = ☐, ☐ × ☐ = ☐) shows which step goes wrong. Recognising a correct option, however, does not show the child can independently construct the steps - pair it with doing.
activities.rationale: Worded problems in varied contexts are curriculum expectations; a plausibility check catches the multiply-the-whole error; talking a problem through may support translating worded language into the structure and should accompany, not replace, the independent practice a procedural skill requires.
sourceClaims: Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: Solve worded problems across contexts: sweets (A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red - how many red?), money (3/5 of 20 pounds), measures (cm), and sets of people (2/3 of 18).
For each, write the two lines of working and name which number divides and which multiplies.
Before accepting an answer, run the plausibility check: a proper fraction of an amount must be smaller than the whole (9 red sweets out of 24 is reasonable; 72 is not).
Optionally talk a problem through aloud with a partner or in-role 'shopkeeper' who poses 'fraction of my stock' problems, explaining each step.
activities.intendedInsight: Translating varied language into the same divide-then-multiply structure prevents pattern-matching one phrasing, and the plausibility check guards against multiply-the-whole errors.

constraints: Keep the two steps explicit and ring-fenced before compressing them: many errors are a collapsed or reversed sequence, not arithmetic slips.
Anchor the procedure in meaning - denominator = how many equal groups, numerator = how many groups taken - so children can self-check which number divides and which multiplies.
A revealed/worked static example shows one case and cannot let the child perform the procedure across varied quantities; use it as a pre-teach, not the main practice.

Recognition-only response formats (selecting a correct option) can assess fluency and surface specific errors but do not elicit independent construction of the two steps; include tasks where the child builds or writes the procedure.
Talking a problem through supports translating worded language into the structure but should accompany, not replace, repeated independent doing for a procedural skill.

Do NOT rely on a visible remainder to flag the divide-by-numerator error in '3/8 of 24': 24 divides evenly by 3, so making 3 groups gives 8-per-group with no remainder. Use a meaning-of-denominator prompt instead.

Watch out for the diagnostic coincidence in '3/8 of 24': the group size (3) equals the numerator (3), so an answer of 3 could mean the child took 3 single counters (treating the numerator as a count of items and ignoring the denominator) or stopped after finding one group (1/8). Neither is divide-by-numerator confusion, which shows up as making 3 groups of 8. Watch what the child actually does, and also use a problem where group size and numerator differ (e.g. 3/4 of 24, group size 6) so these errors can be told apart.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (National Curriculum in England programmes of study) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

The source row's own diagnostic note is self-contradictory: it states the design avoids numerator equal to group size, then states 24 deliberately gives group size 3 and numerator 3. The latter is correct for '3/8 of 24'.

The original 'fraction-of machine' design-note feedback claiming the division visibly stalls (trays won't divide evenly) when a child divides by the numerator does not hold whenever the numerator also divides the whole (as with 3 and 24); it was corrected to a meaning-based prompt in the activity feedback, not relying on a visible remainder.

Claims that a 2D interactive is uniquely 'ideal' or that 3D 'adds nothing', or that doing is inherently superior to talking, are catalog/efficacy judgements not established by the sources; reframed as affordances and qualified limits without asserting necessity or comparative superiority.

probeDeeper: Once they answer, ask 'how did you know to make 8 groups and not 3?' — listen for the denominator meaning, not a recited rule.
'Show me 1/8 of the 24 first — now how do you get to 3/8?' isolates whether the second step is understood or lucky.
Counterexample: 'What if I'd asked for 5/8 of 24 instead?' — a child with the structure re-uses the groups of 3 and takes 5 (=15); a child who pattern-matched the last answer stalls.
'Could your answer be bigger than 24? Why not?' surfaces whether the plausibility check is available.
assess.correctAnswer: 9. The child splits the 24 into 8 equal groups (24 ÷ 8 = 3 in each), then takes 3 of those groups (3 × 3 = 9).

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by the numerator: reads '3/8 of 24' as 24 ÷ 3 and makes 3 groups (or takes just 3 counters), giving 8 or 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning of the denominator: it says how many equal shares. Rebuild with 'how many equal groups does /8 mean?' before touching the numerator.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child makes 3 groups instead of 8, or grabs 3 counters straight away — using the top number as the divisor

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops after one step: finds the unit fraction (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and offers 3 as the answer, not multiplying by the numerator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach division of sets — scaffold the second step only: 'that's 1/8; the question asks for 3/8 — how many of those groups?' Point back at the numerator's job.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child correctly makes 8 groups of 3 then reports '3' — the division is right but the second step is dropped

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the whole by the numerator: computes 24 × 3 = 72, giving an answer larger than the starting quantity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trigger the plausibility check first ('can 3/8 of 24 be more than 24?'), then rebuild the divide-first step with the bar model.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child produces a number bigger than 24 with no partitioning, or multiplies before dividing

responseLevels.gap: Cannot coordinate the two steps: divides by the numerator, or multiplies the whole, or produces the unit-fraction-only answer and cannot get further even with the numerator pointed out.
responseLevels.full: Reliably divides by the denominator then multiplies by the numerator, explains each step by the meaning of the fraction, transfers to a new fraction and a new context (money, measures), and checks the answer is smaller than the whole.
responseLevels.partial: Executes both steps for the practised case (makes 8 groups, takes 3, gets 9) but treats them as a memorised recipe — cannot explain why the denominator divides, or stalls when the fraction changes to 5/8 or the context changes to money.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 24 counters. Find 3/8 of them. Do it however you like, and I'll watch — you don't need to tell me the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the teacher WATCHES the procedure rather than asking about it, the two canonical breakdowns show themselves in the child's actions: a child who divides by the numerator makes 3 groups; a child who stops after one step makes 8 groups but reports 3; only a child who has the divide-then-multiply structure makes 8 groups AND takes 3 of them. 24 is chosen so 3/8 divides evenly (no remainder to mask the error) and the numerator (3) differs from the group size (also 3) is avoided — deliberately 24 gives group size 3 and numerator 3, so watch that they take 3 GROUPS not 3 counters: taking 3 counters instead of 3 groups is the exact tell for divide-by-numerator confusion.
