topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Modelling with multiplication and fractions
topic.description: Model real-world problems involving multiplication, area, fractions, and unit conversion by choosing appropriate representations and interpreting mathematical results in context
evidence: Model a tiling/area problem with an array and write the corresponding multiplication
Represent a recipe-scaling problem as a fraction calculation and interpret the answer in grams
Use a bar model to set up a unit conversion problem (metres to centimetres)
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is solving a real-life problem — like working out the area of a room in square metres — do they choose the right maths tool for the job and interpret the final number in terms of the real situation?

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 the modelling cycle stretches to multiplicative situations — area/array, recipe-scaling with fractions, and unit conversion. The teaching goal is unchanged from the earlier bands but the return trip gets harder: a child must now choose a representation that exposes the multiplicative STRUCTURE (an array shows rows×columns; a bar shows equal parts; a double-scale shows metres against centimetres), run the calculation, and then read the number back into the situation with its unit attached ('so that's 375 grams of flour', not just '375'). The hardest interpret-back at this age is the fractional one: 3/4 of 500g is a quantity of a real thing, not a bare fraction.
bestPractices: Insist on the return trip: after every calculation ask 'what does this number mean in the problem, and what is its unit?' — the model is not finished until the answer is re-clothed in context
Use numberless / number-later problem framing so children build the situation and choose the representation before they grab the numbers (Bushart; CDE guide)
Connect the array/area model to the multiplication sentence explicitly — rows × columns IS the product, area IS l×w — so the picture and the equation are two views of one structure
For recipe-scaling, keep the unit visible through the whole calculation so 3/4 × 500 lands as '375 g of flour', not an abstract 375
Model conversion as a proportional structure (a bar of 1 m cut into 100 cm) rather than a remembered 'move the decimal' rule
keyRepresentations: Array / area model (rows × columns; l × w rectangle)
Bar model for part-whole, scaling and unit conversion
Double number line / scaling ladder (metres against centimetres; grams against portions)
The multiplication / fraction equation written alongside the picture
commonMisconceptions: Stops at the bare number and never re-attaches the unit or meaning ('375') so cannot say what was found
Treats 3/4 of 500 as a fraction answer rather than a quantity of grams of a real ingredient
Reaches for a keyword ('of means times', 'altogether means add') instead of modelling the situation, so mis-sets the operation
Applies a memorised conversion rule (×100) without a structure to check it against, so an inverted conversion (cm to m by ×100) goes unnoticed

learn.summary: For children aged 8–9, mathematical modelling of multiplicative situations (area/array, recipe-scaling with fractions, unit conversion) must complete the full cycle: choose a representation that exposes the multiplicative STRUCTURE, run the calculation, and then take the 'return trip' — read the number back into the situation with its unit and referent attached ('375 g of flour', not a bare '375'). The hardest interpret-back at this age is the fractional one: 3/4 of 500 g is a quantity of a real ingredient, not a bare fraction. Each of the three situations ends in the same interpret-back gate. Guidance centres on a hands-on interactive build where the model and equation are two views of one structure, supported by an in-role client conversation, a labelled primer, and sub-skill checks.

activities.title: Tile a floor, scale a recipe, convert a length — then say what the number means
feedback: Withhold confirmation until both the unit and the referent are right, not just the digits — a correct digit with a stripped unit is not yet a finished model
If the child stops at a bare number, ask 'twenty-four what?' or 'three hundred and seventy-five of what?' and route the answer through 'the number, its unit, and what it is the amount of'
When the array completes, point out that the side lengths are the factors and the filled area is the product — the picture and the equation say the same thing

For the box-ordering step, if a child answers '2 boxes' show that 2 boxes gives only 20 tiles and 24 are needed, so 3 boxes is required — the return trip is what turns '24' into 'enough tiles, so 3 boxes'

For the conversion, check the interpret-back too: '300 cm' should be read as a length (3 m is 300 cm), and an inverted move (treating cm→m as ×100 when it should be ÷100) is caught against the structure of 1 m cut into 100 cm
activities.rationale: Modelling is a full cycle: represent the situation, compute, then interpret results in context and judge whether they are reasonable. A dynamic build lets the child do the modelling and face a mandatory interpret-back gate at the end of each situation, which is the practice itself rather than only the representation. Numberless/number-later framing lets the child build the situation and choose the operation from its structure before a surface keyword can fire. Live examples such as dragging tiles so the equation writes itself, cutting a bar into fractional parts, and stretching a double number line are offered to make the structure concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Modelling is a full cycle — represent the situation, compute, then INTERPRET the mathematical results in context and judge whether they make sense, revising if not; early grades write an equation to describe a situation
A single part-whole bar exposes the underlying structure and lets children choose the operation, and scales to conversion and scaling situations

Suspension of sense-making is common in word problems; keyword-stripping backfires; numberless/number-later framing builds the situation model before numbers so children choose the operation from structure not surface cues
learnerActions: Drag square tiles into a rectangle to build an array; watch the matching equation form alongside (e.g. 6 rows × 4 = 24) so the picture and the equation are two views of one structure
Compute the result, then complete a compulsory interpret-back step: state or type the answer WITH its unit and what it refers to ('24 tiles', '375 g of flour'), not just the digits
Carry a result back into a real decision: if tiles come 10 to a box, work out that 24 tiles needs 3 boxes and that 2 boxes (only 20 tiles) would leave you short
Repeat the same shape with a recipe bar: cut a bar of 500 g into quarters and take 3/4 to get '375 g of flour'

Repeat with a metres-to-centimetres double number line (scaling ladder): read one scale against the other, then complete the same interpret-back gate by stating the converted length with its unit and referent (e.g. '3 m is 300 cm')

At least once, meet a problem where a surface keyword ('altogether', 'of', 'times') points to the wrong operation; use numberless/number-later framing and set the operation from the structure of the situation instead
activities.intendedInsight: A model is not finished until the number is re-clothed in context: every answer needs its unit and referent, and should be sense-checked against the situation. The array/area picture IS the multiplication (rows × columns = product; l × w = area), and scaling and conversion share a multiplicative, proportional structure.

activities.title: Convince the client: 375 of what?
feedback: Have the client accept a number only once the child states its unit and confirms it is reasonable for the real order
If the child gives a bare number, the client asks 'so how much flour do I actually buy?' or 'how many boxes of tiles do I order?' to force the interpret-back in words

If the stated quantity is out of scale, prompt the child to compare it with the starting amount (e.g. if 500 g serves 4 people, going to 6 people is 6/4 = 1.5× as many, so expect more than 500 g but less than double — 1.5 × 500 g = 750 g, not 7500 g)
activities.rationale: Spoken, responsive dialogue with an in-role client can prompt the child to articulate and defend the meaning, unit and reasonableness of a result — the reflective interpretation that completes the cycle. This complements the build by shifting the work into explanation and justification.
sourceClaims: Modelling is a full cycle — represent the situation, compute, then INTERPRET the mathematical results in context and judge whether they make sense, revising if not; early grades write an equation to describe a situation
learnerActions: Work with an in-role client — a baker scaling a recipe, or a decorator ordering tiles — who needs a real answer for a real order
State the result in words with its unit and referent, and justify that the quantity is reasonable for the real order
Respond when the client pushes back ('you said 375 — 375 of what?') by naming the unit and checking the amount makes sense
Decide the practical consequence: how many boxes to buy, how much flour to measure
activities.intendedInsight: Voicing and defending the interpret-back — naming the unit, the referent, and a reasonableness check — is the reflective half of the modelling cycle. The number only means something when tied back to the real decision it informs.

activities.title: Primer: the array beside the equation
feedback: As each label is revealed, restate the link: the two side lengths are the factors, the filled region is the product
Prompt the child to predict a label before tapping, then check against the reveal
activities.rationale: A labelled, reveal-on-tap array/bar can clearly show and name the correspondence between picture and equation, which supports learning the representation. Used as a primer before the hands-on build, it introduces the structure; on its own it does not require the child to do the modelling or the interpret-back, so it is a scaffold rather than the whole practice.
sourceClaims: A single part-whole bar exposes the underlying structure and lets children choose the operation, and scales to conversion and scaling situations
learnerActions: Explore a labelled array or bar where taps reveal the parts: 'this side = number of rows', 'the area = the product = the number of tiles'
Connect each labelled part of the picture to the matching part of the written multiplication or fraction sentence
activities.intendedInsight: Rows × columns IS the product and area IS l × w: the picture and the equation are two views of one multiplicative structure.

activities.title: Sub-skill checks: product and converted length
feedback: Confirm or correct the arithmetic, then hand the result back to the main modelling task with 'now, what does this number mean, and in what unit?'

Flag an inverted conversion (e.g. multiplying when converting cm to m, which should be dividing by 100) by comparing against the part-whole structure (1 m cut into 100 cm) rather than a remembered rule
activities.rationale: Short scored checks can efficiently confirm sub-skills such as array→product or a conversion step, which can feed the main modelling task. A scored check of a stripped digit cannot, on its own, observe the 'what does this mean in context, with its unit' reflection, so it is used to support rather than replace the modelling work.
learnerActions: Check a computed product from a given array (rows × columns)
Check a converted length (e.g. metres to centimetres) for a given structure
activities.intendedInsight: The underlying arithmetic sub-skills (finding a product, carrying out a conversion) must be reliable so attention is free for the modelling and interpret-back.

constraints: The model is not finished until the answer is re-clothed in context: after every calculation, and at the end of each of the three situations, ask 'what does this number mean in the problem, and what is its unit?' and withhold confirmation until the unit and referent are right, not just the digits.

Keep the unit visible through the whole fraction calculation so 3/4 × 500 lands as '375 g of flour', not an abstract 375; and label each quantity's referent before calculating so the referent does not drift (e.g. 'this bar is grams of flour').

Teach conversion as a proportional structure (a bar of 1 m cut into 100 cm), not a memorised 'move the decimal' or '×100' rule, so an inverted conversion (treating cm→m as ×100 when it should be ÷100) can be caught against the structure.

Use numberless / number-later framing so children build the situation and choose the representation and operation from structure before grabbing numbers; discourage reliance on keyword rules ('of means times', 'altogether means add').
The labelled array/bar primer shows and names the representation but does not require the child to model or interpret back; it is a scaffold and is not sufficient alone.
Scored sub-skill checks verify arithmetic only; a correct digit with a stripped or wrong unit still passes such a check, so they cannot on their own observe the modelling and interpret-back.

These situations are planar (arrays, bars, lengths); a 2D array is enough to expose the multiplicative structure here, and 3D is better reserved for genuinely volumetric modelling later — this is a scope choice for this band, not a universal claim about 3D.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 6 × 4 = 24 (consistent); 3/4 × 500 = 375 g (consistent); 500 ÷ 4 × 6 = 750 g (consistent). Going from 4 to 6 people is 6/4 = 1.5×, so 1.5 × 500 = 750 g — the reasonableness check (a bit more than 500, fits; 7500 is out of scale) is sound. Box-ordering: 24 tiles at 10 per box needs 3 boxes (2 boxes = 20 < 24) — correct.

The original design phrase 'a deliberate keyword trap the model defeats' was softened: the activity presents a misleading keyword so the child sets the operation from structure, rather than asserting any representation universally 'defeats' misconceptions.

Legacy fit rankings asserting a quiz 'only assesses' and that '3D adds nothing'/adds 'spatial cost' have been reframed as scoped scaffold limits and a band-level scope choice, not universal pedagogical laws.

The original source's conversion misconception wording ('cm to m by ×100') is noted as the error to catch: cm→m is ÷100, so the activity flags multiplication as the inverted move rather than endorsing it.
reteachPrerequisiteId values (e.g. internal mt_ identifiers) from the assessment are internal IDs and were not carried into learner-facing guidance; the assessment field itself is unchanged.

Independent re-review confirmed the interpret-back gate is present in all three situations (tiles, recipe, conversion), the CDE numberless-framing claim is cited where it is enacted, and no unsupported categorical claims of medium superiority remain; evidence of efficacy is still untested and these remain proposals.

probeDeeper: You said 750 grams — is that more or less than the 500 we started with, and does that make sense for going from 4 people to 6?
If the recipe were for 8 people instead of 6, would you expect the flour to be more or less than 750 g? Roughly how much?
What if I told you the answer came out as 7500 g — would you trust it? How would you know something had gone wrong?
Could you draw me a picture that shows why we divide by 4 and multiply by 6 — what does each step do to the flour?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child treating '750' as unfinished until it is read back into the situation as '750 grams of flour for 6 people', and sense-checking it (6 people is 1.5× as many as 4, so a bit more than 500 g is expected; 750 fits). A child who says only 'the answer is 750' or 'it's 750 people/cups' has done the arithmetic but not the modelling.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the bare number as the finished answer — '750' — and never re-attaches the unit or what it refers to, so cannot say what was found ('it's 750')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refuse the bare number: 'seven hundred and fifty what?' Route every answer through 'the number, its unit, and what it is the amount of' until re-clothing becomes automatic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked what 750 means the child restates the digit or gives no unit, and shows no discomfort that the model is unfinished

errorPatterns.pattern: Attaches the wrong unit or referent — reads 750 as '750 people' or '750 cups' rather than grams of flour — losing track of what the quantity in the model stands for
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go back to the model and label each quantity's referent before calculating: 'this bar is grams of flour', so the answer is grams of flour. Re-run with the referent kept visible throughout.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child confidently supplies a unit but it is not the flour-in-grams the model was about; referent has drifted from the situation

errorPatterns.pattern: Grabs a keyword instead of modelling — hears 'for 6 people' and adds, or 'times' and multiplies the wrong pair — so the operation does not match the situation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Strip the numbers (numberless framing) and rebuild the situation first: what is happening, what is being scaled to what? Choose the representation before any keyword can fire.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child's set-up follows a surface word cue rather than the part-whole/scaling structure of the problem; the representation, if drawn, doesn't match the story

responseLevels.gap: Reports '750' with no unit or referent, or an unrelated unit, and shows no sense that the model is unfinished; cannot say what was found or whether it is reasonable.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, states '750 grams of flour for 6 people', checks it against the situation (1.5× as many people so a bit more flour — fits), would flag an out-of-scale result like 7500, and transfers the same interpret-and-check habit to a fresh scaling or conversion problem.
responseLevels.partial: Attaches the correct unit ('750 grams') when prompted and can describe the steps, but does not spontaneously sense-check the magnitude and needs prompting to relate it back to '6 people, a bit more than 500 g'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A recipe for 4 people uses 500 g of flour. You want to make it for 6 people. A friend works out 500 ÷ 4 × 6 and says '750'. Is the recipe finished being solved? Talk me through what 750 means and whether you'd trust it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely models cannot leave 750 bare — they attach the unit and referent and check it against the situation; a child who only computes says '750' and stops, or mislabels the unit. The prompt deliberately offers a correct calculation so the tell is not arithmetic but whether the return trip happens and whether the magnitude is sense-checked against 'a bit more than 500'.

sources.claim: Modelling is a full cycle — represent the situation, compute, then INTERPRET the mathematical results in context and judge whether they make sense, revising if not; early grades write an equation to describe a situation
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice — MP4 Model with mathematics

sources.claim: Suspension of sense-making is common in word problems; keyword-stripping backfires; numberless/number-later framing builds the situation model before numbers so children choose the operation from structure not surface cues
sources.source: Colorado Dept of Education — Word Problems Guide (Bushart numberless word problems)

sources.claim: A single part-whole bar exposes the underlying structure and lets children choose the operation, and scales to conversion and scaling situations
sources.source: NCETM — The Bar Model

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Fractions on a number line
topic.description: Recognise and use fractions as numbers: place unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators on a number line
evidence: Place 1/2, 1/4, 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1
Identify that 1/3 lies between 0 and 1/2 on the number line
Understand that a fraction is a single number, not just 'part of a shape'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you draw a number line from 0 to 1, can {{name}} mark where 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 should go — without any extra help?

pedagogy.summary: Placing fractions on a number line is the move from 'fraction = part of a shape' to 'fraction = a number with a magnitude', locatable, orderable and equivalence-checkable. The load-bearing idea is that a fraction 1/b is made by splitting ONE unit (the distance between two whole numbers) into b equal SEGMENTS — needing b−1 marks between them — and the point at the a-th mark is a/b. Teach with the unit held visible so children stop treating the whole line as the unit and stop placing 3/4 'between 3 and 4'.
bestPractices: Start from pre-segmented 0-to-1 lines, then minimally-labelled lines with landmarks (0, 1/2, 1, 1½, 2), then unmarked lines to force interval thinking (IES Rec 2)
Teach fourths as four equal SEGMENTS between 0 and 1 made by THREE marks; generalise 1/n needs n−1 marks
Use contrasting cases to kill 'between 3 and 4': locate 3 and 4 on a 0-to-4 line, then 3/4 within 0-1, and discuss why each sits there
Reason with landmarks and distance ('is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or to 0?') so magnitude, not counting, drives placement
Use dual labelling (fifths above the line, tenths below) to show equivalent fractions land on the same point
keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 number line partitioned into equal segments (the core model)
Minimally-labelled landmark line (0, 1/2, 1)
Dual-labelled line (two fractional-unit sequences) for equivalence
Fraction strip laid alongside the line to link area-model and length-model
commonMisconceptions: Treats the number line like a ruler — counts tick marks (or draws 4 marks for fourths) instead of equal segments (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treats the whole line as the unit — e.g. locates 3/4 three-quarters of the way across a 0-to-5 line
Sees a fraction only as part of a shape, not as a single number that has a place on a line
Larger-denominator-is-larger — places 1/8 further from 0 than 1/3

learn.summary: Help 7-8 year olds move from 'fraction = part of a shape' to 'fraction = a number with a place on the line'. The load-bearing idea: a fraction 1/b is made by splitting ONE unit (the distance between two whole numbers) into b equal SEGMENTS, which needs b−1 marks between them, and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th equal segment counted from 0 (for a less than b, this is the a-th interior mark). Keep the unit visible so children stop treating the whole line as the unit and stop placing 3/4 'between 3 and 4'. Core model is a 0-to-1 line partitioned into equal segments; progress to landmark lines and then unmarked lines to force interval thinking, and use dual labelling to show equivalence as the same point.

activities.title: Three marks make fourths: partition and place on an interactive line
feedback: If the child draws or expects four interior marks for fourths, point out four interior marks make FIVE parts; count the equal segments together and confirm three marks give four parts.
If the bead is read as 4/4 or 4/5, recount the equal segments from 0 and name the end of the third segment as 3/4.
If 3/4 is placed between 3 and 4 on the longer line, locate 3 and 4 first, then ask 'is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1?' and relocate it within the first unit.
When 1/2 lands on 5/10, name it: 'same point, two names — that's what equivalent means.'
activities.rationale: Partitioning a unit into equal segments and reading the end of the a-th segment directly targets the ruler-counting error (Roadblock 2.1) and the 'between 3 and 4' error (Roadblock 2.2); dual-labelled lines show equivalent fractions occupying the same point. Live controls (cut-into-parts dial, draggable bead that reports its fraction, length toggle, tenths track) make the segment-counting mechanism and the fixed unit concrete, but are optional ways to realise the task and the same learning can be done on paper.
sourceClaims: Recommendation 2 (Moderate Evidence): use number lines to teach fractions as numbers. Dividing a number line into 1/n units needs n-1 marks between two whole numbers; students err by drawing 4 marks for fourths or treating the whole line as the unit (Roadblock 2.1), and by placing 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction's numbers as separate whole numbers (Roadblock 2.2).

Students often view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), diagnosable by having them label hatch marks on a 0-to-1 number line; equivalent fractions can be shown to occupy the same point using dual-labelled lines.
learnerActions: On a 0-to-1 line, set a 'cut this unit into ___ parts' control to 4 and watch exactly THREE marks drop in, splitting the line into four equal segments.
Say aloud how many marks made four parts (three, not four), and colour each of the four segments, counting SEGMENTS rather than marks.
Drop a bead on the third mark; if the line reports a fraction, check it announces '3/4' and explain why that point is 3/4.

Extend the line from 0-to-1 to 0-to-4, keeping each whole-number unit the same length (or redraw it that way), and notice the 3/4 bead stays three-quarters of the way from 0 to the first '1', nowhere near the '3'.
On a second track below, lined up with the same 0 and 1 and labelled in tenths, slide a 1/2 bead until it lands exactly on 5/10, and state that the two labels name the same point.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction 1/b comes from cutting one unit into b equal segments (needing b−1 interior marks), and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th segment. The unit stays 'one whole' even when the line gets longer, so 3/4 lives between 0 and 1, not between 3 and 4. Equivalent fractions are the same point under different labels.

activities.title: Place and reason on paper lines: pre-marked, landmark, then unmarked
feedback: If a child drifts toward whole-number placement on the longer or unmarked line, return to naming the unit (0 to 1) and ask how many equal parts the denominator calls for.
For 'is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or 0?', prompt: twelfths are small, so compare how far 1/12 sits from 0 against how far it sits from 1/4, rather than which number looks bigger.
If an unmarked line is partitioned unequally, fold or measure to check the segments are the same length before placing the point.
activities.rationale: Fading from pre-segmented to landmark to unmarked lines forces interval thinking and shifts the child from counting to magnitude reasoning (IES Rec 2). Contrasting 3 and 4 with 3/4 on the same 0-to-4 line directly confronts the separate-whole-numbers error. Landmark distance questions support ordering fractions and address larger-denominator-is-larger.
sourceClaims: Recommendation 2 (Moderate Evidence): use number lines to teach fractions as numbers. Dividing a number line into 1/n units needs n-1 marks between two whole numbers; students err by drawing 4 marks for fourths or treating the whole line as the unit (Roadblock 2.1), and by placing 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction's numbers as separate whole numbers (Roadblock 2.2).
learnerActions: On a 0-to-1 line already divided into four equal segments (fourths), place 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 by counting equal segments from 0.

On a minimally-labelled line showing only 0, 1/2, 1, 1½ and 2, place a concrete fraction such as 1¾ using landmarks — reasoning that it sits just below 2 (between 1½ and 2) — rather than counting every mark.
On an UNMARKED 0-to-1 line, decide how many segments you need, make the b−1 marks yourself, then place the fraction.
Answer landmark-reasoning questions such as 'Is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or to 0?' and 'Is 3/4 closer to 0 or to 1?', explaining using distance.
On a 0-to-4 line, place both 3 and 4, then separately place 3/4, and say in your own words why 3/4 does not go between 3 and 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Placement is driven by magnitude and distance from landmarks, not by counting ticks. Children who can partition an unmarked line themselves have internalised that the unit is divided into equal segments, and they keep fractions within the correct whole-number interval.

activities.title: Bridge from the shape model and compare unit fractions
feedback: If the child says a line 'isn't a shape so you can't do fractions on it', use the strip-along-the-line bridge until the shaded part and the point coincide, then name the point.
If 1/8 is placed further from 0 than 1/3, compare one eighth-segment with one third-segment of the same unit: more parts, shorter parts, so 1/8 sits nearer 0.
If a reference point is misnamed, recount the equal segments from 0 and describe the point as 'the end of the a-th of b equal parts'.
activities.rationale: Linking the area model to the length model addresses children who see fractions only as parts of shapes and refuse or randomise line placement. Comparing segment lengths of the same unit partitioned differently reteaches 'more parts means smaller' before ordering, targeting the larger-denominator-is-larger misconception. A labelled reference line supports reading, but being fixed it cannot by itself make the child confront miscounting — pair it with the partitioning task.
sourceClaims: Students often view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), diagnosable by having them label hatch marks on a 0-to-1 number line; equivalent fractions can be shown to occupy the same point using dual-labelled lines.
learnerActions: Shade 3/4 of a fraction strip exactly as long as the 0-to-1 unit, starting the shading at one end, then lay that end at 0 along the line so the shaded part reaches a point; name that point as the number 3/4.
Partition one unit into thirds, then partition an identical unit into eighths, and compare the lengths of a single segment in each.
Place 1/3 and 1/8 on the same 0-to-1 line and decide which is further from 0, explaining using segment length.
State in your own words whether a fraction such as 3/4 is 'a number' or 'just a piece of a shape', and point to where it lives on the line.
Reference check: label 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1 on a line and explain for each point which segment's end it marks.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction names one number and has a single location on the line; the area (shape) model and the length (line) model agree. More equal parts of the same unit means each part is smaller, so 1/8 is closer to 0 than 1/3 — the denominator counts how many parts split ONE whole.

constraints: Hold the unit (the 0-to-1 distance) visible and fixed so children do not treat the whole line as the unit; test transfer on a 0-to-4 or unmarked line, not only on a pre-segmented 0-to-1 line.
Teach fourths as four equal SEGMENTS made by THREE interior marks; generalise that 1/n needs n−1 interior marks. Insist on counting segments, not tick marks.

A fixed labelled reference line can teach and be used while teaching, but on its own it does not require the child to construct segments or re-place a point on a longer line; combine reference-reading with active partitioning and placement.

Fraction strips and paper cutouts have real slight thickness and only approximate the ideal flat model; use them to bridge area and length, and treat any on-screen line as a model of the idealised (zero-thickness) number line.

When comparing unit fractions such as 1/8 and 1/3, keep the SAME whole and compare how one segment's length changes as the denominator changes; describe this as 'more parts means smaller parts', never as a denominator rule that 'flips'.

Placing and comparing points is a construct-and-check task: recognition-only or matching responses can check placement but do not by themselves elicit the child independently partitioning a unit and justifying a location. Include at least one task where the child makes the marks and states the reasoning.

Live controls (cut-into-parts dial, snapping/announcing bead, length toggle, tenths track) are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required equipment; the same learning can be done on paper with careful partitioning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed the two headline errors are 'refuted on contact' and 'die on sight' with a dynamic line, and that a static image 'can't let the child confront miscounting', a dialogue 'can't substitute', and 3D 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-fit assertions, not established efficacy claims; softened here to scoped affordances/limits. Comparative medium superiority is not asserted by the cited Moderate-Evidence source.
Geometry self-audit: a fraction's point on the number line is the END of the a-th equal segment, and b−1 interior marks produce b equal segments; four interior marks would produce five segments.

Landmark question audit: 1/12 ≈ 0.083 and 1/4 = 0.25, so 1/12 is closer to 0 than to 1/4; and 1/8 = 0.125 is closer to 0 than 1/3 ≈ 0.333. These are kept as reasoning prompts for the child to work out, not pre-stated answers. The added example 1¾ = 1.75 sits between 1½ and 2, just below 2.

The Year 3 'count up and down in tenths' curriculum claim was removed from the paper-lines activity (which contains no tenths) to avoid citing a source that supports only the topic context rather than that activity's teaching principle.
Edit this pass: the second activity's landmark-placement action was made concrete (place 1¾ using the 1½/2 landmarks) so it models landmark reasoning rather than leaving the fraction unspecified.

probeDeeper: Is 3/4 closer to 0 or closer to 1? How do you know?
Point to where 1/8 would go and where 1/3 would go. Which is further from 0, and why?
Someone put 3/4 in the space between the 3 and the 4 on this line. What would you tell them?
Is a fraction like 3/4 a number, or just a piece of a shape? Where does that show up on the line?
assess.correctAnswer: The dot is at 3/4, because 0-to-1 is divided into four equal parts (segments) and the dot sits at the end of the third part. On the 0-to-4 line, 3/4 goes three-quarters of the way from 0 towards 1 (just below 1, NOT between 3 and 4) and 1/2 goes halfway between 0 and 1; each is a single number between 0 and 1 because its denominator splits ONE unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rules-the-line like a ruler — counts tick marks (or draws 4 marks for fourths) instead of equal segments, so the point is misread or the unit is mis-partitioned
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show fourths as four equal SEGMENTS made by THREE marks between 0 and 1; have the child colour each segment and count segments, not marks (IES Roadblock 2.1)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads the 3/4 point as 4/4 or 4/5, counts the 0 mark as one, or when drawing puts four interior marks to make fourths

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number placement — treats the numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers and puts 3/4 between the 3 and the 4 on the 0-to-4 line
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrasting cases: locate 3 and 4, then 3/4 as a number between 0 and 1; reteach fraction as a single quantity of one whole before returning to the line (IES Roadblock 2.2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 0-to-4 line marks 3/4 in the interval from 3 to 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction-as-part-of-shape only — can shade 3/4 of a pizza but insists a line 'isn't a shape, you can't do fractions on it' or places it arbitrarily
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bridge the area model to length: lay a fraction strip along the 0-1 line so the shaded part reaches the same point; name the point as the number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses the task, treats the line as decoration, or places the fraction with no relation to the unit

errorPatterns.pattern: Larger-denominator-is-larger — places 1/8 further from 0 than 1/3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Partition the same unit into thirds then eighths and compare segment lengths; reteach more-parts-means-smaller before ordering on the line
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to place unit fractions, puts the one with the bigger denominator further to the right

responseLevels.gap: Counts tick marks, draws four marks for fourths, places 3/4 between 3 and 4, or says a line can't show fractions — treats the two numbers separately.
responseLevels.full: Interprets the marked point as 3/4 by segments, produces 3/4 and 1/2 on a fresh 0-to-4 line both within 0-1 and reasoned by landmarks, and explains a fraction is a single number whose denominator partitions one unit — transferring to locate or compare a new fraction.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and places 3/4 and 1/2 on a pre-marked 0-to-1 line by counting equal segments, but on a 0-to-4 or unmarked line loses the unit (miscounts or drifts toward whole-number placement) and cannot yet say a fraction is one number located relative to landmarks.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First, look at this number line from 0 to 1. There are three marks spaced equally between 0 and 1, and I have put a dot on the third mark. What number is at the dot, and how do you know? Now here is a fresh line labelled from 0 to 4. Put 3/4 on it, and put 1/2 on it, and tell me why each one goes where you put it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting the marked point separates ruler-counting (reads it as 4/4 or miscounts marks) from interval thinking (end of the third equal segment). The 0-to-4 placement is the decisive translate move: a child who treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers puts 3/4 between 3 and 4, which a part-of-a-shape understanding alone cannot avoid, whereas seeing a fraction as one number keeps it inside the first unit.

Dividing a number line into 1/n units needs n-1 marks between two whole numbers; students err by drawing 4 marks for fourths or treating the whole line as the unit (Roadblock 2.1), and by placing 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction's numbers as separate whole numbers (Roadblock 2.2).

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Fractions on a number line
topic.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, number lines, and symbolic equations involving multiplication, fractions, and decimals, explaining what each representation shows
evidence: Represent a sharing problem as both a fraction diagram and a division equation
Explain how a bar model for 4 × 23 connects to the area model and the written method
Translate a decimal on a number line into a fraction and explain the equivalence
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} works on a maths problem involving decimals or fractions, can they move between a fraction strip, a number line, and a written equation — explaining what each one is showing?

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 the web of representations grows to include decimals and the area/distributive model, and the demand is fluency in ALL directions: represent a sharing problem as both a fraction diagram and a division equation, show how a bar model for 4×23 connects to the area model and the written method, and translate a decimal on a number line into a fraction and explain the equivalence (CCSS MP2). Two load-bearing ideas from the IES fractions guide anchor the level: a decimal and its fraction (0.3 and 3/10) are the SAME number — the same point/magnitude on a line, not two different kinds of thing — and area/strip models must be read as a single quantity, not a count of parts. The recurring failure is treating each representation as an unconnected procedure (the area model 'for pictures', the written method 'for answers') rather than as different views of one structure; good teaching keeps asking 'what's the same across these, and where is each number in the other?'
bestPractices: Put fractions and their decimal equivalents on the SAME number line (0.3 and 3/10 at one point) so equivalence is seen as sameness of magnitude, not a conversion trick (IES Rec 2)

Lay the area model, the bar model, and the written method for 4×23 side by side and map each partial product to a region, so the representations are one structure viewed three ways (MP2 coherent representation; NCETM structure)
Use unmarked number lines and 'what single quantity is this?' questioning to stop counting-parts-without-meaning (IES caution)
Translate both ways — diagram→equation AND equation→diagram — and require the child to say what each number represents
Watch decimals for whole-number thinking (0.35 vs 0.5) and route back through the number line's magnitudes
keyRepresentations: Number line carrying fractions and decimals at shared points (equivalence as one position)
Area model / array for multiplication linked to the written method
Bar model for sharing/division and for multiplication structure
Hundredths grid linking a decimal to its fraction
commonMisconceptions: Treats a decimal and its fraction as different kinds of number that can't share a point (0.3 ≠ 3/10 'because one's a decimal')
Applies whole-number thinking to decimals (0.35 > 0.5 'because 35 > 5'; reads 0.3 as 'three')
Reads the area/bar model as a separate procedure from the written method, unable to say how they show the same calculation
Counts parts of a diagram without seeing that numerator and denominator name a single quantity

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, build fluency in moving BETWEEN representations of multiplication, fractions, and decimals: a sharing story, a fraction diagram, a number line, an area/bar model, and a written equation are different views of ONE structure, not separate procedures. Two anchoring ideas: a decimal and its fraction (0.3 and 3/10) name the SAME number — one point/magnitude on a line, not two kinds of thing — and an area or strip model must be read as quantities (each part has a value relative to the whole, and the parts' values combine into the total), not as a bare count of pieces. The recurring failure is treating each representation as its own routine (the area model 'for pictures', the written method 'for answers'); good teaching keeps asking 'what's the same across these, and where does each number live in the other?'

activities.title: Same point on the line: 0.3 and 3/10
feedback: If the child places 0.3 and 3/10 in different spots or calls them 'different numbers because one's a decimal', put both on one number line and on a tenths grid until the shared point is undeniable, and revisit tenths/hundredths equivalence as the same quantity.

If the child reads 0.3 as 'three' or judges 0.35 > 0.5 'because 35 > 5', route placement through magnitude on the line and the tenths/hundredths grid so the value, not the digit string, drives position; revisit decimal place value. (0.35 lies between 0.3 and 0.4, so it is less than 0.5.)

When the child places both at one point, justifies with 'three tenths' reasoning, and carries the same reasoning to the fresh pair, treat that as secure magnitude understanding; transferring such reasoning spontaneously to new pairs is a further sign of security.
activities.rationale: Number lines show the relations among fractions and decimals as the same magnitude at one point, and whole-number thinking misapplied to decimals is a known hazard remedied by magnitude reasoning on a line and grid.
sourceClaims: Number lines show the relations among fractions, decimals and percents (the same magnitude at one point); students misapply whole-number knowledge to fractions/decimals, and area/strip models risk counting parts without seeing a single quantity — remedied by number-line magnitude reasoning.
learnerActions: Mark where 0.3 goes on a number line from 0 to 1, then mark where 3/10 goes, and say whether they land on the same point.
Explain in your own words why both are 'three tenths of the way from 0 to 1' — the same magnitude shown two ways.
Place 0.35 and 0.5 on the line and explain which is bigger and why (0.35 is less than 0.5), checking against a tenths/hundredths grid.
Apply the same reasoning to a fresh pair, e.g. 0.27 and 27/100: place both on the line and explain the equivalence.
activities.intendedInsight: A decimal and its equivalent fraction are the same number — the same position/magnitude on the line — so notation (decimal vs fraction) is not identity; magnitude is.

activities.title: Where do 80 and 12 live? Linking the area model and the written method for 4×23
feedback: If the child can do each separately but cannot say how one shows the other, overlay the area model and the written method and map each partial product to its region, asking 'what's the same, what's different?'

If the child treats the picture as decoration and the algorithm as the 'real' method and cannot point to where 80 and 12 live, go region by region, naming the multiplication each region represents (4×20=80, then 4×3=12) before summing to 92.
Confirm understanding when the child can trace 80 to the 20-strip, 12 to the 3-strip, and explain 92 as their sum in both the picture and the written form.
activities.rationale: Representations reveal a shared mathematical structure; the same structure underlies a bar/area model and the written method, so they should be connected rather than taught as separate procedures.
sourceClaims: Representations reveal a shared mathematical structure; the same structure underlies a bar/area model and the written method, so they should be connected rather than taught as separate procedures.
MP2: create a coherent representation; attend to the meaning of quantities and their referents; move between a situation and its symbolic representation.
learnerActions: Split 23 into 20 and 3 and draw an area model (rectangle) for 4×23, showing the two regions.
Point to the region that is 4×20 and the region that is 4×3, and state their values (80 and 12).
Write out the written method for 4×23 beside the rectangle and match each partial product to its region; check the two regions sum to 92.
Say out loud what is the same and what is different between the picture and the algorithm.
activities.intendedInsight: The area model and the written method are one structure viewed two ways: each partial product (4×20=80 and 4×3=12) is a region of the rectangle, and 80+12=92 is the total.

activities.title: One sharing story, three ways
feedback: If the child can only go one direction (diagram→equation but not equation→diagram, or vice versa), practise the missing direction explicitly, asking what each number stands for each time.
Prompt 'what does this number mean in the story?' whenever the child manipulates symbols without connecting them to the quantity.
Confirm when the child moves fluently between story, diagram, and equation and can name each number's referent in all three.
activities.rationale: Translating between a situation and its symbolic representation, attending to the meaning of quantities and their referents, is the core of coherent representation.
sourceClaims: MP2: create a coherent representation; attend to the meaning of quantities and their referents; move between a situation and its symbolic representation.
learnerActions: Tell a sharing story that 6÷4 (or another division) could represent.
Draw a fraction diagram for it and write the matching division equation.
Say what each number in the equation represents in both the story and the diagram.
Translate the other way too: given a diagram, write the equation; given an equation, draw the diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: A real-world situation, its diagram, and its symbolic equation are different views of the same quantity; fluency means moving in BOTH directions and naming what each number refers to.

activities.title: Convince a doubter: dialogue and discussion
feedback: This discussion is for reasoning, not scoring: focus on whether the child justifies with magnitude ('both are three tenths') and can locate numbers across representations.
If the child only asserts 'they're the same' without showing where each goes, press 'show me where each one lands' — the shared placement plus tenths reasoning is the point.
Encourage the child to address the doubter's specific claim rather than restate a remembered rule.
activities.rationale: Being asked to defend equivalence and shared structure is one way to prompt articulation of why representations coincide; an in-role partner asserting the misconception may elicit the child's reasoning. This is a proposed, untested complement to construction tasks, not a substitute for building and placing representations.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner (classmate, adult, or in-role character) who insists '0.3 and 3/10 must be different — one's a decimal!' and argue, with the number line and a tenths grid, that they share one point.
Have the partner point at an area model for 4×23 and ask 'which bit is the 80, which is the 12?' — answer by tracing each to its region and to the written method.
Explain your reasoning aloud rather than just stating an answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Being asked to defend equivalence and shared structure can push the child to articulate WHY representations coincide, not just that they do.

constraints: Require construction and explanation, not just recognition: the child should build diagrams, place values on lines, write equations, and say what each number means. A matching-type warm-up ('which decimal equals 3/10?') can activate prior knowledge but does not show the child can construct a translation or explain shared structure.

A static side-by-side of story, diagram, area model, and equation with tap-to-reveal links can illustrate connections and serve as a worked example, but it does not let the child build or vary the representations themselves; use it as a scaffold, then move to child-generated work.
Evocative illustrations cannot be trusted for exact decimal/fraction positions — placements on a number line need accurate, marked or verifiable scales.

Optional interactive supports (if available) can make the 'same structure, different view' idea concrete: linked panels where dropping 0.3 on a line snaps 3/10 to the same tick, or an area-model↔written-method splitter where dragging the 20+3 split recolours both the rectangle regions and the partial products together. These are helpful examples, not required mechanisms; the same goals can be met with paper, a drawn number line, and spoken explanation.
When comparing decimals, hold the comparison honest: 0.35 vs 0.5 is about magnitude (0.35 < 0.5), not about which digit string looks bigger — route placement through the value.
4×23 = 92: the partial products are 4×20=80 and 4×3=12, summing to 92. Keep these exact values in any example; '60' is not a valid partial product here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The legacy source labelled all sources 'verified':true and confidence 'high'; this status was not re-checked here and should not be read as fresh validation.

The source recommendation narrative mentioned '60 glowing over the 20-strip' while elsewhere correctly giving 80 and 12 as the partial products for 4×23. The correct value is 4×20=80 (not 60); activities use 80. Any '60' should be treated as an error, not a valid alternative.

Legacy entries asserted that a 3D scene 'adds nothing' and that quizzes can only assess recognition. These are narrowed here to scoped observations (a number line and area model are planar and adequate for this magnitude/structure content; recognition-only items do not elicit construction) rather than universal laws.
The dialogue activity's efficacy relative to other media is untested; it is presented with hedged wording and no source cited for the dialogic mechanism, since no source[].claim supports it.

The fresh-pair transfer (e.g. 0.27 and 27/100) is now issued as an explicit learner task; because it is prompted, feedback credits the child for carrying the reasoning across when prompted and notes spontaneous/unprompted transfer only as an additional sign of security, not as the pass condition.

Reteach prerequisite links (e.g. decimal place-value and area/distributive prerequisites) were referenced in the source; the underlying reteach moves are preserved in feedback but specific internal prerequisite IDs are omitted as non-portable.

probeDeeper: 'Put 0.3 and 3/10 on the line — are they the same point or different? How can you be sure?'
'Where does 0.35 go compared with 0.5? Show me why.'
'In the rectangle for 4×23, point to the part that is the 80 and the part that is the 12. Where are they in the written method?'
'Tell me a sharing story that 6 ÷ 4 could be, and show it as a diagram AND an equation.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child placing 0.3 and 3/10 at the SAME point and explaining they are the same number/magnitude shown two ways (three tenths of the way from 0 to 1), rather than treating decimal and fraction as different kinds of thing living in different places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decimal and fraction seen as different kinds of number that can't share a point: 0.3 ≠ 3/10 'because one's a decimal'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put both on one number line and on a tenths grid until the shared point is undeniable; reteach decimal–fraction equivalence of tenths/hundredths as the same quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child places them in different spots, or agrees they're 'different numbers', treating notation as identity rather than magnitude.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number thinking applied to decimals: reads 0.3 as 'three', or judges 0.35 > 0.5 'because 35 > 5', misplacing the decimal on the line.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Route through the number line's magnitudes and the tenths/hundredths grid so the value, not the digit string, drives placement; reteach decimal place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 0.35 beyond 0.5, or lines decimals up by digit count rather than magnitude.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the area/bar model as a separate procedure from the written method — for 4×23 can do each but cannot say how one shows the other.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the area model and the written method and map each partial product to a region ('what's the same, what's different?'); reteach the area/distributive model as the structure behind the algorithm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the picture as decoration and the algorithm as the 'real' method; cannot point to where 80 and 12 live in the rectangle.

responseLevels.gap: Places 0.3 and 3/10 apart or calls them different numbers; treats each representation as its own procedure.
responseLevels.full: Places 0.3 and 3/10 at one point and explains both are three tenths; maps numbers across diagram, area model, number line and equation (locating 80 and 12 in the rectangle and the algorithm) — and transfers the 'same quantity, different view' reasoning to a new pair (e.g. 0.27 and 27/100) unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Says 0.3 = 3/10 or places them together, but justifies weakly (a remembered rule) or still misplaces 0.35 vs 0.5, or can map one pair of representations but not link the area model to the written method.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate says: '0.3 and 3/10 are different numbers — 0.3 is a decimal and 3/10 is a fraction, so they'd go in different places on a number line.' Do you agree? Show me where each one goes on a line from 0 to 1, and explain what you find. Then tell me how you'd convince the classmate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a magnitude view puts both at one point and can justify it (both are three tenths); a child treating notations as separate 'things' places them apart or can't say they coincide. The prompt is hard to answer right for the wrong reason because merely saying 'they're the same' doesn't survive 'show me where each goes' — the shared placement plus the tenths reasoning is the discriminating act; a notation-bound child cannot produce it.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Fractions on a number line (age 9+)
topic.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, number lines, bar models, and symbolic equations involving multi-digit multiplication, fractions, decimals, and percentages, explaining connections between representations
evidence: Represent a scaling problem as both a bar model and a multiplication equation
Show how 0.35, 35/100, and 35% all represent the same quantity on a hundredths grid
Translate a line-graph reading into a subtraction equation to find the difference
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} solves a problem involving percentages or multi-digit multiplication, can they show the same situation using a bar model, a number line, and an equation — and explain what each one represents?

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 representation fluency is expected across the full spread — real situations, bar models, number lines, multi-digit multiplication, and the fraction–decimal–percentage trio — with the child explaining the connections (CCSS MP2). The signature demand is seeing 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as ONE quantity shown three ways: the IES fractions guide recommends a single representation (a hundredths grid, or one number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below) so the equivalence is a fact of magnitude, not three separate conversion rules. Percentage is the fresh hazard — 'per cent' means 'parts per hundred', and a child who has not internalised that treats 35% as just the number 35 or an unmoored decimal. Scaling problems (bar model ↔ multiplication equation) and reading quantities off a line graph into an equation round out the level; the recurring failure is grabbing visible numbers without asking what quantity each representation is actually showing.
bestPractices: Show 0.35, 35/100 and 35% on ONE representation — a hundredths grid or a single number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below — so equivalence is seen as the same magnitude (IES Rec 2, 4th action step)
Ground percentage in 'parts per hundred' with the hundredths grid before any conversion rule, so 35% is a quantity, not a bare number
Use bar models to expose scaling/multiplicative structure and map each part to the multiplication equation (NCETM structure)
For line graphs, require the child to say what quantity each reading is before choosing an operation — e.g. a difference needs subtraction (MP2 meaning-of-quantities)
Translate in every direction and insist on 'what does each number represent?' at each step
keyRepresentations: Hundredths grid linking fraction, decimal and percentage of the same shaded amount
Single number line carrying fractions, decimals and percentages at shared points
Bar model for scaling/proportion mapped to a multiplication equation
Line graph read into a subtraction/other equation for a difference or change
commonMisconceptions: Treats 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as three different things rather than one magnitude shown three ways
Does not hold 'per cent = parts per hundred', so reads 35% as the number 35 (or a decimal with no meaning)
Grabs both readings off a line graph and adds them instead of asking which quantity and which operation the situation needs
Reads a bar/area model as a separate procedure from the multiplication equation it represents

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, build representation fluency so a child moves between real situations, bar models, number lines, multi-digit multiplication, and the fraction-decimal-percentage trio while explaining the connections and keeping each symbol tied to the quantity it names. The signature demand is seeing 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as ONE quantity shown three ways, located on a single representation (a hundredths grid, or one number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below) so equivalence is a fact of magnitude, not three separate conversion rules. Percentage is the fresh hazard: 'per cent' means 'parts per hundred', and a child who has not internalised that reads 35% as the bare number 35 or an unmoored decimal. Scaling problems (bar model mapped to a multiplication equation) and reading quantities off a line graph into an equation round out the level; the recurring failure is grabbing visible numbers without asking what quantity each representation actually shows.

activities.title: One quantity, three costumes: the linked hundredths grid
feedback: If the child says 35% is bigger than 0.35 'because 35 > nought-point-something', return to the grid: both name the same 35 shaded squares out of 100, so they are the same amount.
If the child converts by a remembered rule without pointing to the shaded region, ask them to show where 35/100, 0.35 and 35% each live on the same grid and the same number-line point.
If the child cannot say what % means, re-ground on '35 out of 100 squares shaded = 35 per hundred = 35%' before touching any conversion rule.
When a new amount is shaded (e.g. 8 squares giving 8/100, 0.08, 8%), confirm the child can state all three forms and tie them back to the shaded area unprompted.
activities.rationale: Locating the same quantity in all three forms on a single hundredths grid or one number line makes equivalence a fact of magnitude and grounds percentage as parts per hundred before any rule. An OPTIONAL live-linker version (shading drives the fraction, decimal and percentage simultaneously and marks the shared number-line point) makes the equivalence vivid by letting the child watch the three notations move together; a static annotated grid can still illustrate the same relationships but does not let the child vary the amount.
sourceClaims: Help students represent fractions as common fractions, decimals and percentages and translate among them; use a single number line (fractions above, decimals/percents below) or a hundredths grid so the same quantity is located and compared in all three forms.
MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
learnerActions: Shade 35 of 100 squares on a hundredths grid and read off the three labels that name the same shaded region: 35/100, 0.35 and 35%.
Change the shading to a different amount (e.g. 8 squares) and state the fraction, decimal and percentage, explaining why all three must still match the shaded area.
Place the same quantity at a single point on one number line that carries fractions above and decimals/percentages below.
Answer the direct challenge: 'Is 0.35 the same as 35%, or is one bigger?' and justify using the shaded area and the per-hundred meaning, not '35 is bigger than nought-point-something'.
Say aloud what the % symbol means ('parts per hundred') and what the quantity is 35% OF.
activities.intendedInsight: 0.35, 35/100 and 35% were never three numbers to convert between; they are one magnitude shown three ways, and 'per cent' means parts per hundred.

activities.title: Scaling bar mapped to a multiplication equation
feedback: If the child treats the bar and the equation as separate procedures, ask them to map each number in the equation onto a part of the bar.
If the multiplier is wrong, check against the bar: how many times the original length is the scaled bar? (4 to 12 is three times, so ×3.)
Confirm the child can explain why the operation is multiplication (equal-group scaling), not addition.
activities.rationale: The bar model exposes multiplicative/proportional structure and connects a situation to its equation, so scaling can be seen as both a bar and a multiplication equation. An OPTIONAL dragging tool where changing the number of equal parts updates both the bar and the × equation can make the correspondence concrete; the mapping can equally be done with a drawn bar and a written equation.
sourceClaims: The bar model exposes multiplicative/proportional structure and connects a situation to its equation, so scaling problems can be represented as both a bar and a multiplication equation.
MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
learnerActions: Represent a scaling situation (e.g. a recipe for 4 scaled to 12) as a bar model showing the equal parts.
Write the multiplication equation that matches the bar (here 4×3=12, a scale of ×3), and point to which part of the bar each number in the equation refers to.
If the scale changes, adjust the bar and update the equation together, explaining why the multiplier changes.
State what quantity each number represents before computing.
activities.intendedInsight: A bar model and a multiplication equation describe the same multiplicative/scaling structure; the bar and the symbols are two views of one relationship.

activities.title: Reading a line graph for meaning before choosing an operation
feedback: If the child adds two readings when a difference is wanted, ask: what quantity is each reading, and what is the question actually asking you to find?
If the child can compute but can't justify subtraction, have them describe the change in words first, then pick the matching operation.
Confirm the child names each reading's quantity before selecting an operation.
activities.rationale: Requiring the child to say what quantity each reading is before choosing an operation keeps symbols tied to their referents and counters number-grabbing. A difference between two readings calls for subtraction because of what the situation asks, not because the numbers are visible.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
learnerActions: On a line graph, name what quantity each point/reading represents before doing any arithmetic.
For a question asking the change or difference between two readings, state which operation the situation needs and why.
Translate the reading into an equation (e.g. a subtraction for a difference) and compute.
Explain why adding the two readings would not give the change.
activities.intendedInsight: Choose the operation from what the situation asks and what each reading means, not by grabbing whichever visible numbers are present.

activities.title: Argue it out: defend equivalence against a doubter
feedback: Accept any correct justification grounded in the shaded quantity and the per-hundred meaning; press for the grid or number-line evidence if the child only asserts 'they're equal'.
If the child agrees with the doubter, go back to the shaded region and the meaning of %.
This dialogue is for reasoning practice and should not be scored.
activities.rationale: Explaining why the forms are the same proportion and what each graph reading means is dialogic, and a doubting partner gives the child something concrete to argue against. This is a reasoning/talk activity, not an assessment; a dialogue can elicit explanation but does not by itself prove the child can construct a representation unaided.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner who claims '35% must be bigger than 0.35 — 35 versus nought-point-something!' by proving sameness on the grid.
Explain in your own words why 35/100, 0.35 and 35% are the same proportion.
When the partner reads a line graph aloud and proposes adding two values to find a change, say whether that is right and correct it, giving your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain and defend why the three forms are one quantity, and why an operation does or doesn't fit, shows understanding beyond rote conversion.

constraints: Show all three notations on ONE representation (a hundredths grid, or one number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below) so equivalence is seen as the same magnitude, not three conversion rules.
Ground percentage in 'parts per hundred' using the grid before introducing any conversion rule, so 35% is a quantity rather than a bare number.
At every step insist on 'what does each number represent?' and translate in every direction.

A static annotated grid or labelled bar model can illustrate equivalence but does not let the child vary the amount or interactively respond to the percentage misconception; treat it as a worked example / scaffold, not the full activity.

Match-the-equivalent exercises test recognition and can reward rote conversion; recognition alone does not elicit independent construction or explanation, so use them only as a warm-up, not as evidence the child can construct the translation or explain the shared magnitude.
The reasoning/argument dialogue is for eliciting explanation and should not be scored.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims are cited where they support the teaching principle (single-representation equivalence, bar-model-to-equation structure, MP2 meaning-of-quantities); citation does not establish that these specific activities were empirically tested or that any medium is superior to another.

The legacy entry asserted some comparative/absolute claims (e.g. a quiz tests recognition 'but not constructing', 3D 'conveys nothing better than a grid', a static image 'can't let the child vary the amount'). These have been softened to scoped scaffold limits; the genuine objective limit retained is that recognition-only matching does not elicit independent construction or explanation.

Arithmetic verified: 35% = 0.35 = 35/100 (thirty-five hundredths); 8 squares = 8/100 = 0.08 = 8%; the scaling example 'recipe for 4 scaled to 12' is ×3 because 4×3=12. The 'is 35% bigger than 0.35' hinge is sound — they are equal.

probeDeeper: 'Shade a different amount — say 8 squares. What are the fraction, the decimal and the percentage now, and why do they all match?'
'What does the little % sign actually mean? 35% of what?'
'Is 0.35 the same as 35%, or is one bigger? Prove it on the grid.'
'On this line graph, what quantity is each point? If I want the change between them, what do I do and why?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising all three name the SAME shaded quantity (thirty-five hundredths), explaining per cent as parts per hundred, and stating that 35% and 0.35 are the same amount — not that one is larger because '35 > 0.35'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction, decimal and percentage treated as three different things, not one magnitude — picks one as 'the' right label or can't relate them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the single hundredths grid / one number line with all three notations on the same region until equivalence is a fact of magnitude; reteach fraction–decimal–percentage as the same quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names only one form as correct, or converts by rote without seeing the shared shaded area; struggles to place all three at one point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Per cent not understood as parts per hundred: reads 35% as the number 35 (so 'bigger than 0.35') or as a meaningless decimal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to 'per cent = out of 100' on the grid, then connect to 35/100 and 0.35; reteach the meaning of the % symbol before any conversion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 35% > 0.35 'because 35 is bigger', or cannot say what the % refers to.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-grabbing off a line graph or bar model: reads values and combines them without asking which quantity or operation the situation needs (e.g. adds two readings when a difference is wanted).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist the child name each reading's quantity first, then choose the operation from the situation; reteach reading representations for meaning before computing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In a graph/scaling task the child pulls the visible numbers and applies an operation without mapping meaning; can't say why subtraction (not addition) gives the change.

responseLevels.gap: Picks one notation as the only right answer or says 35% is bigger than 0.35; treats the forms as separate.
responseLevels.full: Shows all three name the same shaded magnitude, explains per cent as parts per hundred, states 35% = 0.35, and reads graph/scaling representations for their quantities before choosing an operation — transferring the reasoning to a new amount unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the three forms are 'equal' by a remembered rule but can't ground it in the shaded quantity, or wavers on 35% vs 0.35, or maps FDP but grabs numbers on the graph without meaning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a hundred-square, 35 squares are shaded. One classmate says 'that shows 35/100', another says 'no, it's 0.35', another says 'it's 35%'. Who is right? Explain how these three are related, and show me on the grid. Then tell me: is 35% a bigger amount than 0.35, or the same?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds proportion-as-one-magnitude says all three are the same and 35% = 0.35; a child treating notations as separate quantities picks one 'right' answer or claims 35% is bigger. The last question is the hinge: '35 versus nought-point-something' tempts the notation-bound child into 'bigger', while a child who understands per-cent-as-per-hundred sees they coincide. Hard to answer right for the wrong reason — saying 'same' must be backed by the grid and the per-hundred meaning.
