topic.name: Fractions on a number line
topic.description: Understand and use place value for decimals, measures, and integers of any size; extend the number system to include all positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a single number line
evidence: Identify the value of any digit in numbers of any size including decimals
Place positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line
Use place value to compare and order numbers across the full number system
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} place a mix of numbers — like 3, −2, 0.5, −1.75, and ¼ — all on the same number line, in the right order?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of ANY size; extend the number system so all positive/negative integers, decimals and fractions sit on a single number line.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size' and 'order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions' on one line.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.6 (position integers and rationals on the number line, opposites) and 6.NS.C.7 (understand ordering of rational numbers).
• Operational details: Consolidate the ×10/÷10 place-value structure as UNBOUNDED in both directions — no largest, no smallest place — and unify previously separate representations (whole numbers, decimals, negatives, fractions) onto ONE number line. Stress that every number, however written, names a single point; the line is the common ground where mixed forms can be compared.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'State the value of the 7 in 4,700,000 and in 0.007.' Tier B: 'Place −3/4, 0.6, −2 and 1.25 on one number line.' Tier C: 'Explain why the place-value system has no largest and no smallest place.'
bestPractices: Present place value as a single unbounded ×10/÷10 structure — no largest or smallest place — rather than a table that stops at millions or thousandths
Unify whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions onto ONE number line so mixed forms share a common reference for comparison
Insist every representation (numeral, fraction, decimal) names a single POINT on the line
Convert between forms to a common representation (usually decimal or a common denominator) before comparing across types
Use magnitude/scale reasoning ('the value of a digit is its face value times its place') for numbers of any size
keyRepresentations: Single number line hosting integers, decimals, negatives and fractions together
Place-value chart extended arbitrarily far left and right of the decimal point
Zoomable number line to locate decimals/fractions between integers
Form-conversion cards (fraction ↔ decimal) feeding points onto the line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking place value 'runs out' at a largest place (millions) or smallest place (thousandths)
Treating whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions as living on separate scales rather than one line
Placing negatives as if their magnitude sets their order (−3/4 to the left of −2)
Assuming a fraction and its decimal (3/4 and 0.75) are different points rather than the same point
Comparing mixed forms by surface features (digit count) rather than converting to a common form

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: extend place value as an unbounded ×10/÷10 structure (no largest or smallest place) and unify whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions onto ONE number line, where every number — however written — names a single point. Learners locate and order mixed forms by position relative to zero and to integer landmarks, recognising that a fraction and its decimal (e.g. 3/4 and 0.75) are the SAME point, and that on a standard (left-to-right) line ordering follows leftmost-is-smallest across all number types.

activities.title: Many forms, one line
feedback: If a fraction is placed by its visible digits (e.g. 1/2 put near the 2), convert it to a decimal or locate it between integer landmarks: 1/2 = 0.5 sits halfway between 0 and 1, not near 2.
If negatives are ordered by magnitude (e.g. −3/4 placed left of −2), anchor zero: on a standard line every point further left is smaller, so −2 < −3/4 because −2 is further from zero on the left.
If 3/4 and 0.75 are placed at different points, convert 3/4 to 0.75 and confirm both describe three-quarters of the way from 0 to 1 — they are literally one point.
activities.rationale: Placing mixed representations on a single line forces a common measure of size and confronts the misconceptions that different number types live on separate scales and that notation digits dictate position. This supports ordering integers, decimals and fractions on one line.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
6.NS.C.6/C.7: position integers and rational numbers on the number line and understand ordering of rational numbers.
learnerActions: Draw a single number line and place each of these numbers on it: −3/4, 0.6, −2, and 1.25. Then, on a separate zoomed-out view using an appropriate scale, mark a large integer such as 4,700,000, noting that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs both views.
For each number, say in words where it sits relative to zero and to the nearest whole-number landmarks (e.g. '1.25 is a quarter of the way from 1 to 2').
Place 3/4 and 0.75 separately, then check that both land on exactly the same point; write one sentence explaining why they must coincide.

Write all the numbers in order from smallest to largest, treating 3/4 and 0.75 as one point, and justify the order using position on the line, not the digits (−2 < −3/4 < 0.6 < 3/4 = 0.75 < 1.25 < 4,700,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions all belong to one number line governed by a single ×10/÷10 structure; each names a single point and equivalent forms name the same point. On a standard (left-to-right) line, size is read as position (leftmost is smallest) across every type, even when very large and very small values must be shown at different scales.

activities.title: Zoom in — is there a smallest place?
feedback: If the line is treated as discrete ('the next number', only a few slots between landmarks), zoom one segment and mark finer divisions to show more and more numbers fit — any fraction or decimal has a place.
If the learner claims place value 'runs out' at thousandths or at millions, point to the column-naming continuing with each zoom: the pattern is ×10/÷10 repeated, with no final column.
activities.rationale: Progressive subdivision makes the unbounded ×10/÷10 place-value structure concrete, addressing the misconception that place value stops at a largest or smallest place; it also illustrates (informally) that the line keeps subdividing so any decimal or fraction has a place.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
learnerActions: Take the segment from 0 to 1 and subdivide it into tenths; label 0.6 among them.
Zoom into a tenth (e.g. between 0.6 and 0.7) and subdivide into hundredths; place a value such as 0.65.
Zoom again into hundredths and mark thousandths; keep a note of which place column you are in at each step (tenths → hundredths → thousandths…).
Argue in writing whether this subdividing ever stops, and state what that means for a 'smallest place' in the place-value system.
Repeat the reasoning outward: explain why there is likewise no largest place as the ×10 structure grows.
activities.intendedInsight: The ×10/÷10 place-value structure continues without end in both directions — there is no smallest place and no largest place. Informally, between any two points more numbers can always be found, so any decimal or fraction has a location between landmarks.

activities.title: Value of a digit at any scale
feedback: If only the face value (7) is given, prompt for the place: the 7 in 4,700,000 is 7 hundred-thousands = 700,000; the 7 in 0.007 is 7 thousandths = 0.007.
If columns are miscounted on the decimal side, count rightward from the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
activities.rationale: Magnitude/scale reasoning for digits of any size consolidates place value as a single unbounded structure rather than a table that stops at millions or thousandths.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
learnerActions: State the value of the 7 in 4,700,000 and the value of the 7 in 0.007.
For each, say which place column the 7 occupies and compute face value × place value.
Explain in one or two sentences why the same digit can represent vastly different amounts depending on its place.
Optional extension: explain to a partner (or in writing) why the place-value system has no largest and no smallest place.
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's value is its face value times its place value, and this scaling reasoning works for numbers of any size, large or small.

activities.title: Which is smaller, and why
feedback: Correct ordering: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75. −3 is smallest because it is furthest left of zero, regardless of number type.
If 1/2 is ranked below −3 ('it's less than one'), anchor zero: every negative lies left of every positive, so −3 < 1/2 whatever the digits suggest.
If 2.75 is ranked by '275', relocate it as three-quarters of the way from 2 to 3 and compare positions.
activities.rationale: This diagnostic comparison exposes ordering-by-magnitude-of-negatives and reading-by-digits, and the justification for '−3 smallest' reveals whether the learner reasons by position across types.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.6/C.7: position integers and rational numbers on the number line and understand ordering of rational numbers.
learnerActions: Place −3, 1/2 and 2.75 on one number line relative to zero and to each other.
Order them from smallest to largest.
Explain how you know −3 is the smallest, referring to its position rather than the size of the digit 3.
Name a number between 1/2 and 2.75, and then another number between those two, to show many values lie between any pair.
activities.intendedInsight: On a standard (left-to-right) number line, across all number types the leftmost position (furthest below zero) is smallest; a negative can be smaller than a small positive fraction even though its digit looks large. Informally, infinitely many numbers also lie between any two points.

constraints: Learners should construct placements and justifications themselves; multiple-choice or slider checks can consolidate the unified-line idea afterwards, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent placing, converting and justifying that evidences full understanding.

When comparing mixed forms, convert to a common representation (decimal or common denominator) or locate each between integer landmarks before ordering; do not compare by surface features such as digit count. Fractions remain comparable numbers; the common-reference requirement is about positioning represented portions consistently.

A static, annotated line showing several forms on one axis can illustrate the unification and is a useful scaffold, but it cannot be re-scaled by the learner, so pair it with hands-on subdividing/zooming when demonstrating that the structure is unbounded and that more numbers always fit between landmarks.

Treat large integers and sub-unit decimals at appropriate separate scales when a single drawn line cannot show both; the point is that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs each, so the unification is conceptual even when two views are used.
The number system here is one-dimensional, so a single line is the correct representation; avoid adding extra spatial dimensions that would misrepresent ordering.

'Leftmost is smallest' assumes the conventional left-to-right orientation of the number line; use that standard orientation and make it explicit rather than treating it as an intrinsic property of the numbers.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited standards were marked verified:false in the source and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source value-of-digit example checked: the 7 in 4,700,000 is 700,000 (7 hundred-thousands) and the 7 in 0.007 is 7 thousandths; both are internally consistent and retained.

Ordering checked: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75 and −2 < −3/4 < 0.6 < 1.25 < 4,700,000 are correct; the source's own stated misconception 'placing −3/4 left of −2' is correctly treated as an error to correct, not taught.

The subdividing/zoom demonstration illustrates (does not formally prove) the unbounded place-value structure and that numbers always lie between any two points; density is a true mathematical property but is not attributed to the cited standards, which support ordering and place value rather than density.
Optional interaction examples (zoomable/subdividing line, slider placement, snapping equivalent forms to one point, place-value read-out) are preserved as illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: Why is −3 to the left of 1/2 when 3 is bigger than a half?
How did you decide exactly where 2.75 goes between the whole numbers?
Is 1/2 the same point as 0.5 on this line? How do you know?
Name a number between 1/2 and 2.75 — and another between those two.
assess.correctAnswer: −3 sits three to the LEFT of zero; 1/2 halfway between 0 and 1; 2.75 three-quarters of the way from 2 to 3. Ordered: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75. −3 is smallest because it is furthest left / below zero, regardless of the type of number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude — argues 1/2 is the smallest 'because it's less than one', and −3 is not really small because 3 is a decent-sized number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor zero on the line; show every negative lies left of every positive, so −3 < any positive including 1/2, whatever the digits say.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/2 is the smallest, because it's less than one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 1/2 below −3, or is surprised −3 is least.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a fraction/decimal by its visible digits — places 1/2 near 2, or ranks 2.75 by '275'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert to a common frame (all as decimals, or all located between integer landmarks) so 1/2 = 0.5 lands between 0 and 1, not near 2.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/2 goes near the 2 on the line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Placement or ordering tracks a digit in the notation rather than the number's value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Consecutive-number thinking — believes there is a 'next' number and only a few values sit between landmarks, so a fraction has one fixed slot with gaps around it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Zoom a segment (0 to 1) and mark tenths, then hundredths, to show the line is dense — any decimal or fraction has a place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats the line as discrete, unsure where non-integers 'fit' or claims spots are 'taken'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place mixed types on one line; orders by digits or by magnitude of negatives.
responseLevels.full: Locates and orders integers, fractions and decimals on a single line by position relative to zero and to integer landmarks, and justifies size by leftmost-is-smallest across all types.
responseLevels.partial: Places and orders correctly when types are separated, but muddles when integers, fractions and decimals must be compared together, or reverts to magnitude for the negative.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On one number line you have to place −3, 1/2 and 2.75. Where does each go relative to zero and to each other — and how do you know −3 is the smallest?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Placing mixed representations on ONE line forces a common measure of size. A child with full place-value/number-system understanding orders across integers, fractions and decimals by position. A child who orders negatives by magnitude, or who cannot locate a fraction/decimal without a whole-number cue, is exposed — and the reason for '−3 smallest' is the tell.

topic.name: Fractions on a number line (age 11+)
topic.description: Order positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values including negative numbers and mixed representations
evidence: Order a mixed set of positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions
Use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ correctly in mathematical statements

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a mixed list like 2.5, −3, ¾, 0, and −0.5, can they put them in order from least to greatest using a number line if needed?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions on a number line; use =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values, including negatives and mixed representations.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.7 — understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers; write, interpret and explain statements of order (e.g. −3 > −7).
• Operational details: Order by POSITION on the number line (left = less), which handles negatives and mixed forms uniformly. Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) or place each on the line before applying symbols. Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ alongside <, >, = and distinguish strict from inclusive. Interpret order statements in context ('−3 > −7 means −3°C is warmer').
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'True or false: −5 < −2.' Tier B: 'Order 0.75, 3/4, −0.8, 7/10.' Tier C: 'Write a single statement using ≤ that is true for all of 2, 2.0, 4/2.'
bestPractices: Order by position on the number line (leftmost is least) so negatives and mixed forms are handled by one rule, not sign-specific tricks
Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) before comparing, and verify by placing on the line
Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ explicitly alongside <, >, = and contrast strict (<) with inclusive (≤)
Read comparison statements aloud in context ('−3 is greater than −7 because it is warmer / further right')
Bait the 'bigger digit = bigger value' error deliberately with negatives (−5 vs −2) and unequal-length decimals
keyRepresentations: Number line as the arbiter of order (left → right = least → greatest)
Common-form conversion (3/4 → 0.75) to compare across representations
Symbol cards =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ placed between two values
Sorting track / ordering slots that snap items into line positions
commonMisconceptions: Ordering negatives by magnitude (−5 placed as greater than −2)
Comparing fractions and decimals by surface features instead of converting to a common form
Confusing < and > direction (the 'alligator eats the bigger' heuristic misapplied)
Treating ≤/≥ as identical to </> and missing the equality case
Assuming a longer decimal or larger denominator is automatically larger/smaller

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions on a single number line (leftmost = least), and use =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values, including negatives and mixed representations. The core principle is that POSITION on the line — not sign, digit count, or denominator size — is the single rule that orders every kind of number, and that equal values (e.g. 0.75 and 3/4) sit at the same point, so neither < nor > holds between them; = is the precise relation, and ≤ and ≥ are also true. The primary activity is a hands-on positional sort of mixed-form cards with a common-form conversion check; supporting activities consolidate symbol conventions, interrogate wrong orderings, and read statements in context.

activities.title: Drop mixed-form numbers onto one number line and choose the symbol between neighbours
feedback: If negatives are ordered by magnitude (e.g. −1.5 written as less than −2, or −2 placed to the right of −1.5): anchor on position — further left = smaller; −2 is left of −1.5, so −2 < −1.5. Reason from where it sits, not from digit size.
If 0.75 and 3/4 are placed at different points or not joined by '=': convert one form to the other (3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) and land both on the same point, then compare.
If ≤ is used where = or < is meant, or the inequality opens toward the smaller value: read the statement aloud in words — the open side faces the larger value, and ≤ means 'less than OR equal'.

If a longer decimal or larger denominator is assumed automatically larger: place both on the line to test — e.g. 0.8 vs 0.75, where the shorter decimal 0.8 is the larger value, so more digits does not mean larger. (For negatives the extra wrinkle is that −0.8 < −0.75.)
activities.rationale: Ordering mixed forms is decided by position, so letting the learner perform the sort, convert to a common form to check, and attach symbols between neighbours makes the one positional rule visible and surfaces the equal-values-coincide case. Dragging, the decimal-conversion toggle, and stacking of coincident cards are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms, and their comparative effectiveness over other media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions and use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
learnerActions: Take a set of mixed cards — 0.75, 3/4, −0.8, −0.75, 7/10, −2, −1.5, 1/2 — and place each at its correct position on a shared number line.
Use a 'show as decimal' conversion (e.g. 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) to check cross-form values before placing them.
Notice that 0.75 and 3/4 land on the IDENTICAL point and coincide there.
Between each adjacent pair of placed cards, select a symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ and justify the choice.
Confirm that between the two coincident cards the strict symbols < and > (and ≠) are false; = is the most precise choice, and the inclusive ≤ and ≥ are also true because they allow equality.
Deliberately test the surprise case: see that −0.8 sits LEFT of −0.75, so −0.8 is smaller, even though 0.8 > 0.75 for positives — defeating the 'bigger magnitude wins' instinct for negatives.
activities.intendedInsight: Position on the number line (left = less) is a single rule that orders integers, decimals, fractions, positives and negatives uniformly; equal values coincide, so < and > cannot hold between them, while = (and the inclusive ≤, ≥) are true.

activities.title: Consolidate the symbol conventions with true/false and ordering checks
feedback: For '−5 < −2': it is TRUE because −5 is further left on the line than −2.
If ≤ and < are treated as identical: recall ≤ also holds when the two values are equal, so a statement using ≤ can be true for equal values like 2, 2.0 and 4/2 (all equal to 2).
If a sequence mis-ranks negatives or equal forms: re-place the items on a line to check before fixing the symbols.
activities.rationale: Recognition and selection items are a useful consolidation companion for the symbol conventions, best used after the positional meaning is established. These items check and reinforce convention use; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an ordering.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions and use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
learnerActions: Judge true/false statements such as '−5 < −2' and explain the reasoning from position.
Match order statements to the correct symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
Order a mixed-form set smallest to largest as a sequence.
Write a single statement using ≤ that is true for all of 2, 2.0, 4/2.
activities.intendedInsight: Order statements and symbol conventions (including strict vs inclusive) can be applied fluently once positional ordering is understood.

activities.title: Interrogate and repair a wrong ordering in discussion or context
feedback: If the learner cannot say why −5 belongs left of −2: tie '−5 < −2' to temperature — −5°C is colder, so smaller, and sits further left.

If strict and inclusive are confused: have them state in words whether equality is possible for the pair; < needs the values to be different, while ≤ is true both when the first is smaller and when they are equal, so ≤ is the natural choice when equality could hold.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can interrogate a wrong ordering and surface reasoning, and reading statements in context ('warmer / further right') supports interpretation of order statements such as −3 > −7. This complements, rather than replaces, performing the positional sort.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7: understand ordering of rational numbers and write/interpret statements of order such as −3 > −7.
learnerActions: Examine a given ordering that mis-ranks negatives (e.g. −5 placed to the right of −2) and explain why it is wrong, referring to position.
Read comparison statements aloud in context, e.g. '−3 > −7 means −3°C is warmer / further right than −7°C'.
Decide when ≤ would be used instead of < between two values, and say why.
State an inference about relative size from a placement, e.g. which of −2 and −1.5 is smaller and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating WHY an ordering is right or wrong — in words and in real contexts like temperature — reinforces positional reasoning and distinguishes strict from inclusive comparison.

constraints: Order by POSITION on the number line (leftmost is least) so negatives and mixed forms are handled by one rule rather than sign-specific tricks.
Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) before comparing, and verify by placing on the line.
Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ explicitly alongside <, >, = and contrast strict (<) with inclusive (≤), making the equality case explicit.

Deliberately bait the 'bigger digit = bigger value' error two ways: with negatives (−5 vs −2, where the larger-magnitude number is smaller; and −0.8 vs −0.75, where −0.8 < −0.75) and with unequal-length positive decimals (0.8 vs 0.75, where the shorter decimal is larger) so the misconception is confronted directly rather than accidentally confirmed.
Recognition/selection items (true/false, matching) check convention use but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an ordering; use the hands-on positional sort for that.

A static labelled line with forms placed and symbols shown can illustrate a completed ordering but does not let the learner perform the sort or select symbols with feedback; it is a worked-example scaffold, not the full task.

Position-order for this objective is represented along a single line (one dimension), so a third spatial dimension is not needed here; this is a scoped observation about representing order, not a general claim that 3D 'adds nothing'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Both cited sources carry verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Math check: −0.8 < −0.75 (−0.8 is further from zero on the negative side, hence further left); −2 < −1.5; 0.75 = 3/4; 1/2 = 0.5; 7/10 = 0.7. Full order of the 8-card activity set: −2 < −1.5 < −0.8 < −0.75 < 1/2 < 7/10 < 3/4 = 0.75. The smaller 5-item diagnostic answer −2 < −1.5 < 1/2 < 3/4 = 0.75 is consistent for its own set.

Original-row inconsistency: the recommendation names −0.75 as the surprise neighbour but never lists it among the cards (0.75, 3/4, −0.8, 7/10, −2). This was corrected by including both −0.8 and −0.75 so the intended comparison is actually available; the original wording is retained only as an uncertainty note.
The 'alligator eats the bigger' heuristic is listed as a common misconception in the source; it is reframed here as reading the open side as facing the larger value, rather than taught as a mnemonic.

Efficacy/necessity of the hands-on track relative to the consolidation checks, static image or dialogue is not established by the standards documents, which support the objective rather than any medium's superiority.

probeDeeper: Is 0.75 the same as 3/4? Convert one to check, then place both.
On the line, which is further left, −2 or −1.5 — and so which is smaller?
Put the correct symbol between −1.5 and −2, and say why.
When would you use ≤ instead of < between two of these?

errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor on the number line: further left = smaller. −2 is left of −1.5, so −2 < −1.5. Reason from position.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the line −2 sits nearer zero than −1.5, or the inequality between them is reversed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot compare across representations: treats 0.75 and 3/4 as different sizes, or ranks 0.75 > 3/4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert one form to the other (3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) and land both on the same point; then compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 0.75 and 3/4 are placed at different points, or = is not chosen between them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misuses the strict vs inclusive symbols, or reverses < / >
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read each statement aloud as words; the open side faces the larger value, and ≤ means 'less than OR equal'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses ≤ where = or < is meant, or opens the inequality toward the smaller value.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a mixed set: −2, 0.75, 3/4, −1.5, 1/2. Say: 'Place these on a number line and order them smallest to largest. Then put the right symbol between 0.75 and 3/4, and between −1.5 and −2.'

Placing them on ONE line and choosing = vs <,> reveals whether the child translates between forms and reasons about negative position rather than digit size.

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 6 strawberries and eats half of them, can they write that as "1/2 of 6 = 3" — and explain why 2/4 and 1/2 are the same amount?

pedagogy.summary: Writing simple fractions of quantities (1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognising the first equivalence: 2/4 = 1/2. Equivalence means two differently-written fractions name the SAME amount (the same-sized piece, cut into a different number of parts). This is the child's first encounter with the idea that a fraction has many names, and the natural place to confront the whole-number bias that '2/4 must be more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger'.
bestPractices: Establish equivalence by overlaying identical wholes cut two ways (two quarters exactly cover one half)
Derive equivalence from sharing (four pizzas among eight children = 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2 - IES)
Write the fraction sentence alongside the model (1/2 of 6 = 3) so notation records a known amount
Confront the 'bigger numbers = more' intuition head-on with a predict-then-check comparison
Ask for more than one name for the same amount to normalise many-names-one-value
keyRepresentations: Two identical bars, one halved and one quartered, with two quarters overlaid on one half
A fraction wall aligning 1/2 with 2/4
A set of 6 shared into two equal groups (1/2 of 6 = 3)
Number line with 1/2 and 2/4 landing on the same point
commonMisconceptions: 2/4 is more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger (whole-number bias)
Two fractions written with different numbers cannot name the same amount (no concept of equivalence)
Errors computing a unit fraction of a quantity (1/2 of 6) by not sharing equally

learn.summary: Year 2 children (ages 6-7) write simple fractions of quantities (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and meet their first fraction equivalence: 2/4 = 1/2. Equivalence means two differently-written fractions name the same amount - the same-sized piece, cut into a different number of parts. This is the natural place to confront the whole-number bias that '2/4 must be more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger'. The core teaching move is predict-then-check: the child predicts a comparison, then overlays two quarters onto one half to see them coincide exactly.

activities.title: Overlay check: proving 1/2 = 2/4 by covering
feedback: If the child predicts 2/4 is more because '2 pieces is more than 1' or 'the numbers are bigger', let them do the overlay: the two quarters cover the half exactly, so the amounts are equal despite the larger numbers.
If the pieces don't line up, check that both bars were the same size to start and that each bar was cut into equal pieces; re-cut and overlay again.
Reinforce correct work: 'You found two names for the same amount - 1/2 and 2/4 are equal.'
When they find a further equivalent such as 3/6, confirm that it too covers one half, so the same amount can have many names.
activities.rationale: Overlaying identical wholes cut two ways lets the child see directly that two quarters coincide with one half. Starting from a prediction makes the whole-number bias explicit before it is contradicted. Using identical-sized wholes removes any 'it depends on the bar' escape, keeping attention on the fractions themselves.
sourceClaims: Children view fractions with larger denominators/numbers as larger (whole-number bias), which obstructs seeing 2/4 = 1/2
Year 2 pupils write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
learnerActions: Take two identical chocolate bars (or paper strips of the same length). Cut one into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4 equal pieces.
Before moving anything, predict and say aloud: are 2 pieces from the four-piece bar MORE, LESS, or the SAME as 1 piece from the two-piece bar? Give your reason.
Place the two quarter-pieces exactly on top of the one half-piece and check whether they cover it with nothing left over and no overlap.
Write the result as a fraction sentence: 1/2 = 2/4, and say in words 'the same amount, cut into a different number of parts'.
Find at least one more name for the same amount (for example cut another identical bar into 6 and check that 3/6 also covers one half).
activities.intendedInsight: Two quarters cover exactly one half, so 2/4 and 1/2 name the same amount even though 2/4 uses bigger numbers. A fraction has many names for one value. The prediction step surfaces the 'bigger numbers = more' intuition so the overlay can confront it directly.

activities.title: Equal sharing: deriving equivalent fractions
feedback: If the child treats 4/8 and 1/2 as different amounts, lay the shares side by side so they see each child's portion is identical.
Confirm when they connect the sharing result to equivalence: 'Each child gets half a pizza - that's why 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2.'
activities.rationale: Equal-sharing scenarios with common factors give a meaningful route into equivalence, complementing the overlay model.
sourceClaims: Equivalence can be developed from equal-sharing scenarios with common factors (e.g. four pizzas among eight children give 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2)
learnerActions: Share 4 pizzas equally among 8 children by drawing or using counters; work out how much each child gets.
Write the share each child receives as a fraction (4/8), then show by grouping that this is also 2/4 and 1/2.
Explain in your own words why 4/8, 2/4 and 1/2 all describe the same share.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions arise naturally from equal sharing: the same real share can be written with different numbers, and these names are equal.

activities.title: Finding a fraction of a quantity by equal sharing
feedback: If the child gives a wrong value for 1/2 of 6, check that the counters were shared into two EQUAL groups before counting one group.
If the child struggles to make four equal groups from 6 whole counters, point back to the equivalence 2/4 = 1/2 so they can compute 1/2 of 6 = 3 instead; both routes give 3.
Confirm correct sentences: 'Half of 6 is 3, and because 2/4 is the same as 1/2, 2/4 of 6 is also 3.'
activities.rationale: Grounding 'fraction of a quantity' in equal sharing addresses the error of not dividing into equal groups and links computation back to the written notation. The final answer 2/4 of 6 = 3 is a whole number, but making four equal groups of whole counters is awkward (6 shared four ways is 1.5 each), so routing through the known equivalence 2/4 = 1/2 keeps young learners on whole-counter sharing while reinforcing why equivalent fractions give equal results.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
learnerActions: Take a set of 6 counters. Share them into 2 equal groups and count one group to find 1/2 of 6.
Write the sentence 1/2 of 6 = 3 next to your groups.
Try 1/2 of 10 by sharing 10 into 2 equal groups, and write 1/2 of 10 = 5.

Now find 2/4 of 6. Sharing 6 counters into 4 equal groups does not give whole counters (each group would be one and a half), so use the equivalence 2/4 = 1/2: since 1/2 of 6 = 3, we know 2/4 of 6 is also 3.
activities.intendedInsight: A unit fraction of a quantity is found by sharing equally into the number of parts named by the denominator and taking one group. Because 2/4 = 1/2, taking 2/4 of a quantity gives the same result as taking 1/2 of it.

activities.title: Many names on one point: number line and matching
feedback: If the fractions land on different points, check the line was divided into equal parts; re-measure.
If the child matches by digit size rather than value, return to the overlay or number line to show the true equal pairs.
Confirm: 'Both sit on the same point, so 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount.'
activities.rationale: A number-line view and matching/recognition tasks consolidate equivalence after the hands-on overlay. Matching and choosing answers check recognition of equivalent pairs; they do not by themselves show the child can construct or explain an equivalence, so pair them with the explaining and overlay work.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
learnerActions: Mark 0 and 1 at the ends of a strip or line. Fold or measure to place 1/2, then divide the same line into quarters and place 2/4.
Check that 1/2 and 2/4 land on exactly the same point.
Match written fractions to their equal partners (for example pair 1/2 with 2/4), explaining why each pair is equal and why a 'bigger numbers' pairing would be wrong.
Say or write a short justification: 'They are at the same point, so they are the same amount.'
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same position on the number line, giving another way to see that different names can mean one value. Matching tasks let the child rehearse recognising equivalent pairs and rejecting 'bigger-number' traps.

constraints: Use identical-sized wholes (same-length bars or strips) when demonstrating equivalence by overlay; different-sized wholes let the child escape with 'it depends on the bar' and break the comparison. This common-whole requirement applies to comparing the represented portions; as numbers, 1/2 and 2/4 remain comparable (indeed equal).
Every whole must be cut into EQUAL parts before counting or sharing; unequal parts invalidate both the fraction-of-a-quantity work and the overlay.

Matching and multiple-choice tasks assess recognition of equivalent pairs; they do not elicit independent construction or explanation, so include tasks where the child builds a model and states why in words.

A printed fraction wall or equivalence poster is a useful reference but is fixed: the child cannot test the overlay on it. Pair reference images with an activity where the child actually cuts and overlays pieces.
Keep the prediction step before the check: recording the child's reason first is what makes the whole-number bias visible and the overturning meaningful.

When a quantity does not share cleanly into the number of groups named by a denominator (e.g. sharing 6 whole counters into four equal groups), route the task through an equivalent unit fraction (2/4 of 6 via 1/2 of 6) rather than forcing fractional counters.

All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The original probeDeeper prompt '1/2 of 6 is 3 - what is 2/4 of 6?' invites forming four equal groups of 6, which does not give whole counters (6 shared four ways is 1.5 each). The activity now computes 2/4 of 6 via the equivalence 2/4 = 1/2, giving 3. The final value (3) is correct either way; only the intermediate whole-counter grouping is awkward. Original phrasing retained here for reviewer awareness.
Arithmetic checks: 1/2 of 6 = 3 and 1/2 of 10 = 5 are correct; 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2 and 3/6 = 1/2 are correct equivalences; 2/4 of 6 = 3.

The equal-sharing example (4 pizzas among 8 children) and whole-number-bias framing come from the IES/WWC guide claims; efficacy or necessity of any one representation is not asserted beyond what those claims state.

Independent re-audit found no new learner-facing errors, contradictions, or unsupported categorical modality claims; removed catalogue rankings and the '3D adds nothing'/'dialogue is poor' dismissals were not reintroduced.

assess.poeTask: Show two identical chocolate bars. Ask the child to predict and justify: is 2 pieces from the four-piece bar MORE, LESS, or the SAME as 1 piece from the two-piece bar? Record the reason. Then place the two quarter-pieces exactly on top of the one half-piece; observe they cover it exactly. The pre-observation reason is diagnostic - a 'bigger numbers / more pieces' justification reveals the whole-number bias that the overlay then contradicts (2/4 = 1/2).
probeDeeper: Can you find another fraction that is the same amount as 1/2?
Is 2/4 always equal to 1/2, even for a bigger bar?
1/2 of 6 is 3 - what is 2/4 of 6?
Why can two fractions that look different be the same amount?
assess.correctAnswer: The same amount. 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent - they name the same-sized piece, just cut into a different number of parts. Two quarters cover exactly one half. (Tier 2: 1/2 = 2/4.)

errorPatterns.pattern: 2/4 is more than 1/2 - 'two pieces is more than one', or 'the numbers are bigger' (whole-number bias)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Predict-then-overlay two quarters onto one half (see poeTask); they coincide, so the amounts are equal.
errorPatterns.distractor: The second one - 2/4 is more than 1/2 because 2 is more than 1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the four-piece bar as more and justifies by piece-count or digit size

errorPatterns.pattern: Two fractions written with different numbers cannot be the same amount - no concept of equivalence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Same amount, different name: overlay the pieces and show one point on a number line; collect other names for 1/2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists 1/2 and 2/4 must differ because they are written differently

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot compute a unit fraction of a quantity (e.g. 1/2 of 6) reliably
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share 6 into two equal groups; write 1/2 of 6 = 3 alongside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a wrong value for 1/2 of 6 by not sharing into two equal groups

responseLevels.gap: Says 2/4 and 1/2 differ because the numbers differ, or picks 2/4 as more; no equivalence idea.
responseLevels.full: Recognises 2/4 = 1/2 as the same amount with different names, explains it with a model, computes unit fractions of quantities, and finds or tests a further equivalent (e.g. 3/6).
responseLevels.partial: Accepts 2/4 = 1/2 when shown a diagram but cannot generate another equivalent name or explain why, or cannot compute 1/2 of a quantity.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two identical chocolate bars. One is cut into 2 equal pieces and you take 1 piece; the other is cut into 4 equal pieces and you take 2 pieces. Ask: 'Do you have the same amount of chocolate, more, or less? How do you know?' Then ask: 'So what can you say about the fractions 1/2 and 2/4?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-bias child says the 2/4 bar is more 'because 2 pieces / bigger numbers', giving a clear wrong reason; a child with the equivalence idea says 'the same' and names 1/2 and 2/4 as equal. Identical bars remove any 'depends on the bar' escape, so the judgement is purely about the fractions.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Unit fractions
topic.description: Recognise, find, and write fractions of a discrete set of objects: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators
evidence: Find 1/4 of 12 objects by dividing into 4 equal groups
Find 3/4 of 12 objects
Write the fraction of a set that is shaded or selected
topic.assessmentPrompt: If there are 15 books on a shelf, can {{name}} work out how many two-thirds of them is — and check by grouping the books into three equal piles?

pedagogy.summary: Finding a fraction of a discrete SET treats the whole set as the '1': the denominator says how many EQUAL GROUPS to share the objects into, and the numerator says how many of those groups to take. So 1/4 of 12 means share 12 into 4 equal groups of 3 and take one group (3), and 3/4 of 12 means take three of those groups (9). Because the whole is the set, the SAME fraction gives a DIFFERENT count for a different-sized set (1/4 of 12 is 3, but 1/4 of 8 is 2).
bestPractices: Physically share the objects into 'denominator' equal groups first, then take 'numerator' groups — grounding the fraction in equal sharing/division
Stress that the whole is the whole SET, so 1/4 of a set is a number of objects, not the digit 4
Distinguish the numerator's job (how many groups to take) from the denominator's (how many groups to make), especially for non-unit fractions like 3/4
When naming the fraction of a set that is coloured, count coloured objects against the WHOLE set (part-to-whole, 3/12), not against the uncoloured ones (part-to-part, 3/9)
Vary the set size so children see 1/4 is a relationship, not a fixed number of things
keyRepresentations: Counters shared into equal groups (12 → four groups of 3)
Array / grouping diagram
Bar model of the set partitioned into b parts with a shaded
Double number line (objects ↔ fraction of the set)
commonMisconceptions: Takes the denominator as the answer: 1/4 of 12 is '4' because the fraction has a 4
For a non-unit fraction, finds 1/4 (=3) and stops, giving 3 for 3/4 instead of 9
Names a coloured set part-to-part (3 coloured, 9 not → 3/9) instead of part-to-whole (3/12)
Divides by the numerator instead of the denominator

learn.summary: Teaches fractions of a discrete set by treating the whole SET as the '1': the denominator tells how many equal groups to share the objects into, and the numerator tells how many groups to take. 1/4 of 12 means share 12 into 4 equal groups of 3 and take one group (3); 3/4 of 12 means take three groups (9). Because the whole is the set, the same fraction gives a different count for a different-sized set (1/4 of 12 = 3, but 1/4 of 8 = 2). Also targets naming a coloured part part-to-whole (3/12), not part-to-part (3/9).

activities.title: Share the set into equal groups, then take some
feedback: If the child grabs 4 counters for 1/4, share the 12 into 4 equal groups on the tray; one group (3 counters) is 1/4 — the 4 counts the GROUPS, not the objects.
If the child gives 3 for 3/4, ask how many of the four groups 3/4 wants — three of them — and count 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
When the set changes from 12 counters to 8 and is re-shared, point out each ring now holds 2: the same fraction 1/4 gives a different amount because the whole set has changed.
activities.rationale: Grounding the fraction in physically sharing the set into equal groups and then taking groups makes the distinct jobs of numerator and denominator visible, and varying the set size directly confronts the 'fraction = fixed number' and 'denominator = answer' misconceptions. Dragging counters into rings, a live set-size control, and a '3/4 of 12 = 9' readout are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; paper rings and dealt counters achieve the same. An array/grouping diagram, a bar model of the set partitioned into equal parts with some shaded, or a double number line (objects ↔ fraction of the set) are alternative representations of the same equal sharing.
sourceClaims: A unit fraction 1/b is the quantity formed by one part when the whole is partitioned into b equal parts, and a/b is a parts of that size; fractions are grounded in equal partitioning/sharing.

Year 3 pupils must 'recognise, find and write fractions of a discrete set of objects: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators', and Year 2 non-statutory guidance connects unit fractions of a set to equal sharing and grouping and to 'unit fractions as a division of a quantity' — grounding the 'share the set into denominator equal groups, take numerator groups' method.

NCETM's KS1 fractions guidance teaches the part-whole stem sentence 'the whole is divided into __ equal parts and we have __ of them', and cautions that with sets of objects teachers should 'keep the focus on visually dividing them into equal parts, rather than saying, for example, "we have eight strawberries, so one-quarter of the strawberries is two"', and that children should read the name ('one-quarter') not 'one-over-four' — directly targeting the denominator-as-count reading and the 'out of' part-to-part naming this record assesses.
learnerActions: Start with 12 counters and the request 'show me 1/4'. Set the denominator to 4 and form four group-rings (or draw four rings/circles on paper).
Deal the 12 counters out one at a time so each ring holds an equal share — 3 each. If any group is unequal, keep dealing until they match.
Take one group for 1/4: say and record '1/4 of 12 = 3'.
For 3/4, light up / shade / move three of the four groups and count 3 + 3 + 3 = 9; record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Change the set size: re-share 8 counters into four equal groups and see each group is now 2, so 1/4 of 8 = 2. Compare with 1/4 of 12 = 3.
State in words why 1/4 means making 4 equal groups rather than just taking 4 counters.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole is the whole SET; the denominator counts the equal groups to make and the numerator counts the groups to take. The same fraction names a different quantity when the set changes, so a fraction is a relationship, not a fixed number of objects.

activities.title: Name the coloured fraction of a set — part to whole
feedback: If the child writes 3/9, point out they compared coloured to uncoloured; count the coloured against the WHOLE set (all 12): 3 out of 12 = 3/12. The denominator is the whole, not the leftover.
Reinforce reading the name aloud ('three twelfths') to avoid treating the digits as a count.
activities.rationale: Comparing the coloured part to the whole set directly addresses the part-to-part naming error (3/9), reinforcing that the denominator represents the whole. A mode that shows a coloured set and corrects part-to-part attempts, or a selection item offering 3/12 versus 3/9, can make this concrete during practice.
sourceClaims: NCETM's KS1 fractions guidance teaches the part-whole stem sentence 'the whole is divided into __ equal parts and we have __ of them', and cautions that with sets of objects teachers should 'keep the focus on visually dividing them into equal parts, rather than saying, for example, "we have eight strawberries, so one-quarter of the strawberries is two"', and that children should read the name ('one-quarter') not 'one-over-four' — directly targeting the denominator-as-count reading and the 'out of' part-to-part naming this record assesses.
learnerActions: Look at a set of 12 counters with 3 coloured. Decide what fraction is coloured.
Count the coloured objects (3) and then count the WHOLE set (all 12), not the uncoloured ones.
Write the fraction as coloured-over-whole: 3/12.
Explain why it is 3/12 and not 3/9: the denominator is the whole set, not the leftover uncoloured counters.
Say the fraction by name ('three twelfths') rather than 'three over twelve'.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming a fraction of a set is part-to-whole: compare the coloured objects to the whole set, not to the uncoloured remainder.

activities.title: Predict before you re-share
feedback: A prediction of 'same 3' signals the fixed-count belief; share the 8 and let the observed 2 do the correcting, then discuss why the answer changed.
If the child cites 'the digit 4' as the answer for 1/4, re-share into 4 groups and show one group is 3 — the 4 counts the groups.
If 3/4 of 12 is given as 3, ask them to take three of the four groups of 3 and total 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 (for 8 counters, three groups of 2 make 6).
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain sequence makes the misconception visible and lets the physical outcome, not the teacher, refute it, with the correction resting on the equal-sharing grounding of the fraction. The follow-up 'why 4 groups not 4 counters' question separates grouping by rote from genuine understanding of the denominator's role.
sourceClaims: A unit fraction 1/b is the quantity formed by one part when the whole is partitioned into b equal parts, and a/b is a parts of that size; fractions are grounded in equal partitioning/sharing.
learnerActions: Share 12 counters and establish that 1/4 of 12 is 3.
BEFORE sharing again, predict: 'What will 1/4 of these 8 counters be — the same 3, or different?' Give a reason.
Now share the 8 into four equal groups — 2 each — and compare the observed 2 with the prediction.
Answer follow-up prompts: Is someone right that '1/4 of 12 is 4 because there is a 4 in the fraction'? For 3/4 of 12, how many of the four groups of 3 do you take, and why three?
Explain in your own words why 1/4 means making 4 equal groups, not just taking 4 counters.
activities.intendedInsight: A child who thinks a fraction names a fixed number predicts 3 for 1/4 of 8; sharing reveals 2, refuting the 'fixed count' idea and showing 1/4 is a relationship to whatever the whole set is.

constraints: Choose set sizes that divide evenly by the denominator so sharing yields equal whole-number groups (e.g. 12 and 8 for quarters); keep denominators small as required for this age.

A static grouped-set picture with tap-to-reveal (e.g. 'one group = 1/4 = 3 counters') can serve as a reference aid, but it does not let the child do the sharing or vary the set size, so it is a scaffold rather than the main activity.

Recognition-only or selection items can check the result without requiring the child to construct the groups or explain the reasoning: a '1/4 of 12' item with answer options such as 3, 4 and 48 surfaces the denominator-as-count error (4) and a multiply slip (48), while a separate 'what fraction is coloured?' item offering 3/12 versus 3/9 surfaces the part-to-part naming error.

Keep the focus on visually dividing the set into equal parts; avoid phrasing that treats the answer as a fact to recall ('eight strawberries, so a quarter is two') rather than the result of equal sharing.
Encourage reading fraction names ('one-quarter', 'three twelfths') rather than 'one-over-four', which can feed the digit-as-count error.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original flagged 3D/depth and in-role conversation as 'poor fit' with rationales like 'depth adds nothing' and insight 'comes from sharing, not dialogue'. These are reframed as scoping notes rather than universal laws: the grouping/quantity focus means a 2D sharing manipulation or paper materials fit the objective well, without asserting other media can never contribute.
Arithmetic checked: 1/4 of 12 = 3, 3/4 of 12 = 9 (3+3+3), 1/4 of 8 = 2; coloured 3 of 12 = 3/12, not 3/9. All consistent across pedagogy, assessment, and recommendation fields.

The '48' answer option for '1/4 of 12' presumably represents multiplying (12×4) rather than dividing; it is retained only as a plausible wrong option, never a valid answer, but it is worth confirming it matches an intended error pattern during review.

Array/grouping diagrams, a bar model of the partitioned set, and a double number line are carried over from the original representations as optional alternatives; their relative effectiveness here is untested.

assess.poeTask: Share 12 counters and establish that 1/4 of 12 is 3. Then, BEFORE sharing again, ask: 'What will 1/4 of these 8 counters be — the same 3, or different?' Have the child predict and give a reason. A child who believes a fraction names a fixed number of objects predicts 3; a child who understands the set is the whole predicts fewer. Then share the 8 into four groups — 2 each — and the observed 2 refutes the 'fixed count' idea, showing 1/4 is a relationship to whatever the whole set is.
probeDeeper: If 1/4 of 12 is 3, what is 1/4 of 8 — the same or different? Why?
Here are 12 counters with 3 coloured — what fraction is coloured?
Someone says 1/4 of 12 is 4 because there is a 4 in the fraction — are they right? Why not?
For 3/4, how many of your four groups do you take, and why three?
assess.correctAnswer: 1/4 of 12 = 3 (share into 4 equal groups of 3, take one group); 3/4 of 12 = 9 (take three of the four groups). The denominator 4 says how many equal groups to make; the numerator says how many groups to take — 4 is the number of groups, not the number of counters.

errorPatterns.pattern: Takes the denominator as the answer — grabs 4 counters for 1/4 'because there's a 4 in the fraction'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share the 12 into 4 equal groups on the tray; one group (3 counters) is 1/4. The 4 counts the GROUPS, not the objects.
errorPatterns.distractor: 4 counters (because the fraction has a 4 in it)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Selects 4 counters for 1/4 rather than sharing into 4 groups; tier-2 reason cites the digit

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 3/4 the same as 1/4 — finds one group (3) and stops, giving 3 for 3/4 instead of 9
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask how many of the four groups 3/4 wants — three of them — and count 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 3 for 3/4; does not take three of the four groups; cannot say the numerator means 'how many groups to take'

errorPatterns.pattern: Names a coloured set part-to-part — 3 coloured and 9 not, so writes 3/9 instead of 3/12
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the coloured against the WHOLE set (all 12): 3 out of 12 = 3/12. The denominator is the whole, not the leftover.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 'what fraction is coloured?' probe, compares coloured to uncoloured rather than to the whole set

responseLevels.gap: Takes 4 counters for 1/4 (denominator as count), gives 3 for 3/4, or writes 3/9 for a coloured set; no sense of the whole set shared into equal groups.
responseLevels.full: Finds 1/4 (=3) and 3/4 (=9) by grouping, explains denominator = number of equal groups and numerator = groups taken, recognises 1/4 of a different set gives a different count, and names a coloured set part-to-whole.
responseLevels.partial: Finds 1/4 of 12 = 3 by making 4 groups, but stumbles on 3/4 (forgets to take three groups) or cannot explain why it is 4 groups not 4 objects, or wobbles when the set size changes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 12 counters. Show me 1/4 of them, and then 3/4 of them. Then tell me: why does finding 1/4 mean making 4 equal groups, rather than just taking 4 counters?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Tier 1 (show 1/4 and 3/4) can be reached by grouping. Tier 2 — why 4 groups and not 4 counters — is where understanding shows. A child who reads the denominator as a count takes 4 counters for 1/4; a child who treats 3/4 like 1/4 gives 3 for 3/4; a secure child shares into equal groups and explains the denominator's role. Reasoning correctly and reasoning wrongly give visibly different actions and different tier-2 answers.
