pedagogy.summary: This is the iteration idea: a/b is built by counting copies of the unit fraction 1/b — 3/5 is 'three one-fifths', 7/4 is 'seven one-quarters'. It reframes a fraction from a static shaded region into a COUNT of equal units, exactly parallel to how a whole number is a count of ones. The pivotal move is that the count can pass the whole: iterating 1/4 past the fourth copy (4/4 = 1) gives 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — improper fractions that are perfectly ordinary numbers with a home on the number line. This unit-fraction-as-building-block view is the seed of adding fractions with like denominators (join the counts), of multiplication (a/b = a × 1/b), and of mixed numbers.
bestPractices: Teach 1/b as the unit you iterate, then build a/b by repeated addition of that unit — '1/5, 2/5, 3/5' spoken as 'one fifth, two fifths, three fifths' so the count is audible.
Use the number line as the primary model: start at 0 and make equal jumps of 1/b, landing on a/b; this makes iteration a physical count and naturally continues past 1 into improper fractions.
Deliberately cross the whole: iterate 1/4 to 4/4 = 1 and keep going to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4, so improper fractions arise as the natural continuation of counting units, not as a strange new object.

Link the count to notation: the numerator IS the number of unit-fraction copies, the denominator names the unit — so 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... (seven times), and adding like fractions just adds the counts.
Contrast unit-counting with the wrong move of adding denominators (1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8): on the line, two quarter-jumps land at 2/4, not at a smaller point, refuting it visually.
keyRepresentations: Number line with equal 1/b jumps from 0, continuing past 1 (0, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4=1, 5/4, 6/4, 7/4)
Fraction strips / identical unit tiles laid end to end (seven 1/4-tiles making 7/4)
Repeated-addition equation 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4
Bar model spanning more than one whole to show 7/4 as one whole plus three more quarters (1 3/4)
Skip-counting sequence in unit-fraction language ('one-fifth, two-fifths, three-fifths...')
commonMisconceptions: Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so an improper fraction like 7/4 'isn't a real/proper number' or must be an error.
Adding denominators when joining unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 rather than 2/4.
Whole-number bias in placing improper fractions: reading 7/4 as near 7 (or treating the 7 as the dominant number) rather than as seven quarters just past 1 3/4.
Losing the unit: writing 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 but unable to say the denominator stays 5 because each part is the same size 1/5.
Thinking the number line 'stops' at 1 for fractions, so not continuing the jumps past the whole.

learn.summary: Teach a/b as a COUNT of unit fractions 1/b: 3/5 is 'three one-fifths', 7/4 is 'seven one-quarters'. The pivotal move is letting the count pass the whole — iterating 1/4 past 4/4 = 1 to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4, landing exactly on 1 3/4 — so improper fractions appear as the ordinary continuation of counting equal units on the number line, not a strange new object. This unit-as-building-block view seeds like-denominator addition (join the counts), multiplication (a/b = a × 1/b), and mixed numbers.

activities.title: Stamp the unit-fraction jumps and cross the whole
feedback: If a learner expects to stop at 1: iterate 1/4 aloud past 4/4 — 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each is one more quarter landing on a definite point; a/b counts copies of 1/b, so the count can exceed the denominator.

If two quarter-jumps are placed at a smaller point (2/8 thinking): on the line, two equal 1/4-jumps land at 2/4, not somewhere smaller; each jump is the SAME unit, so joining counts adds numerators while the unit (denominator) stays 4.
If 7/4 is placed far right near 7: count the seven small quarter-jumps together — they reach only 1 3/4, not near 7; the denominator sets the size of each counted unit.
Reinforce: at the fourth jump the point is 4/4 = 1 whole, and counting does not have to stop there.
activities.rationale: Letting the learner iterate the unit themselves and watch both count and position update makes iteration a physical, audible act and makes the crossing of the whole visible — the point where improper fractions stop being strange. A live count/value tally and growing equation make the numerator=number-of-copies link concrete. Live manipulation is proposed as a way to let the learner build the count by their own action; a pre-built illustration (below) conveys the same decomposition but without the learner's own iteration.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
Pupils should understand a fraction a/b as a sum of unit fractions 1/b (e.g. 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5) and connect this to multiplication of a unit fraction by a whole number.
learnerActions: Work on a number line marked 0 to 2 with whole-number anchors at 1 and 2.
Add one 1/4 jump at a time starting from 0, saying each landing aloud: 'one quarter, two quarters, three quarters'.
Keep a running record that shows BOTH the count (number of copies) and the value n/4, alongside a growing equation 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 ...
On the fourth jump, notice the marker lands exactly on 1 and the tally reads 4/4; then deliberately keep going — tap again to step to 5/4, past the whole, still a definite point on the line.
Continue to the seventh jump, landing exactly on 1 3/4, with the equation showing seven 1/4's and the side note 7/4 = 1/4 × 7.

Switch the unit to 1/3 and repeat while keeping the whole-number anchors 1 and 2 fixed, counting up to six jumps (6/3 = 2) on this 0–2 line. To continue to seven jumps (7/3 = 2 1/3), extend the line past 2 first. Each jump is now larger: three third-jumps reach the same point 1 that four quarter-jumps reached.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction a/b is just a count of equal units 1/b; nothing forces the count to stop at the whole, so improper fractions like 7/4 are ordinary points on the line. The denominator names the size of the unit you are counting.

activities.title: Walk through a pre-built iteration and read the decomposition
feedback: If the learner thinks the count must stop at 1: point to the flap at 4/4 and the jumps beyond it — the sequence continues to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4.
If the learner loses the unit: have them restate that every tile and every jump is 1/4, so the denominator stays 4 the whole way.
activities.rationale: A pre-built reveal communicates the decomposition and crossing-the-whole clearly and is useful when a live iterator is unavailable; its limit is that the count is pre-baked rather than built by the learner's own action, so pair it with construction when possible.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Study a 0–2 number line showing seven quarter-jumps, revealing the running total jump by jump (1/4, 2/4, ... 7/4).
At the 4/4 mark, read the flap '= 1 whole, keep going' and continue tracing to 7/4.
Read the side card showing 7/4 = 1/4 × 7 and 7/4 = 1 3/4.
Lay out seven identical quarter-tiles end to end and match them to the seven jumps, then state in words that each part is the same size 1/4.
activities.intendedInsight: Seven copies of 1/4 decompose 7/4, the count continues naturally past 1, and 7/4 equals exactly 1 3/4 — the same unit-count read from a worked layout.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: where do seven quarter-jumps land?
feedback: Full understanding looks like: seven equal 1/4-jumps passing 4/4 = 1 without pause to land exactly on 1 3/4, 7/4 written as seven 1/4's, and 7/4 justified as a real number because it is seven copies of the unit 1/4 — a definite point — with the same reasoning transferred to 7/3 on request.
Partial understanding: iterates and writes the sum correctly but hesitates to cross the whole, or places 7/4 correctly yet cannot explain WHY in terms of counting units.

If the learner says 7/4 'isn't a real fraction' or 'isn't a number', or stops at 1: iterate aloud past 4/4 — 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each one more quarter on a definite point. (7/4 is indeed an improper fraction, but it is still a real number.)
If the learner writes 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 or growing denominators: show two 1/4-jumps landing at 2/4 and re-establish that joining equal units adds numerators while the unit stays 4.
activities.rationale: The reason behind the prediction is the diagnostic part: a learner expecting the jumps to stop at or before 1 reveals the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief. The second-tier 'how do you know it's a number' separates lucky placement from understanding. This surfaces outcomes and misconceptions rather than teaching the iteration, so it complements, not replaces, the construction activity.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Before making any jumps, PREDICT where seven jumps of 1/4 from 0 will land — before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 — and state WHY.
Iterate the seven quarter-jumps, crossing 4/4 = 1 and landing exactly on 1 3/4.
Explain any mismatch between the prediction and the result.

Answer probing questions: Why doesn't 7/4 land near 7 when there's a 7 in it? If it were 7/3 instead of 7/4, would the jumps be bigger or smaller, and would you land further from or closer to 0, and why? When you write 7/4 as seven 1/4's, why does the bottom number stay 4 and not grow? At the fourth jump you reached exactly 1 — what is that point as a fraction, and why doesn't counting have to stop there?
Write 7/4 as a sum of unit fractions and answer: is 7/4 a real number, and how do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason, not just a landing spot, reveals whether the learner holds the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief or the add-denominators error, and distinguishes a lucky correct placement from genuine understanding that 7/4 is a count of seven units.

activities.title: Spot and refute the add-denominators move
feedback: Correct: two 1/4-jumps land at 2/4 — adding denominators would wrongly shrink the result; each jump is the same 1/4.
If jumps shrink across the sum: re-establish that every term is the identical unit 1/4, so the size does not change as you add more.

In ordering 3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4: 7/4 sits between 5/4 and 9/4 and lands at exactly 1 3/4 on the line, while 9/4 lands at 2 1/4 (just past 2) — compare by the count of quarters, not the numerator against unrelated wholes.
activities.rationale: Contrasting unit-counting with the common add-denominators error and refuting it visually on the line targets a specific, documented misconception directly; the number line makes the equal-size units concrete.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 and test it on the number line by making two equal quarter-jumps from 0.
Mark where the two jumps actually land and compare it with where 2/8 would sit.
State in your own words why joining two copies of the same unit gives 2/4, not 2/8.

Answer a quick check: 5/8 = 1/8 + 1/8 + __ (fill the remaining 1/8 terms to make five eighths — three more are needed); then order 3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4 on a line long enough to reach 9/4 (use a 0–3 line, since 9/4 = 2 1/4 lies past 2).
activities.intendedInsight: Joining unit fractions keeps the unit (denominator) fixed and adds the counts (numerators); the jumps stay the same size.

constraints: Use the number line as the primary model with equal 1/b jumps from 0, extending past 1 so improper fractions arise as the natural continuation of counting; this representation is recommended by the cited guide.
Speak the count aloud ('one fifth, two fifths, three fifths') so the iteration is audible and the numerator is heard as the number of copies.
Deliberately cross the whole (4/4 = 1, then 5/4, 6/4, 7/4) rather than stopping at 1.

Keep the denominator fixed while counting copies of a unit. If the denominator changes, keep the whole-number anchors fixed and change the jump size: thirds reach1 in three jumps, quarters in four jumps.
When a task uses values beyond a whole (e.g. ordering up to 9/4 = 2 1/4), draw the line long enough to contain them rather than clipping to 0–2.
A pre-built reveal or worked illustration conveys the decomposition but does not have the learner iterate themselves; pair it with learner construction when possible.
Unit tiles and fraction strips are physical approximations of the ideal equal jumps; keep each tile the same size to represent equal units.

A quiz or fill-in check can verify the outcome (expressing a/b as a sum, placing an improper fraction), but recognition or selection alone may not elicit the learner's own construction of the sum or placement; use such checks alongside tasks where the learner builds and justifies, not as the sole learning surface.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

The original row rated in-role dialogue and 3D rendering as 'poor' fit; these were catalog fit judgements, not pedagogical laws. They are reframed as narrowly scoped observations (iterating a unit along a line is inherently 1D/planar; a narrating character adds little over learner-built iteration) rather than universal claims that such media cannot teach.

Arithmetic checked: 7/4 = 1 3/4 EXACTLY (one whole plus three quarters), so seven 1/4-jumps land ON 1 3/4, not 'just past' it; seven 1/4's sum to 7/4; two 1/4's sum to 2/4; after two 1/8 terms, three further 1/8 terms are needed to total 5/8; 9/4 = 2 1/4. The ordering feedback references the set's actual neighbours (5/4 and 9/4) and now uses a 0–3 line so 9/4 fits.
The original row's probeDeeper and correctAnswer described 7/4 as a point 'just past 1 3/4'; this is an original error (7/4 = 1 3/4 exactly) and has been corrected in all learner-facing text here.
The add-denominators distractor (1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8, or 7/4 = 7/28) is intentionally presented only as a wrong move to refute, never as a valid answer.
Recognition/selection checks are scoped as not themselves eliciting independent construction (an observable affordance limit), not as a categorical 'quiz only assesses' claim.

assess.poeTask: Before making any jumps, ask the child to PREDICT where seven jumps of 1/4 from 0 will land: before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 — and to say WHY. The stated reason is the diagnostic part: a child expecting it to stop at or before 1 reveals the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief. Then iterate the seven quarter-jumps together, crossing 4/4 = 1 and landing at 1 3/4, and have the child explain the mismatch with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You made seven jumps and landed just past 1 3/4. Why doesn't 7/4 land near 7, when there's a 7 in it?
What if the fraction had been 7/3 instead of 7/4 — would your jumps be bigger or smaller, and would you land further from or closer to 0? Why?
When you write 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... seven times, why does the bottom number stay 4 the whole way and not grow?
At the fourth jump you reached exactly 1. What is that point as a fraction, and why does the counting not have to stop there?
assess.correctAnswer: Seven equal jumps of 1/4 from 0, landing at 1 3/4; 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. Yes, 7/4 is a real number — it is seven quarters, a definite point just past 1 3/4 on the line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a fraction must be less than 1, so 7/4 'isn't a proper number' or must be a mistake — stops the jumps at 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate 1/4 aloud past 4/4 on the line: 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each is just one more quarter and lands on a definite point. Reteach that a/b counts copies of 1/b, so the count can exceed the denominator.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 isn't a proper number — the top can't be bigger than the bottom, so it must be written a different way.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to place 7/4 beyond 1, or says it should be written only as a mixed number because '7/4 isn't allowed'; answers the second tier with 'it's not a real fraction'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds denominators when summing unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8, so the sum can never build to 7/4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the line, two 1/4-jumps land at 2/4, not at a smaller 2/8 point. Re-establish that each jump is the SAME unit 1/4, so joining counts adds numerators while the denominator (the unit) stays 4.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... = 7/28, because you add the bottoms too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/4 as a sum whose terms have growing denominators, or claims 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8; the jumps get smaller instead of staying equal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias: places 7/4 near 7 (or treats the 7 as dominant) rather than as seven quarters just past 1 3/4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the quarters together onto the line so 7/4 is felt as seven small jumps reaching only 1 3/4. Contrast with 7 whole-ones. Reteach that the denominator sets the size of each counted unit.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 is close to 7 on the number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Marks 7/4 far to the right near 7, or orders it as if larger than 6/4-and-under by the numerator alone without regard to the unit.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build a/b by iterating 1/b; stops at 1, denies 7/4 is a number, or adds denominators so the sum never reaches 7/4. Reads the numerator as a whole-number magnitude.
responseLevels.full: Makes seven equal 1/4-jumps, passes 4/4 = 1 without pause to land at 1 3/4, writes 7/4 as the sum of seven 1/4's, and justifies 7/4 as a real number because it is seven copies of the unit 1/4 — a definite point on the line. Explains the denominator names the unit being counted and transfers the reasoning to a different unit (e.g. 7/3) on request.
responseLevels.partial: Iterates 1/b correctly and writes 7/4 as seven 1/4's, but hesitates at or cannot justify crossing the whole, or places 7/4 correctly yet cannot explain WHY it is a legitimate number in terms of counting units — lists the copies without the relational 'count of a unit' reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show 7/4 on a number line from 0 to 2 by making equal jumps, and write 7/4 as a sum of unit fractions. Then tell me: is 7/4 a real number, and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands iteration counts seven equal 1/4-units, passes 4/4 = 1 without stopping, and defends 7/4 as an ordinary number. A child who believes fractions must be less than 1 balks at the improper form, stops at 1, or declares 7/4 'not proper'. A child who adds denominators writes 1/4+1/4=2/8 and cannot make the sum reach 7/4. The second tier — 'how do you know it's a number' — separates a lucky correct placement from genuine understanding of the unit-count.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding fractions
topic.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, and symbolic equations involving three-digit numbers and fractions, explaining what each part represents
evidence: Write an equation with three-digit numbers to match a measurement or money word problem
Draw a bar model to represent a fraction problem and use it to solve
Explain how a number line diagram relates to the quantities in a word problem
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} works through a maths problem involving fractions or three-digit numbers, can they switch between drawing a diagram, using a number line, and writing an equation — and explain what each one shows?

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 connecting representations widens to include the NUMBER LINE and to bigger numbers and fractions: a child writes an equation with three-digit numbers to match a measurement or money problem, draws a bar model to represent and solve a fraction problem, and explains how a number-line diagram relates to the quantities in a situation (CCSS MP2). The number line is the pivotal new representation, and the IES fractions practice guide makes it central: it shows a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude — a length/position, not two separate whole numbers stacked. This is where the load-bearing misconceptions live: children place 3/4 between 3 and 4 (treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers), or count tick marks/parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity. Alongside, the operational equals-sign habit persists into multi-step money/measurement sentences. Good teaching keeps every symbol tied to its referent and uses unmarked number lines and bar models to force attention to the quantity, not the count of parts.
bestPractices: Use the number line as the central tool for fractions-as-numbers: partition 0–1 into equal parts, mark whole numbers as fractions too (e.g. 5/5), and contrast where 3 and 4 sit versus where 3/4 sits (IES Rec 2)
Use unmarked-between-endpoints number lines and 'what quantity is this?' questioning to prevent counting parts without understanding that numerator and denominator name a single number (IES caution)
Keep every number in an equation tied to its referent in the money/measurement story — units included — so translation stays meaningful (MP2)
Draw bar models to expose fraction and multi-step structure before computing (NCETM: reveals structure, precursor to algebra), then map the diagram to the equation
Translate in all directions among situation, bar/number line, and equation, explaining what each representation shows
keyRepresentations: Number line (fractions as lengths/positions; whole numbers labelled as fractions; equivalent fractions stacked above/below)
Bar/strip diagram for fractions and multi-step money/measurement problems
Part-whole and comparison bar models with an unknown
Symbolic equation with three-digit numbers and units tied to the story
commonMisconceptions: Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, reading numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers
Counts tick marks or parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity
Partitions with the wrong number of marks (four hash marks for fourths) or treats the whole line as the unit
Keeps the operational equals-sign habit in multi-step money/measurement sentences and drops units off the numbers

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds, connecting representations widens to include the NUMBER LINE, bigger (three-digit) numbers, money/measurement, and fractions. The core objective: move fluently among a real situation, a number line, a bar model, and a symbolic equation, explaining what each part represents and keeping every number tied to its referent (including units). The pivotal new representation is the number line, which shows a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude — a length/position — not two whole numbers stacked. The load-bearing misconceptions: placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 (reading numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers), and counting tick marks/parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity. The operational equals-sign habit (left-to-right compute; drop units) also persists into multi-step money/measurement sentences. Teaching keeps every symbol tied to its referent and uses partitioning on number lines plus bar models to focus on quantity rather than count of parts.

activities.title: Place a fraction on a number line as a length
feedback: Target whether the fraction is placed as ONE magnitude, not whether a point was tapped: 'What single quantity is this point?'
If placed between 3 and 4: contrast directly — 'Locate 3, then 4, then find 3/4 between 0 and 1. Which is less than one whole?'
For partitioning: 'Dividing 0–1 into fourths needs three marks between 0 and 1 — how many marks did you use and why?'
When 5/4 is placed correctly: 'Good — a fraction can be more than one whole; say why the length passes 1.'
activities.rationale: The IES fractions guide makes the number line central for showing fractions as magnitudes and names the between-3-and-4 error as a documented whole-number misapplication; comparing the point's distance from 0 makes magnitude felt. An interactive placer with live length feedback and a whole-number/fraction toggle can make the mechanism concrete, but a fixed, well-drawn number line with the same partitioning task can also teach this — the interactive tool is proposed, not required.
sourceClaims: Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Given a number line that runs 0 to 4, decide where 3/4 belongs before marking it.

If you first place it between 3 and 4, judge how far that point is from 0 — it stretches past 3, far too long for 'three quarters' (an interactive tool can light up this length, but you can equally read the distance on a fixed, accurately drawn line).
Drag or redraw 3/4 back between 0 and 1, partition that first unit into four equal parts, and mark three of those steps from 0.
State the single amount that point names in one sentence (e.g. 'three of four equal parts of one whole, which is less than 1').
Use a whole-number/fraction view to contrast where 3 and 4 sit versus where 3/4 sits.
Extend: place 5/4 and explain how a fraction can be more than 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction is a single number with a magnitude — a length/position from 0 — not a numerator and a denominator parked side by side as two whole numbers.

activities.title: Partition an unmarked line and name the quantity
feedback: 'What ONE quantity is this point?' — answers that only recount marks have missed the goal.
If the wrong number of partitions appears (e.g. four hash marks for fourths): 'How many equal parts, and how many marks between 0 and 1 does that take?'
Praise answers that name the point as a single magnitude and justify the number of marks.
activities.rationale: The IES guide cautions that area/strip manipulatives can lead to counting parts without understanding, and suggests unmarked number lines with 'what quantity is this?' questioning; it also notes partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks. This activity focuses attention onto the named quantity rather than the count.
sourceClaims: Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Start from a number line with only its endpoints (0 and 1) marked — no interior tick marks.
Cut the space from 0 to 1 into the number of equal parts needed for the fraction you want (e.g. four parts for fourths).
Say how many marks you had to add between 0 and 1 and why that many (fourths need three interior marks).
Point to the exact spot for the fraction and state what single amount that point represents — do not just count marks.
activities.intendedInsight: A point on the line names one quantity; the numerator and denominator together specify a single number, and partitioning into n equal parts needs n−1 interior marks.

activities.title: Build a bar model and equation for a money/measurement story, units attached
feedback: If the child grabs the visible numbers or computes left-to-right: 'Which quantity is the whole here? Map the bar before writing the equation.'
If units are dropped or mismatched: 'Put the unit back on each number and convert to one unit first — what does 3/4 of a metre measure in cm?' (3/4 m = 75 cm).
Check units match (metres vs centimetres) before combining — convert and name both quantities, so 245 cm and 3/4 m are expressed in the same unit, then subtract (170 cm).
Reward explanations that tie each symbol to the story and that identify whole vs part correctly.
activities.rationale: NCETM describes the bar model as revealing problem structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) and bridging concrete to abstract; MP2 requires keeping symbols tied to referents and units, which here includes converting to a common unit before combining. Falkner, Levi & Carpenter document the entrenched operational view of '=' and recommend relational routines to remedy it.
sourceClaims: The bar model reveals problem structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) and is a precursor to algebra; it bridges concrete experience and abstract symbols.
MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.

The operational view of '=' ('compute; the answer follows') is entrenched and persists with age; it interferes with writing structurally faithful equations, and is remedied by relational routines (true/false and open number sentences).
learnerActions: Read a measurement or money story, e.g. 'A ribbon is 245 cm long; 3/4 of a metre is cut off.'
Draw a bar model that shows the whole, the parts, and where the unknown sits.
Before combining any numbers, convert so every quantity is in the SAME unit — e.g. 3/4 of a metre = 75 cm — so you are not subtracting 3/4 from 245.

Write a matching equation in which each number keeps its referent and a unit, using the common unit you converted to (for this ribbon, every quantity in cm, e.g. 245 cm − 75 cm = ? cm; use £ or pence consistently when the story is about money).
Say aloud what each number in the equation points back to in the situation, then solve using the bar (245 cm − 75 cm = 170 cm).
Translate in both directions: given an equation, describe the story and draw its bar; given a story, write the equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Equations should be structurally faithful to the situation — each number carries a referent and unit, quantities must share a unit before combining, and '=' means 'the same amount as', not 'compute left to right'.

activities.title: Argue it out: where does 3/4 really live?
feedback: Never scored; push every answer to a because-clause with a reason about magnitude.
If the child guesses 'between 0 and 1' without partitioning: ask the follow-up — 'Show me the exact spot and how many equal parts.'
Accept a correction only when the child names 3/4 as a single quantity less than 1 and justifies the partition.
activities.rationale: Explaining how a number-line diagram relates to quantities is dialogic; presenting the documented misconception and asking the child to argue against it can check whether magnitude is genuinely understood rather than only recognised. MP2's emphasis on coherent, referent-tied representations supports mapping the proposed equation to the story.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.

Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner (real or in-role) who places 3/4 between 3 and 4, saying 'because it's got a 3 and a 4 in it.'
Say whether you agree, then show and explain where 3/4 really belongs and how you found its exact spot.
Finish a because-clause: 'It goes between 0 and 1 because…'.
Judge a candidate equation the partner proposes for a money problem, and map each number to the story.
Tackle a follow-up — 'Is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1?', 'Where would 5/4 go?' — to defend your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining why 3/4 is not between 3 and 4 — and why the numerator/denominator pair names one magnitude — consolidates the concept and can expose shaky reasoning that a correct-looking placement might hide.

activities.title: Linked worked example: one story, four representations
feedback: Use as a worked example, not as evidence of mastery — follow with a construct-it-yourself task.
If the child relies on the highlighting to answer, remove it and ask them to produce the links from scratch.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal matched quadruple can illustrate correspondences but does not itself let the child place a fraction, partition a line, or respond to the magnitude misconception; it is a scaffold toward the construction tasks above, not a substitute for them.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.
learnerActions: Study a matched set: a story, its bar model, its number line, and its equation side by side.
Highlight (e.g. tap) one part and see the matching parts in the other representations light up.
For each representation, say what it shows that the others make less visible (magnitude on the line; whole/part structure on the bar; the exact relation in the equation).
Then, without the linked view, reconstruct the bar, line, and equation for a new story yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: The four representations describe the same quantities; seeing the correspondences prepares the learner to construct and translate among them independently.

constraints: Reading/placing a correct point on a number line, or selecting a correct equation, is recognition; it does not by itself show the child can CONSTRUCT the translation or explain magnitude/structure. Pair any recognition warm-up (e.g. 'which point is 3/4?') with a construction-and-explanation task.

Illustrations and diagrams that are evocative rather than measured cannot be trusted for precise fraction positions; use tools or drawings where the partition is exact when the point itself is the learning target.

Unmarked number lines and 'what one quantity is this?' questioning are the intended scaffold against counting-without-understanding; if a line is pre-marked, the child may count ticks and bypass the concept.
Area/strip manipulatives remain useful but carry a known risk of children counting parts without seeing a single quantity — pair them with magnitude language and the number line.

Keep units on every number in money/measurement work and confirm units match (m vs cm), converting to a common unit BEFORE combining; the objective includes referent- and unit-faithful equations, not just a numeric answer.

The linked/tap-to-reveal worked example is a scaffold: it shows correspondences but does not require the child to place a fraction, partition a line, or confront the misconception, so it should lead into construction tasks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: 'a ribbon 245 cm long, cut off 3/4 of a metre' mixes centimetres and metres; this is a genuine unit-conversion step (3/4 m = 75 cm; 245 cm − 75 cm = 170 cm) kept deliberately as a referent/unit-tracking challenge. The conversion is now an explicit learner action and feedback item, not only a reviewer note, so a child cannot be left subtracting 3/4 from 245 directly.

The original 'the number line's refusal to lie' and 'the recompute makes fraction-as-magnitude felt' are motivational framing for a particular interactive tool; retained as an optional live-length mechanism, not asserted as the only way to teach magnitude.

Claims that fraction magnitude 'is not spatial-3D' and that a quiz 'cannot' show connecting representations were softened: recognition formats have an objective limit (they do not elicit independent construction), but no categorical medium-superiority claim is asserted.
Internal reteach-prerequisite references from the assessment field are left as source-internal data and are not surfaced as learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: 'Is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1? So which two whole numbers must it sit between? Show me why.'
'Cut the space from 0 to 1 into the right number of parts — how many marks do you need, and why that many?'
'Point to the exact spot for 3/4 and tell me what single amount that point is.'
'Where would 5/4 go — and does that show a fraction can be more than 1?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting the between-3-and-4 placement, treating 3/4 as ONE number with a magnitude less than 1, and locating it by partitioning the unit from 0 to 1 into four equal parts and counting three — explaining that numerator and denominator together name a single quantity, not two whole numbers.

errorPatterns.pattern: Numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers: places 3/4 between 3 and 4 because 'it has a 3 and a 4' — applies whole-number knowledge to a fraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a documented false belief — confront with contrasting cases (locate 3 and 4, then 3/4 between 0 and 1) and reteach placing unit and non-unit fractions on a number line as lengths from 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child agrees with the between-3-and-4 placement, or locates fractions by their digits rather than by magnitude; may say 4/3 'isn't a number'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts tick marks/parts without seeing one quantity: gets a location by counting marks (or draws the wrong number of partitions) rather than treating the numerator/denominator pair as a single magnitude.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use an UNMARKED number line and ask 'what one quantity is this point?'; teach that dividing into 1/n needs n−1 marks between whole numbers and that the point names a single number (IES).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts marks to land somewhere, or partitions into the wrong number (four hash marks for fourths), and cannot say what single quantity the point represents.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational equals sign / number-grabbing in multi-step money/measurement sentences: writes a left-to-right compute or combines the numbers present without preserving the situation's structure or units.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a bar model to fix which quantity is the whole and keep units on each number; reteach connecting the situation to the representation before symbolising.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In a money/measure story the child produces a compute-then-answer equation, drops units, or grabs the visible numbers without mapping whole vs part.

responseLevels.gap: Places 3/4 between 3 and 4 (or by counting digits/marks); treats numerator and denominator as two whole numbers.
responseLevels.full: Places 3/4 between 0 and 1 by partitioning the unit into four equal lengths and counting three, explains numerator and denominator together name a single number, keeps referents and units when matching the equation — and transfers the magnitude reasoning to a new case (e.g. locating 5/4 beyond 1) unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Knows 3/4 is less than 1 or belongs between 0 and 1, but locates it by counting marks or can't justify the partitioning — lists the steps without explaining the point as one magnitude; or handles the line but drops structure/units in the money equation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate is putting fractions on a number line that goes from 0 to 4. They put 3/4 in the space between the 3 and the 4, saying 'because it's got a 3 and a 4 in it.' Do you agree with where they put it? Talk me through where 3/4 really belongs and how you know — and show me how you'd find its exact spot.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands fractions as numbers places 3/4 between 0 and 1 and can justify it by partitioning a unit into a length; a child applying whole-number thinking reads '3' and '4' as separate whole numbers and puts it between them — the two produce visibly different placements and different reasons. The prompt is hard to answer right for the wrong reason: guessing 'between 0 and 1' without the partitioning reason doesn't survive the follow-up, and a child who truly sees magnitude cannot place it between 3 and 4.

sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP2

Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Rec 2)

sources.claim: The bar model reveals problem structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) and is a precursor to algebra; it bridges concrete experience and abstract symbols.
sources.source: NCETM, 'The Bar Model'

sources.claim: The operational view of '=' ('compute; the answer follows') is entrenched and persists with age; it interferes with writing structurally faithful equations, and is remedied by relational routines (true/false and open number sentences).
sources.source: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999), Children's Understanding of Equality, Teaching Children Mathematics 6(4)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding fractions (age 7+)
topic.description: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct place-value and fraction vocabulary, specify units in measurement answers, and use notation accurately
evidence: Consistently specify units in measurement answers (e.g. '35 cm' not '35')
Use fraction vocabulary precisely (numerator, denominator, equivalent)
Write equations with correct notation including £/p, >, <, = and fraction symbols
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} gives a maths answer involving measurements or fractions, do they include the correct units — like "3½ metres" or "2.5 kg" — and use the right symbols throughout?

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 precision consolidates into consistent conventions: always specifying units in measurement answers ('35 cm', not '35'), using fraction vocabulary precisely (numerator, denominator, equivalent), and writing equations with correct notation (£/p, >, <, =, and fraction symbols). The teaching emphasis is that a written mathematical statement must be readable by anyone without guesswork — '£3.5' is ambiguous where '£3.50' is not, and calling the top number 'the denominator' confuses a listener. Precision here is about shared, agreed conventions that carry meaning, in line with CCSS MP6's call to communicate precisely and use clear definitions.
bestPractices: Require the unit as part of every measurement answer and money to be written to two decimal places (£3.50), because a bare or truncated number can be misread (CCSS: specify units, appropriate precision)
Attach each fraction term to its role — numerator counts the parts we have (top), denominator names how many make the whole (bottom) — and use 'equivalent' only for fractions of equal value
Have children proofread statements for a reader: 'could someone misunderstand this?' — turning precision into an act of communication
Read notation aloud in words (>, <, =, ¾) so the symbol and its meaning stay linked (CCSS: state the meaning of symbols)
Model correct money and fraction notation consistently and correct drift promptly, so conventions become automatic
keyRepresentations: Measurement answers written with units (35 cm, 2 kg, 500 ml)
Money notation to two decimal places (£3.50)
Fraction written with numerator and denominator labelled
Comparison and equation notation (>, <, =)
Fraction bars / number line linking symbol to quantity
commonMisconceptions: Omits or is inconsistent with units — writes '35' for 35 cm (CCSS)
Writes money imprecisely — '£3.5' for £3.50, or mixes symbols as '£3.50p'
Swaps or avoids fraction vocabulary — calls the top number the denominator, or says 'the bottom number' rather than denominator
Uses 'equivalent' loosely for any related fractions rather than only equal-value ones

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, the objective is communicating with mathematical precision: always specifying units in measurement answers ('35 cm', not '35'), using fraction vocabulary accurately (numerator for the top that counts the parts, denominator for the bottom that names how many make the whole, 'equivalent' only for equal-value fractions), and writing notation correctly (money in pounds with £ and two decimal places, e.g. £3.50, or in pence with p, e.g. 350p, but not both symbols; >, <, =, fraction symbols). The core insight is that a written mathematical statement should be readable by anyone without guesswork: '£3.5' invites misreading where '£3.50' does not, and the equals sign must mean 'is the same as' so that false statements like 7+5=12+3 are rejected. Precision here is treated as an act of communication grounded in shared, agreed conventions.

activities.title: Maths proofreader's bench: fix the almost-right statements
feedback: For '£3.5', point out that amounts in pounds are written to two decimal places: without the trailing convention a reader could take '£3.5' to mean three pounds and five pence (£3.05) rather than three pounds fifty, so writing '£3.50' makes the amount unambiguous. (Note that in strict decimal £3.5 equals £3.50; the point is that dropping the convention invites a reader's misreading, not that £3.5 literally equals £3.05.)

If a length is written as '35', ask '35 of what? Could someone read this as 35 metres?' and have the unit added so the meaning is fixed (contrast 35 cm, 35 m and 35 mm to show how the unit changes the meaning).
When the fraction sentence is corrected, link each word to the bar: the numerator (top) counts the parts we have; the denominator (bottom) names how many make the whole.

For '7 + 5 = 12 + 3', work out each side (left is 12, right is 15); because the two sides are not the same value the statement is false, and the equals sign always means the two sides are equal in value.
activities.rationale: Showing a reader act on imprecise notation makes the cost of ambiguity concrete and turns correction into communication rather than rule-following; the equals-sign item targets a documented tendency to read '=' operationally and accept false statements. The misreading of '£3.5' is used as an illustrative communication device about convention, not as a claim that £3.5 equals £3.05 or about any specific real till.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely

The equal sign must be used consistently to mean 'is the same as'; children who read it operationally accept false statements like 7+5=12+3 — evidence that notation must carry an agreed, precise meaning
learnerActions: Work through a set of statements that are almost right and repair each one: '£3.5' (a price), '35' (a length), 'the top number is the denominator', and '7 + 5 = 12 + 3'.

Submit each statement first as it is written — the sloppy version — to a reader that acts only on what is written and may misread nonstandard notation, then submit the repaired version and compare what the reader does with each. For example, when the two-decimal-place convention is dropped, a reader could misread '£3.5' as three pounds and five pence (£3.05) and short-change the customer; writing '£3.50' removes that ambiguity.

Repair the price to '£3.50', add 'cm' to the 35, and rewrite the fraction sentence as 'the top number is the numerator', checking it against a fraction bar where the numerator counts the shaded parts.
Decide whether '7 + 5 = 12 + 3' is true, and state why the equals sign means 'is the same as' rather than 'here comes the answer'.
Proofread each finished statement by asking 'could someone misunderstand this?'
activities.intendedInsight: A written mathematical statement should be readable by anyone without guesswork; a dropped unit, a missing decimal place, or a swapped term can change the meaning a reader takes from it, so following shared conventions is an act of communication, not a nitpick.

activities.title: Dialogue with a literal reader
feedback: If the character shows a possible misreading of the money, prompt: 'You wrote £3.5 — amounts in pounds are written to two decimal places, so write £3.50, and use £ or p, not both,' which makes the amount unambiguous.

If the child says 'the bottom number' or swaps the terms, ask them to attach each word to its role against a fraction bar — numerator counts the parts (top), denominator names how many make the whole (bottom) — before continuing.
Reinforce correct statements by having the character act correctly, confirming the notation was unambiguous.
activities.rationale: A responsive in-role listener can produce the repair through back-and-forth and may surface the child's reasoning about why the convention matters; this supports the precision objective and complements, rather than replaces, written practice.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Give notation to a character (a shopkeeper or robot) who acts only on what is written and may misread nonstandard notation: writing '£3.5' lets the character show how it could be misread as three pounds five pence (£3.05), even though £3.5 strictly equals £3.50, and writing '35' with no unit leaves the character unable to tell whether cm, m or mm is meant, so it cannot act correctly.
Correct the notation in response to what the character does: fix £3.5 to £3.50, add the missing unit, and name the numerator and denominator correctly when asked for fraction words.
Explain to the character why the corrected version removes the confusion.
activities.intendedInsight: Precision repairs can come from seeing a listener try to act on exactly what was written or said; the child supplies the convention that prevents the misreading and says why it matters.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and write-it-correctly screener
feedback: Confirm correct rewrites; for a missed item, show the precise form and name the convention (units as part of the answer, pounds to two decimal places and only one of £ or p, numerator/denominator by role).
Where a child only recognises but does not rewrite, follow up with an open task that asks them to construct the corrected statement and say why it matters.
activities.rationale: Spot-the-error items efficiently screen for which conventions need work, but they target recognition and rewriting; they do not on their own elicit the child's full reasoning about why a convention carries meaning, so pair them with the bench or dialogue for that.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Work through short items that present units, money, and fraction-vocabulary slips (e.g. '35' for a length, '£3.5', '£3.50p', 'the top number is the denominator') and either flag the error or rewrite the statement correctly.
For each flagged item, write the corrected version.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and rewriting common notation slips builds fluency and shows which conventions are not yet automatic.

constraints: Precision tasks should have the child produce or repair notation (write/say the corrected statement), not merely recognise a correct label; a static labelled example or reference card can support but cannot accept the child's input to host the production/repair practice.
Recognition-only or spot-the-error items screen for slips efficiently but do not by themselves elicit the child's reasoning about why a convention matters — use open prompts for that.

Keep fraction vocabulary tied to roles: numerator counts the parts we have (top); denominator names how many make the whole (bottom); 'equivalent' applies only to fractions of equal value, not to any related fractions.
Money in pounds is written with £ and two decimal places, and money in pence is written with p and no decimal point (e.g. '£3.50' or '350p'); never use both symbols ('£3.50', not '£3.5' or '£3.50p').
A fraction bar or number line that links the symbol to the quantity helps keep the term attached to its meaning; this is a representation choice, not a required mechanism.

In strict decimal '£3.5' equals '£3.50'; the till/character device illustrates how dropping the two-decimal-place convention invites a reader's MISREADING (e.g. as £3.05), and must not be stated as £3.5 literally equalling £3.05.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Mathematically '£3.5' = '£3.50'; the original's 'till reads £3.5 as £3.05' was reframed in all learner-facing text as a possible human misreading when the convention is dropped, so the guidance does not teach a false decimal equivalence.

The legacy row rated a static labelled example and 3D as 'poor' with claims like '3D adds nothing' and that a static example 'cannot host the practice'; these are catalog-fit judgements. Retained only the genuine, narrowly scoped limit (a static display cannot accept input, so recognition does not elicit independent construction) and softened the rest.

The MP6 claim supports the precision objective the dialogue and screener activities teach but does not independently evidence that any one medium outperforms another; medium efficacy is left as proposed/may.
reteachPrerequisiteId and quiz-step/screener-feeding-the-bench vocabulary were internal routing details and were not carried into learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: You wrote 35 — 35 of what? Could I think you meant 35 metres?
Is '£3.5' the same as '£3.50'? What might someone think '£3.5' means?
In ¾, which is the numerator and which the denominator — and what does each one tell you?
Why does it matter that we all use 'denominator' to mean the same thing?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child correcting '£3.5' to '£3.50' (money to two decimal places / pounds and pence) and correcting 'the top number is the denominator' to numerator (the top counts the parts; the bottom, the denominator, names how many make the whole), and for saying why the conventions matter (£3.5 could be misread; the wrong word confuses the listener). Surfaced for discussion, not scored.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits or is inconsistent with units — writes '35' for a length that is 35 cm
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist the unit is part of the answer; contrast 35 cm with 35 m and 35 mm so the unit visibly changes the meaning. Reteach calculating with standard units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives bare numbers for measurements and is untroubled by '35 what?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes money imprecisely — '£3.5' for £3.50, or '£3.50p' mixing the symbols
errorPatterns.nextMove: Money is written to two decimal places, and £ OR p not both; show how £3.5 could be read as £3.05. Reteach in place — a convention, not a gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces £3.5 or £3.50p and does not see how a reader could misinterpret it

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps or avoids fraction vocabulary — names the top number the denominator, or says 'the bottom number' instead of denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Attach each term to its role against a fraction bar — numerator counts the parts (top), denominator names the size of the whole (bottom). Reteach fraction notation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mislabels numerator/denominator or avoids the terms altogether

responseLevels.gap: Gives bare numbers, writes money loosely (£3.5), and mislabels or avoids fraction vocabulary, without noticing a reader could misunderstand.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, specifies units and correct money notation, uses fraction vocabulary precisely, writes equations with correct symbols, and can explain why shared, exact conventions are needed to be understood.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, adds units, corrects to £3.50, and can name numerator and denominator, but does not apply the conventions consistently or spontaneously.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child wrote the price as '£3.5', and said 'in three-quarters, the top number is the denominator.' Are these written and said correctly? Fix anything that isn't quite right, and tell me why it matters.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child attending to precision spots BOTH the money-notation slip and the swapped fraction term and can say what goes wrong; a child who is loose reads straight past them. Both are almost-right on the surface, so only genuine attention to convention — not arithmetic — separates the children.

sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice — MP6 Attend to precision

sources.claim: The equal sign must be used consistently to mean 'is the same as'; children who read it operationally accept false statements like 7+5=12+3 — evidence that notation must carry an agreed, precise meaning
