topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding fractions (age 9+)
topic.description: Construct and present logical mathematical arguments involving multiple steps; critique others' reasoning about fractions, angles, or calculations and clearly explain errors or alternative methods
evidence: Prove that 3/4 > 2/3 using a common denominator argument and a visual model
Find and explain an error in a long multiplication where a partial product was misaligned
Present a chain of reasoning to show that angles in a triangle sum to 180° by tearing and arranging
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} and a classmate solve the same maths problem differently, can {{name}} compare the two approaches, explain which method is more efficient, and identify any errors in either working?

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 arguments become genuinely multi-step and start reaching toward proof: a child proves 3/4 > 2/3 not by drawing two bars and eyeballing them but by converting to a common denominator (9/12 vs 8/12) and stating why that settles it, and critiques a peer's long multiplication by finding a misaligned partial product and explaining the place-value consequence. The practice now spans three arenas at once — fractions, angles, calculation — and the SMP3 demand sharpens: an argument must be a connected logical progression, and a critique must name the flawed step AND offer why the correct method works. This is the empirical-to-deductive transition Hoyles & Küchemann document as slow and fragile: children will still offer 'I tried it and it worked' as proof, and the teaching job is to make them feel the gap between a convincing example and a watertight general reason.
bestPractices: Demand a general reason, not a confirming example: after a child checks 3/4 > 2/3 with a picture, ask 'would that convince someone who couldn't see your drawing?' and push toward the common-denominator argument
Use deliberately flawed peer work across all three arenas (a misaligned partial product, a mis-added angle, a wrong common denominator) and require 'which step and why', per SMP3's explain-the-flaw
Teach the tear-and-arrange angle demonstration as an argument, not a fact to memorise — the arrangement into a straight line IS the reasoning that the three angles sum to 180°
Introduce the counter-example as a tool: one case that breaks a claim disproves it, whereas any number of confirming cases does not prove it (the asymmetry Hoyles & Küchemann flag)
Insist on because/therefore connectives linking each step to the next so a list of true facts becomes a valid chain
keyRepresentations: Common-denominator conversion (3/4=9/12, 2/3=8/12) as the engine of a size argument
Column/grid long-multiplication layout for locating a misaligned partial product
Tear-and-rearrange triangle (three corners meeting on a straight line) as a visual proof of the 180° angle sum
A because/therefore chain frame connecting givens to conclusion
commonMisconceptions: Treating a confirming example (or a careful drawing) as a proof of the general claim
Comparing fractions by whichever has the bigger numerator or bigger denominator rather than by a common referent
Critiquing by answer-agreement — 'the total's wrong' — without locating the misaligned step or explaining the place-value error
Believing the tear-and-arrange result is a lucky fact of that one triangle rather than a general property

learn.summary: For children aged 9-10, this guidance supports the empirical-to-deductive transition in mathematical reasoning (SMP3): constructing multi-step arguments and critiquing others' reasoning across fractions, angles, and calculation. The core teaching objective is to make learners feel the gap between a convincing example (or careful drawing) and a watertight general reason, and to critique flawed work by naming the specific broken step AND explaining why the correct method works - not merely noticing the answer is wrong. Dialogue with a skeptic is proposed as a strong vehicle because the defining moves are dialogic, while constructed-argument workspaces, annotated correct-vs-flawed comparisons, and limited recognition warm-ups each have a distinct, more limited role noted below.

activities.title: Convince the skeptic without a picture
feedback: If the learner offers more examples or a neater drawing, ask: 'How many would it take before you were CERTAIN? Is there any number that would make it a proof?'
If the learner converts to twelfths, revoice their chain back: 'so 3/4 is 9/12, 2/3 is 8/12, 9 is more than 8 - and that holds whatever you drew.'
Name success as locating a reason that covers every case at once, not as getting the right verdict.

If the learner senses the drawing isn't enough but stalls, scaffold: 'you're right it's not settled - what could you turn both fractions into so they're easy to compare?' and let them complete the chain.
activities.rationale: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates at this age and the shift to deductive reasoning is slow; a skeptic who accepts only a because-chain targets the empirical-proof habit and exercises argument construction (one half of SMP3). A dialogic format may respond to the child's over-reliance on examples in real time.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.

Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the empirical→deductive transition is slow and fragile; a general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false, whereas confirming examples cannot establish a general truth.

The describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder: convincing may be confident but incomplete, whereas justifying is a correct, complete because/therefore chain; recognising that specific examples do not constitute watertight proof is a key developmental step.
learnerActions: State a claim, e.g. 3/4 > 2/3, and offer your first justification however you like (a drawing is fine to start).

When challenged ('your drawing looks close - how do I know you didn't just draw it that way? Convince me without the picture'), reach for a general reason: convert to a common denominator - 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, and 9/12 > 8/12.
State explicitly why this reason settles it for ANY representation, not just your drawing.
Respond to repeated pressing ('but ALWAYS?') and refuse to let 'I tried it and it worked' count as proof.
Try the same argument on a fresh pair, e.g. 5/8 versus 2/3, to test whether your method generalises (work out the common-denominator comparison rather than guessing).
activities.intendedInsight: A confirming example or a careful drawing can persuade, but a reason that holds independent of any picture is what actually settles a general claim.

activities.title: Find the broken step in a long multiplication
feedback: If the learner only says 'the total's wrong', redirect: 'which step caused it, and what did the misalignment do to the place value of that partial product?'
Confirm success when the learner links the misaligned column to the partial product sitting in the wrong place value.

A column/grid layout makes the misaligned partial product easier to locate; nudging a partial product in and out of column alignment can make the place-value cost felt (optional illustration, not required).
activities.rationale: Critiquing multi-step work by locating the flawed step and explaining why the correct method works is the critique half of SMP3. Using deliberately flawed work targets this directly rather than rewarding mere answer-agreement.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.
learnerActions: Examine a worked long multiplication in which one partial product has been shoved one column to the right of where it belongs (misaligned).
Identify WHICH step is wrong, not just that the final total is off.

Explain the place-value consequence: the partial product for the next higher-place digit should sit one column further LEFT than the previous partial product (or, equivalently, end in a placeholder zero). Shoved one column to the right, it lands in a place value that is too low, so it is added into the wrong columns and contributes only one tenth of its true value.
State what the correct alignment should be and why that fixes the value.
activities.intendedInsight: A valid critique names the flawed step and explains the underlying place-value error, which is deeper than noticing answer-disagreement.

activities.title: Tear and rearrange: from evidence to a reason why ALL triangles have angles summing to 180 degrees
feedback: If the learner treats the result as specific to their triangle, prompt: 'would this happen for a long thin triangle too? Try one and watch what the corners do.'

Name success as telling apart what the demonstration shows (strong evidence of about 180 degrees for the triangles tried) and a general reason that covers every triangle, not just reporting the 180 degree sum.

A draggable triangle that keeps re-forming the straight line as you deform it can make the pattern vivid (optional), but it is still a series of examples. Note the approximation: tearing and placing corners is imprecise, so a paper demonstration can only look close to a straight line. The exact 180 degree result is about the idealised mathematical triangle and is established by a general argument.
activities.rationale: Teaching the demonstration as evidence that motivates a general argument, rather than as a fact to memorise or as a proof in itself, connects a visual action to a general geometric claim. It also counters the belief that the result is coincidental for one triangle, and stays consistent with the point that confirming examples alone do not prove a general claim.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.
learnerActions: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them so their vertices meet at a point along a straight edge.
Observe that the three angles together appear to form a straight line (about 180 degrees, within the precision of the tearing).

Treat the arrangement as evidence, not yet a proof: the corners appearing to meet on a straight line suggests that the three angles sum to 180 degrees. A torn paper triangle is only one approximate example, so ask what general reason would make this happen for every triangle.

Repeat with a differently shaped triangle (or deform a draggable on-screen triangle) and see that the corners again appear to form a straight line. Note that each successful case makes the claim more convincing, but more cases on their own still do not prove it for every triangle.

State the general claim that the angles of ANY triangle sum to 180 degrees, and explain the general reason (with teacher support): draw a line through one corner parallel to the opposite side. The other two angles reappear at that corner as equal (alternate) angles, so the three angles together fill a straight line, which is 180 degrees. This reason does not depend on the triangle's shape.
activities.intendedInsight: Tearing and rearranging corners convincingly suggests that a triangle's angles sum to 180 degrees, and repeating it builds confidence. But only a general reason (such as the parallel-line argument) shows that it holds for ALL triangles; examples alone are not a proof.

activities.title: Counter-examples and the asymmetry of proof
feedback: If the learner holds 'bigger denominator wins', have them test it on 1/4 versus 1/3 (equal numerators, larger denominator) and watch it fail; if they hold 'bigger numerator wins', have them test it on 3/8 versus 1/2 (differing numerators) and watch that fail - match the test case to the rule they actually hold.
Reinforce the connectives: ask the learner to join their true statements with 'because' and 'therefore' so the argument reads as a chain, not a list.

Distinguish an incorrect comparison rule (a false belief about fraction size) from a reasoning gap; if the learner misranks fractions, revisit comparison via a common denominator or a benchmark before judging their reasoning.
activities.rationale: Introducing the counter-example as a tool teaches the logical asymmetry between refutation and confirmation, a developmental step flagged as key; insisting on because/therefore connectives turns true facts into a valid chain. The 1/4 vs 1/3 case holds the numerator fixed to break the bigger-denominator rule, while the 3/8 vs 1/2 case has both parts differing and is used to break the bigger-numerator rule (3 > 1, yet 3/8 < 4/8 = 1/2). These vary different quantities to refute different single-component rules; this is not a denominator rule 'flipping'. Fractions remain comparable as numbers throughout.
sourceClaims: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the empirical→deductive transition is slow and fragile; a general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false, whereas confirming examples cannot establish a general truth.

The describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder: convincing may be confident but incomplete, whereas justifying is a correct, complete because/therefore chain; recognising that specific examples do not constitute watertight proof is a key developmental step.
learnerActions: Consider a claim such as 'the fraction with the bigger denominator is always bigger' or 'the fraction with the bigger numerator is always bigger'.
Test the bigger-denominator claim where the numerator is held fixed: compare 1/4 and 1/3 - the denominator 4 is larger, yet 1/4 is smaller than 1/3, so that claim fails.

Test the bigger-numerator claim on a case where the numerators actually differ: compare 3/8 and 1/2 - the numerator 3 is larger than 1, yet 3/8 is smaller than 1/2 (since 1/2 = 4/8), so that claim fails too.
State each breaking case as a counter-example that disproves the rule.
Articulate the asymmetry: one counter-example disproves a general claim, but any number of confirming examples does not prove it.
Build a because/therefore chain linking the givens to the conclusion so a list of true facts becomes a connected argument.
activities.intendedInsight: One counter-example is enough to refute a general claim, whereas confirming examples alone never establish one - and each step of an argument should be linked by because/therefore.

constraints: Do not accept a correct verdict (e.g. agreeing 3/4 > 2/3) as evidence of reasoning; a child can be right for the wrong reason via a single-component comparison rule. The discriminating act is explaining WHY examples don't settle it and producing the general reason.

Fixed-answer or 'spot the misaligned step' recognition tasks can serve as a warm-up but do not elicit a constructed general justification or a flaw explained in the child's own words; a score on such a task is not evidence of the reasoning practice, and recognition formats can inadvertently reward the confirming-example habit. Recognition alone does not elicit production.

Annotated correct-vs-flawed comparisons with tap-to-reveal explanations can seed critique talk but do not themselves respond to a child's over-reliance on examples or capture a constructed chain; use them to launch discussion, not as the assessment.

A single confirming example or drawing is a starting point for talk, not a proof; always push toward a reason that holds independent of the representation. Fractions remain comparable as numbers; the common-whole caveat applies only to comparing represented portions within a drawing.
Separate two distinct causes of wrong fraction comparisons: a faulty comparison rule (reteach comparison) versus a reasoning-articulation gap (scaffold and scribe); treat them differently.

Paper-corner tear-and-arrange uses physical cutouts as an imprecise, concrete approximation of idealised angles; a draggable on-screen triangle is a model of the same relationship. Both offer repeated examples that make the pattern vivid, but neither proves the general claim by itself, and neither is universally required.

Optional interaction examples (draggable triangle re-forming the straight line, nudging partial products in/out of column alignment, linked fraction/angle/multiplication tools) are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory features. Comparative claims that one medium uniquely teaches, or that another 'cannot', are not established by the sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research, re-reviewed independently without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original row's confidence was 'high' and its sources were marked verified; this review does not re-verify them and does not upgrade or downgrade that status.

Arithmetic confirmed: 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, 9 > 8, so 3/4 > 2/3; 1/4 < 1/3; 3/8 < 1/2 (= 4/8); 5/8 = 15/24 and 2/3 = 16/24, so 5/8 < 2/3 (the 5/8 vs 2/3 pair is used only as a generalisation test, with no answer asserted in the activity).

Long-multiplication critique: a partial product belonging to a higher-place digit should be shifted one column to the LEFT; if instead shoved one column to the right it lands in a place value that is too low, so that partial product contributes too little. The source gives no concrete numeric example and describes this only as the 'wrong place value', so the net total direction is not asserted (an earlier candidate claim that the misalignment 'inflates the total' was incorrect - rightward columns are lower place values - and has been removed).

The original framed a 'doubting Thomas'/skeptic persona and claimed dialogue uniquely targets both halves of SMP3 and 'directly attacks' the empirical-proof habit; comparative necessity claims, or that other formats 'cannot' teach, are not established by the source citations and have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

Counter-example wording was tightened: 1/4 vs 1/3 holds the numerator fixed to break the bigger-denominator rule, while 3/8 vs 1/2 is a case where both numerator and denominator differ (used to break the bigger-numerator rule, since any numerator-rule counter-example must vary both parts). This is a fair test of single-component rules, not a denominator rule 'flipping'.

probeDeeper: 'How many examples would it take before you were CERTAIN? Is there any number that would make it a proof?'
'Turn both fractions into twelfths for me — now what does that let you say, for sure?'
'A classmate says 3/4 > 2/3 because 4 is bigger than 3. Is that a good reason? Test it on 1/4 and 1/3.'
'Would your common-denominator argument still work for 5/8 versus 2/3? Show me.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that confirming examples/drawings do not constitute a general proof, and offering (or reaching for) a common-denominator argument (3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, 9/12 > 8/12) as the reason that settles it independently of any picture.

errorPatterns.pattern: Empirical proof scheme: treats confirming examples or a careful drawing as proof — 'I tried it and it worked, so it's true.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the asymmetry: 'How many pizzas would you have to try to be SURE? Could there ever be one where it's different?' Then co-build the common-denominator reason and name it as the kind of argument that covers every case at once.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses the classmate ('yes, that settles it') and, asked to show it themselves, offers another example or a neater drawing rather than a general reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares fractions by a single component — bigger numerator or bigger denominator wins — so any 'reason' given rests on a faulty comparison rule.
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a false belief about fraction size, not an argument-skill gap — reteach comparison via a common denominator or a benchmark using bars. Do not accept the correct verdict as evidence of reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child justifies 3/4 > 2/3 with '4 is bigger than 3' or '3 is bigger than 2' rather than by a common referent; may get the right verdict for the wrong reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Senses that 'drawings can be misleading' matters and rejects the example-proof, but cannot yet articulate the common-denominator reason — reasoning outruns the ability to state it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT read as not-knowing. Scribe/revoice: 'you're right it's not settled — what could you turn both fractions into so they're easy to compare?' Let the child complete the chain; the discriminating instinct is already there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'no, that's not really a proof' or 'you need a proper reason' but stalls when asked to give one; may gesture toward twelfths without completing the chain.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts the examples/drawing as settling it and offers only more examples when asked to show it themselves.
responseLevels.full: Recognises confirming examples don't prove the claim AND produces a common-denominator (or benchmark) argument that settles it independent of any picture, explaining why that reason covers every case — and spontaneously applies the same 'examples aren't proof' stance to a new comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Is uneasy with the example-proof or gives the correct verdict, but justifies by a single-component rule or an unexplained drawing; can describe a comparison but not a reason that generalises.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate says: 'I checked and 3/4 is bigger than 2/3 — I drew them and the 3/4 bar looked longer, and I tried it with a pizza too, so it's definitely true.' Do you think that settles it? How would YOU show whether 3/4 is bigger than 2/3, and would your way convince someone who says drawings can be misleading?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has crossed toward deductive reasoning is uneasy with 'I drew it and tried a pizza' and reaches for a reason that holds regardless of the drawing; a child still in the empirical-proof scheme is fully satisfied by the examples and sees nothing to add. The prompt separates them because it explicitly offers the empirical justification as 'settled' — a correct reasoner pushes past it, an empirical reasoner endorses it. Reasoning right for the wrong reason is hard here: agreeing 3/4 > 2/3 is easy, but explaining WHY the examples don't settle it and producing the common-denominator reason is the discriminating act.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding fractions (age 10+)
topic.description: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, coordinate grids, algebraic expressions, tables, and symbolic equations involving fractions, ratio, and algebra, explaining connections between representations
evidence: Translate a word problem into an algebraic equation and also represent it on a bar model
Plot data from a table onto a coordinate grid and interpret the relationship
Explain how a pie chart, a fraction, and a percentage all represent the same proportion
topic.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is working on an algebra or ratio problem, can they move fluidly between a graph, a table of values, a written equation, and a real-world story — explaining how each representation shows the same relationship?

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 representation fluency reaches its primary ceiling and turns toward algebra: a child translates a word problem into an algebraic equation AND a bar model, plots table data on a coordinate grid and interprets the relationship, and explains how a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage all show the same proportion (CCSS MP2). Two threads from the verified bank become load-bearing. First, the bar model is now explicitly a precursor to algebra (NCETM): the same part-whole/scaling structure that sized a bar now sizes an equation with a letter for the unknown. Second, the equals sign becomes decisive for algebra — Falkner, Levi & Carpenter show with 4x + 27 = 87 that a child who reads '=' as 'do the calculation' cannot understand why you subtract 27 from both sides, and can only memorise rules to misapply; a RELATIONAL '=' (the two sides name the same amount) is what lets a word problem become a solvable equation. Proportion equivalence (pie chart = fraction = percentage) extends the fraction–decimal–percentage identity of the previous level to a new representation.
bestPractices: Build algebra on the bar model: represent 'a number ×4, add 27, gives 87' as a bar with an unknown part, then as 4x + 27 = 87, mapping each symbol to the bar (NCETM precursor-to-algebra)

Insist on a RELATIONAL equals sign for solving — the two sides are the same amount, so you may do the same to both — not '= means work out the left side'; this is the documented key to moving from arithmetic to algebra (Falkner/Levi/Carpenter)
Ground proportion equivalence: show a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage of the same whole and require the child to explain why they represent one proportion
For coordinate grids, name what each axis and each point's coordinates MEAN in the situation before reading a relationship (MP2 meaning-of-quantities)
Translate in all directions among situation, bar, equation, table, grid and chart, explaining connections at each step
keyRepresentations: Bar model with a labelled unknown mapped to an algebraic equation
Algebraic equation (e.g. 4x + 27 = 87) read relationally as a balance
Coordinate grid plotting ordered pairs from a table
Pie chart / fraction / percentage showing one proportion of a whole
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' in an equation as 'work out the left-hand side' (operational), so cannot justify doing the same operation to both sides
Treats a bar model and an algebraic equation as unrelated — can draw one but not see it as the other's structure
Treats a pie chart, fraction and percentage as different things rather than one proportion of the whole
Reverses coordinates or reads a point's value without connecting it to the quantity the axis represents

learn.summary: For learners aged 10-11, this guidance builds the bridge from arithmetic representation fluency to algebra. Three connected objectives: (1) translate a word problem into BOTH a bar model with a labelled unknown AND an algebraic equation (e.g. 4x + 27 = 87, where x = 15), mapping each symbol to each part of the bar; (2) read the equals sign RELATIONALLY — the two sides name the same amount, so you may do the same operation to both — rather than as 'work out the left-hand side'; (3) explain why a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage that show the same portion of the same whole all represent one proportion. A supporting objective is plotting ordered pairs from a table onto a coordinate grid and stating what each axis and point MEANS in the situation before reading the relationship. The relational equals sign is the load-bearing idea: research on children's understanding of equality (e.g. Falkner, Levi & Carpenter) reports that many learners read '=' as 'do the calculation'; that reading gives no reason for subtracting 27 from both sides, so learners who hold it may fall back on memorised rules that they can misapply.

activities.title: Build the bar, build the equation, balance it
feedback: If the learner writes the equation but cannot locate x or +27 in the bar, overlay the two and ask 'where is the x in your bar? where is the 27-block?' until each symbol maps to a part.
If the learner subtracts 27 from only one side, ask what happens to the balance — the two sides no longer name the same amount, so the equation is no longer true.
If the learner recites 'move the 27 over, change the sign' without a reason, ask them to justify it using the balance idea: both sides must stay equal.
Target feedback at relational equality and the bar-to-equation mapping, not only at reaching the number for x.
activities.rationale: The bar model is a precursor to symbolic algebra: the same part-whole/scaling structure that sizes a bar sizes an equation with a letter for the unknown. A relational understanding of '=' is a documented foundation for moving from arithmetic to algebra; without it learners tend to rely on memorised solving rules. Constructing both representations and justifying the both-sides move targets this productive core.
sourceClaims: The bar model is a precursor to symbolic algebra: it represents unknowns and exposes the structure that an equation encodes, so a situation can be shown as both a bar and an algebraic equation.

A relational understanding of '=' is a major foundation for algebra: with 4x + 27 = 87, students who see '=' only as 'do something' cannot understand why one subtracts 27 from both sides and can only memorise rules to misapply; understanding '=' as expressing that both sides are the same is what enables equation solving.
learnerActions: Take the word problem: 'I think of a number, multiply by 4, add 27, and get 87.'
Draw a bar model: four equal unknown parts plus a 27-block, all equal in length to an 87-bar.
Write the matching equation 4x + 27 = 87 beneath, and point to where the x, the +27 and the 87 each appear in the bar.

Treat the equation as a balance with two equal sides. Try removing 27 from only one side and say what would go wrong; then remove 27 from BOTH sides (leaving 4x = 60) and explain why the two sides stay equal.
State in your own words why '=' lets you do the same thing to both sides, and finish solving (4x = 60, so x = 15).

If a dynamic model is available, size an unknown bar and watch the equation assemble; in a balance-beam mode, removing weight (such as the 27) from only one pan tips the beam, so removing it from both becomes a felt necessity, and the 27 vanishing on both sides at once mirrors the equation step.
activities.intendedInsight: A bar model and an algebraic equation are the same structure in two forms; the equals sign is a promise that both sides are the same amount, which is exactly why you may apply the same operation to both sides.

activities.title: Argue a classmate out of the operational equals sign
feedback: If the learner merely repeats the rule, prompt: 'Your partner still thinks = means compute the left side — what reason convinces them you can operate on both sides?'
If the learner says the three proportion forms are different, have them show all three on the same whole and name the shared amount.
Reward reasoning that names 'both sides are the same amount' and 'one proportion of the same whole', not just the final verdict.
activities.rationale: Justifying why you may subtract 27 from both sides, and why a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage of the same whole are one proportion, is well suited to dialogue; voicing the operational-equals error and having the learner refute it can surface the relational meaning. This is offered as one effective option, not the only route to the insight.
sourceClaims: A relational understanding of '=' is a major foundation for algebra: with 4x + 27 = 87, students who see '=' only as 'do something' cannot understand why one subtracts 27 from both sides and can only memorise rules to misapply; understanding '=' as expressing that both sides are the same is what enables equation solving.
Fractions, decimals and percentages of the same whole represent one quantity in different forms; equivalence should be understood as sameness of magnitude/proportion.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner (real or role-played) who claims: '= just means work out 4x + 27, and the answer is 87.'
Explain why that reading breaks down when you need to solve for x, using the balance idea that both sides name the same amount.

Respond to the same partner, who points to a pie slice that is 40% of the whole and claims '40% is a different thing from that pie slice' — argue why the slice, the fraction 2/5 (40/100) and 40% of the same whole are one proportion.
Keep the exchange as justification, not a scored answer: push every assertion to a reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Relational equality and proportion equivalence become more convincing when you have to defend them against a plausible wrong view, not just assert them.

activities.title: One proportion, three pictures
feedback: If the learner converts by rule but calls the forms 'different', ask them to point to the same whole in each and name the single proportion.
If the learner reverses or mislabels a percentage, return to the shaded whole and count the proportion directly before converting.
activities.rationale: Proportion equivalence extends the fraction–decimal–percentage identity to the pie-chart representation; when comparing represented portions, equivalence is sameness of magnitude for the same whole, which requires explaining the shared whole, not just converting by rule.
sourceClaims: Fractions, decimals and percentages of the same whole represent one quantity in different forms; equivalence should be understood as sameness of magnitude/proportion.
learnerActions: Look at a pie chart with one quarter shaded.
State the fraction (1/4) and the percentage (25%) it represents.
Explain whether these are the same amount or three different things, pointing to the same whole in each form.
Repeat with another proportion of your choice, converting among pie chart, fraction and percentage and justifying the shared magnitude.
If a linked display is available, change one form (e.g. drag the pie slice) and watch the fraction and percentage update together.
activities.intendedInsight: A pie chart, a fraction and a percentage are different representations of one proportion of the same whole, not three separate quantities.

activities.title: Plot the table and say what the points mean
feedback: If the learner reverses coordinates, re-read the axes' meanings and re-place the point so it matches the situation.
If the learner reads a value without connecting it to the quantity, ask 'what does that number stand for here?' before describing the relationship.
activities.rationale: Attending to the meaning of quantities across representations (decontextualising into symbols and recontextualising by probing referents) is the reasoning target; naming axis and point meaning before reading a relationship enacts it.
sourceClaims: MP2: decontextualize a situation into symbols and contextualize by probing referents; attend to the meaning of quantities across representations.
learnerActions: Take a small table of paired values and plot each pair as an ordered point on a coordinate grid.
Before reading any relationship, name what the horizontal axis means and what the vertical axis means in the situation.
For one point, say what its two coordinates MEAN (e.g. 'at 3 hours the cost is £12'), not just the numbers.
Describe the relationship you see between the quantities, in words tied to the situation.
Check for reversed coordinates by asking whether the point lands where that situation should put it.
activities.intendedInsight: A coordinate point carries situational meaning: naming what each axis and coordinate represents is what turns plotted dots into an interpretable relationship.

constraints: The equation should be CONSTRUCTED and the both-sides step JUSTIFIED by the learner; recognition-only tasks (e.g. 'which equation matches the bar?') can check a match but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the translation or the relational explanation, so use them only as a warm-up.

A static, tap-to-reveal set linking story, bar, equation and chart can illustrate the connections but cannot let the learner operate on a balance or plot points; treat it as a worked-example scaffold, not the productive activity.

When describing the balance, the required move is to keep the two sides equal (do the same to both); do not let a learner finish having only chanted 'move it over, change the sign' without the balance reason.
For the coordinate work, require the situational meaning of axes and coordinates before any relationship is read, to prevent number-reading without interpretation.

Dynamic recolouring, balance-beam tipping, draggable bars and linked updating displays are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not mandatory, and the reasoning can also be done on paper.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Arithmetic self-check: 4 × 15 = 60 (partial products 40 + 20), and 60 + 27 = 87, so x = 15 is consistent; the '60' here is the correct value of 4x, not an error. The equation 4x + 27 = 87 is internally sound.

On source scope: the Falkner/Levi/Carpenter claim is attached to the dialogue activity because it supports the relational-equality CONTENT being argued, not because the source endorses dialogue as a medium; efficacy of the dialogic route is stated as proposed/one option, not established.

The source materials lean toward strong single-format and necessity claims (e.g. that an operational equals sign 'cannot' justify both-sides operations, that scored items reward rule-following, that a dynamic linker is uniquely suited). The 'cannot justify' finding is a documented misconception pattern from Falkner/Levi/Carpenter and is stated here as such; the comparative/necessity and medium-superiority framings are not established as universal laws by the cited sources and are retained only as narrowly scoped design observations with stated affordances and limits.
The partner/dialogue activity and the static-linked-set scaffold are preserved as genuine alternatives with distinct purposes, not as inferior copies of one preferred format.

probeDeeper: 'If the equals sign just meant "work out the left side", how would you explain what to do with 4x + 27 = 87? Does that story break down?'
'Point to the x in your bar model. Where is the +27? Where is the 87?'
'Why is it fair to subtract 27 from BOTH sides — what would go wrong if you only did it to one?'
'A pie chart shows one quarter shaded. What fraction and percentage is that — and are they the same amount or three different ones?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting the operational reading and treating '=' relationally (the two sides are the same amount), mapping the word problem to both a bar with an unknown part and 4x + 27 = 87, and justifying 'subtract 27 from both sides' by the balance idea (keeping the two sides equal) rather than by a memorised rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational equals sign blocking algebra: reads '=' as 'compute the left side; the answer follows', so cannot justify operating on both sides — can only memorise rules for solving equations (the documented arithmetic→algebra stumbling block).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild '=' as balance with true/false and open sentences and a balance-beam model until 'same amount both sides' is felt; then re-derive 'subtract from both sides' from it. Reteach in place — relational equality is the new work here.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses 'work out 4x + 27', or 'solves' by a chanted rule ('take 27 over, change the sign') with no reason; can't say why both sides get the same treatment.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bar model and algebraic equation treated as unrelated: can draw the bar or write the equation but not see them as the same structure, so the translation is mechanical.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the bar and the equation, mapping each part to each symbol ('where is the x in your bar?'); reteach representation fluency connecting bar/equation across situations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces one representation but can't map the unknown part of the bar to the x, or the 27-block to the +27; treats them as two separate tasks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Proportion equivalence not seen: treats a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage of the same whole as different quantities.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show all three on the same whole and require the child to justify the shared proportion; reteach fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence as one magnitude.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the pie slice, the fraction and the percentage are 'different', or can convert by rule but not explain they are one proportion of the whole.

responseLevels.gap: Endorses 'work out the left side', or solves by a rule with no reason; can't connect the bar to the equation or justify operating on both sides.
responseLevels.full: Rejects the operational reading, maps the word problem to both a bar (unknown part) and 4x + 27 = 87, justifies subtracting 27 from both sides by keeping the two equal sides balanced, and explains pie chart/fraction/percentage as one proportion — transferring the relational-equality reasoning to a new equation unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Produces the bar and the equation, or rejects the operational reading, but can't fully justify 'both sides' by the balance idea — lists the solving steps without the relational reason; or maps bar↔equation but wavers on proportion equivalence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate is solving 4x + 27 = 87. They say: 'The equals sign means work out 4x + 27, and the answer is 87.' First: do you agree that's what the equals sign is telling us here? Then take this problem — 'I think of a number, multiply it by 4, add 27, and get 87' — show it as a bar model AND as an equation, and explain why you're allowed to subtract 27 from both sides.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a relational equals sign explains that both sides name the same quantity, so any operation must be done to both to keep them equal; a child with an operational view thinks '=' announces the answer and can only recite 'move the 27 over' without saying why. The prompt is hard to fake: the bar model plus the both-sides justification requires the relational meaning, and a child who truly holds it cannot endorse 'work out the left side'.

sources.claim: MP2: decontextualize a situation into symbols and contextualize by probing referents; attend to the meaning of quantities across representations.
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP2

sources.claim: The bar model is a precursor to symbolic algebra: it represents unknowns and exposes the structure that an equation encodes, so a situation can be shown as both a bar and an algebraic equation.
sources.source: NCETM, 'The Bar Model'

sources.claim: A relational understanding of '=' is a major foundation for algebra: with 4x + 27 = 87, students who see '=' only as 'do something' cannot understand why one subtracts 27 from both sides and can only memorise rules to misapply; understanding '=' as expressing that both sides are the same is what enables equation solving.
sources.source: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999), Children's Understanding of Equality: A Foundation for Algebra, Teaching Children Mathematics 6(4)

sources.claim: Fractions, decimals and percentages of the same whole represent one quantity in different forms; equivalence should be understood as sameness of magnitude/proportion.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Rec 2)
